goal: Teach one concrete operator lesson with specific examples and conviction.
expected_facts: Early-stage startups can sell to CIOs if the value is differentiated and the risk to the buyer is contained.

answer:
So I had this interesting conversation recently with a very senior IT leader at one of SaaStr Fund’s portfolio companies that sells into enterprises, especially larger ones (think $100m+ ACV).  They are doing well now, but when they started off, they didn’t really understand how to sell up.  To the CIO level, the VP level, the business process owners.
A few years back, we did a deep dive on “how to sell to CIOs” with the CIO of Workday,
a great session you can watch here:
But my experience is most founders aren’t sure how to do it.   They want their product to be used by everyone across an enterprise, ideally starting with the CEO and going all the way down through sales reps and engineers.  But most CEOs don’t know enough to buy software themselves, no matter how cool it is.  And most CIOs will want nothing to do with anyone who hasn’t worked in tech for decades, unless they’ve been truly vetted as part of their own network.  That leaves VPs of Sales and Engineering … often the #2 and #3 folks in any org.  Not exactly what many start-ups want to try to sell to.
The thing is, if you can get past them — they’ll almost always buy more than just your core app.  More features, more seats, more modules, etc.  So there is real revenue there, even with just an 8-person team.  It’s hard to close big deals without a brand behind you.  Or so it seems.
Here was our experience at Adobe Sign / EchoSign:
We closed some pretty big deals early on ourselves, but once we got past a few $500k-$1m deals, we needed a partner with us.  We added a local reseller, and then later, a channel manager, and then eventually, a global channel director.  Later still, we hired a Global Channel Head from Salesforce to build out a full channel strategy.

answer:
I've been doing this for a while now. And I have a pet peeve that I want to share with you today, because there's just so much bad information out here on how start-ups sell to enterprises, especially big companies and to CIOs. Everyone wants to go into Salesforce and Workday and Oracle and all these big places. And people will give you advice like "Oh yeah, you gotta get on airplanes. You gotta build a team." But no one ever tells you what actually happens once you're inside those doors. So let me tell you my story, because we started off as eight person company selling to CIOs. And if you know anything about SaaS and enterprise sales, you'll hear something different than what most people are telling you. My first real job was at Adobe Sign / EchoSign back when it was a six-person company. It didn't take us long to figure out we had to sell to CIOs. Our product was great. We had 50,000 customers using our free version. But they wanted to buy more from us. They needed security, compliance, audit trails, all this stuff. But we couldn't even ship any of that ourselves yet. So we decided to sell directly to CIOs. This was crazy. Most people say you can't sell to CIOs unless you're already huge. Well, maybe you can't sell to their budget owners per se. But you can definitely sell to their point guys. Their help desk, their business systems analysts, whoever's responsible for deploying new software within your organization. What we found out early on is that this social contract exists between vendors and IT folks. Here's how it works:
First, you show up. That means you respond to emails fast. You answer calls quickly.

answer:
So we’ve done so many SaaStr deep dives on Monday before, I didn’t think there was much more to learn.  But boy, I was wrong!  A lot has changed since our last deep dive:
Monday IPO’d
and is now worth $15B (!)
has gone multi-product
and added Marketing and IT as its third core vertical (in addition to Sales & Service) — although we’re still seeing the earliest signs here
has become very enterprise
, with almost half their customers paying $50k+ annually
is going global fast,
with over 100 countries using its product
And that’s just for starters!!   The latest data:
$500M ARR, Growing 93%
110% NRR overall, And 125% From Its Largest Accounts
126% Revenue Growth Year Ago When It Was At $240,000,000 in ARR
A Stunning 86% Growth Rate in New Customers This Year
What We Can All Learn:

#1. 120% NRR from 10-Seat Deals = Plenty Of Room For Expansion
.  As you can see below, Monday gets even better NRR once your deal goes into double digits.  So if you haven’t really gone all-in on adding more products after $10k deals close … well, maybe start ASAP.
#2.  85% NRR from Smaller Customers Still Drives Them To $250m ARR and Beyond
.  Even small accounts grow quickly.  You don’t need perfect NRR at first.  Just enough to scale quickly.
#3.  40% of Customers Use More Than One Product, Up From 28% a Year Ago.  Push Harder Here
.  Another example of how important multiple products often are.  Especially when they aren’t truly natural extensions like Slack + HypeChat.
#4.  60% of Customers Are Outside North America, and That’s Where They Are Really Accelerating
.  This is a reminder to go where your competition isn’t strong.

retrieval_hits.text:
We
last looked in on Monday.com at $240m ARR
, but it’s grown so incredibly quickly, and so effectively, it’s worth checking in again at $400,000,000 in ARR.
Because at $400,000,000 in ARR …  Monday is growing a stunning 91% (!) year-over-year.  Goodness gracious!
5 Interesting Learnings:

#1.  Revenue up 91%, Customer Count Up “Just” 34%.  The math of going upmarket
.  I personally get a little worried when this ratio falls below 2:1, if only because sometimes upsell can mask lower growth in new accounts.  The real story with Monday is going upmarket.  $50k+ customers are up 200%, to 793 from 264 a year ago.  That’s a key driver to Monday’s hyper-growth as it approaches $500,000,000 in ARR.
#2.  10+ Users the Sweet Spot now
.  As part of going upmarket, Monday’s 10+ seat customers are now 72% of total revenue, up from 63% just a year ago.  Asana has seen similar dynamics, but Monday seems to be going upmarket even faster than Asana.

#7.  Monday.com is growing 68% (!) at $550m in ARR.  No SMB deceleration here!
Not much, at least.  Monday’s growth has slowed a little bit, but in absolute terms, the growth is just incredible even now.

.

So Monday.com has
filed to IPO
with some pretty incredible numbers, especially considering just how competitive the space is.
At $240m in ARR, they are growing a stunning 85% year-over-year!  And that’s with direct and indirect competition from Asana, Atlassian, Clickup, Wrike, Smartsheet, Notion and so many others.
Pretty incredible for a product that just launched in 2014.
Whoa.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  121% NRR from 10+ seat customers, 107% overall, ~85% from smallest customers.
This is a super-helpful breakdown for anyone selling to customers both smaller and larger.  65% of its revenue comes from 10+ seat deals and they have 121% NRR.  The remaining 35% is from smaller deals.  For those to average to 107%, NRR is likely around 85% for self-service and < 10 seat deals (about the same as
Squarespace
).
So those seem like good yardsticks to shoot for if you sell to SMBs of all shapes and sizes and are somewhat like Monday.  The tiniest of customers may have only 85% NRR.  But once you cross 10 seats, you should start to see the benefits of account growth and 120% NRR like Monday.

answer:
So we've talked on SaaStr a lot over the years about Monday.com. I think when they first IPO'd, many folks thought they were just a project management tool. But boy, what's happened since then. It was a great example of going multi-product early, which we do love to talk about, how that can really help you scale faster and longer than being single product. They now have four core products all powering their 100 million ARR run rate.
But one thing I wanted to dig into here today because it's something I want founders listening to think carefully about is this question of how do you balance your existing base versus investing in new markets? Because Monday's been doing well for years. And so, if you're seeing big disruption coming from AI agents, maybe even if your business is doing well, you might need to invest more there. Let me break down five interesting learnings from Monday.com. Number one, they are still growing a stunning 85% at 250 million dollars in ARR.
That's incredible, especially given where we are right now in software. Now, as part of that, they are benefiting from price increases, which is common in vertical SaaS. So, while 80% of their growth comes from net new customers, 20% comes from pricing increases. So, that's important to keep in mind as we look at some of these ratios later on. This is fairly common in vertical SaaS where you're charging more per seat, often as you go upmarket.

last looked in on Monday.com at $240m ARR
, but it’s grown so incredibly quickly, and so effectively, it’s worth checking in again at $400,000,000 in ARR.

#1.  Revenue up 91%, Customer Count Up “Just” 34%.  The math of going upmarket
.  I personally get a little worried when this ratio falls below 2:1, if only because sometimes upsell can mask lower growth in new accounts.  The real story with Monday is going upmarket.  $50k+ customers are up 200%, to 793 from 264 a year ago.  That’s a key driver to Monday’s hyper-growth as it approaches $500,000,000 in ARR.
#2.  10+ Users the Sweet Spot now
.  As part of going upmarket, Monday’s 10+ seat customers are now 72% of total revenue, up from 63% just a year ago.  Asana has seen similar dynamics, but Monday seems to be going upmarket even faster than Asana.

#7.  Monday.com is growing 68% (!) at $550m in ARR.  No SMB deceleration here!
Not much, at least.  Monday’s growth has slowed a little bit, but in absolute terms, the growth is just incredible even now.

.

filed to IPO
with some pretty incredible numbers, especially considering just how competitive the space is.

Squarespace
).

answer:
I’ve been doing this for quite some time now.  And I’m convinced there’s one thing that truly helps candidates stand out … besides being super smart:
It shows they have done their homework on the company before the interview
And in particular,
they show up with at least one very good question for each interviewer
that isn’t just generic.
A bit more here:
So what makes a candidate really stand out? In any role?
Having done the research ahead of time and bringing 2-10+ thoughtful, insightful questions for
each
interviewer?
Yes, those questions can be simple. But they also should be thoughtful and insightful. It shows respect for the position, and the job itself. You know, when most folks hear “thoughtful” — they think “easy.” They think someone who asks thoughtful questions has asked easy ones. That doesn’t matter as much as having thought about your answers.
How do we build a high-performing team? How do we increase revenue per lead? What does success look like in this role? The best candidates ask questions that demonstrate their ability to learn, grow, and contribute to the organization immediately. Ask open-ended questions that encourage sharing information rather than yes/no responses. If you’re interviewing for an entry-level position, ask how the company approaches training new hires and professional development. For management roles, inquire about strategic initiatives and expectations for performance.

–

–
**Pro Tip**

answer:
So we've talked over the years on SaaStr how to do well at job interviews. What's different today? Well, first, I think there's so much competition for jobs these days that if you're going into any interview without preparation, knowing your stuff cold, having done your research ahead of time, you're probably wasting your time. That's always been true, but it's even truer now. Second, it seems like most folks just aren't as hungry anymore. They're sort of doing the bare minimum. So if you can find some way to show up with high energy and a real desire to truly make a difference where you work, I bet that will carry the day. And finally, we all know that AI has changed everything. We've talked before on this channel about whether we should be excited about AI changing our roles, or worried because they could take them away. The reality is, it does both. But one thing is clear. If you haven't figured out what you're going to do with AI in your role, get on it fast. Because everyone else is. You'll fall behind quickly. Now let me give you two questions you ask during an interview that will immediately stand out as thoughtful and interesting:

What did you learn from someone who failed in their last role?
And then secondly,
what was something you were proud of that didn't go exactly according to plan?

These two answers almost always stand out as good ones. They show you've thought deeply about things and have learned lessons. When I interviewed hundreds of SDRs and AEs, I never heard anyone say, "Hey, I worked really hard, closed lots of deals." No one says that. It doesn't matter. Everyone thinks they close lots of deals. So instead, they'd tell me stories about how they helped a CEO build his brand by writing blog posts, or how they got creative and built a community. Those are the types of answers that stood out.

Dear SaaStr: How Do I Build a Great SDR Team?
Building a great SDR team is one of the most critical steps in scaling a SaaS company, especially when you’re selling to the C-suite or enterprise. SDRs are the engine of your pipeline, and if you get this right, it can transform your sales organization.
Here’s how to do it:

1. Hire for “Fire in the Belly”
–
**What to Look For**
: SDRs don’t need prior experience in sales, but they need grit, hunger, and a relentless drive to succeed. Look for candidates who are coachable, curious, and have a strong work ethic. These traits are far more important than a polished resume.
–
**Pro Tip**
: Many great SDRs come from unconventional backgrounds—teachers, military veterans, or recent grads. They’re often looking for a career change and bring fresh perspectives.

[train_3205]
7. Create a Career Path
– **Why?**: SDRs are often entry-level hires, and they’ll want to see a path forward. Without it, you’ll lose them to other companies.
– **What It Looks Like**:
SDR → Senior SDR → AE or other roles (e.g., Customer Success, Marketing)
Promote internally whenever possible. It’s less risky, and they already know your product and processes.
–
**Pro Tip**
: Highlight success stories of SDRs who’ve moved up in the company to inspire your team .

So this one I think we've talked to before on SaaStr. It's Mark Roberge, co-founder managing director stage two capital. And I'm really excited he's here because mark is an incredible researcher. He was CRO at HubSpot for many years, built out their sales team with very high efficiency. So that's what we're gonna do today. We'll dig into what makes scaling up sales teams work, how you can scale more efficiently than most folks seem to be able to do so far. Mark
00:01:30
Okay. Thanks jay. So my goal today is just to share some research insights as well as practical experience around building high velocity revenue organizations. And I believe there are three core elements that I'd like to focus on. The first is understanding the demand side of your business. What does the market look like? How big is it? Who should you target based upon who will buy now versus later? The second piece is hiring the right people for each segment of the funnel. And the third piece is ensuring alignment across all parts of the organization. These are things that have evolved over time. When I started off doing research back in the day, these were kind of the foundational principles. But as the company scales, they become even more important. Now let me start by talking a little bit about demand generation. In particular, we did a lot of research recently looking at different types of customers.

answer:
In a stunning deal announced on July 29, 2025,
Salesforce will acquire Informatica for approximately $8 billion
—a move that completes an extraordinary journey spanning over three decades for one of enterprise software’s most resilient companies. This isn’t just another acquisition; it’s the culmination of a remarkable odyssey that took Informatica through two IPOs, multiple near-death experiences, and a transformation so dramatic it would make even the most seasoned SaaS veterans take notice. The Story That Defines Resilience
Founded in 1988 by Gaurav Dhillon and Diaz Nesamoney as a small startup in Menlo Park, California, Informatica began life focused on data integration solutions. What started as a “data warehousing” company quickly evolved into something much bigger—becoming the world’s largest independent pure-play enterprise software company. But this wasn’t your typical Silicon Valley success story. Informatica faced challenges that would break lesser companies cold:
The Dot-Com Crash (1999)
Informatica went public during the peak dot-com era in May 1999. When the bubble burst, shares plummeted. The company found itself struggling financially, eventually being forced to lay off nearly half of its workforce. Yet rather than folding, they used their $500 million war chest to survive—and transform. The Private Equity Rescue (2009)
After years of fighting, Informatica found new life under private equity ownership in 2009 when Permira led a consortium buying out the firm for roughly $5.3 billion. Under new leadership, including former IBM executive Anant Jha and CFO Michael Bleier, they set about rebuilding what had been destroyed.

1. Salesforce: +9,296% (Marc Benioff – Founder)
IPO Date:

The numbers are so staggering they require a double-take. After accounting for Salesforce’s 4-for-1 stock split in 2013, Marc Benioff’s cloud computing revolution delivered returns that approach 100x.
Benioff didn’t just create a company—he created an entire industry. When Salesforce went public in 2004, cloud software was still a radical concept. His vision of “No Software” seemed almost absurd to enterprise buyers accustomed to on-premise installations.
What Made It Legendary:
Category Creation:
Literally invented cloud software for enterprises
Platform Vision:
Built the AppExchange ecosystem that became a $4B+ marketplace
Relentless Innovation:
Never stopped evolving from CRM to AI to complete customer platform
20-Year Execution:
Sustained hypergrowth for two decades as a public company
$10,000 invested at IPO would be worth $939,636 today.

So Salesforce has now grown into the active granddad of SaaS.  Maybe not growing quite as fast as it once did.  But it’s matured into a true force of nature.  Only Microsoft, Oracle and now Salesforce have crossed $40 Billion in enterprise software ARR:
$40 Billion in ARR
Growing 9%
33% Non-GAAP Operating Margins (19% GAAP)
Generating $13B of free cash flow a year!!
Perhaps most importantly, Salesforce has leaned deeply into AI … and while the early usage is impressive, so far it hasn’t materially changed growth.  So far:
Since October, closed 5,000 Agentforce deals, including more than 3,000 paid just 90 days after officially launching
Salesforce says
Agentforce has managed 380,000 conversations
, with only 2% escalated to humans and an 84% resolution rate
So far, at the public company level, it’s the infra players that are seeing the crazy AI growth.  Nvidia, Google Cloud, Azure, etc.  But how about 2026+?  We’ll see.  As Marc Benioff notes below, Salesforce’s just started.  It’s only been selling AgentForce for a few months.  He’s incredibly excited and bullish on where it’s going.  It’s rejuvenated him.  Maybe AI will for all of us.

answer:
So what do you know about Informatica?  I'm sure some folks have heard of it -- they've been around since '92! But beyond that, probably less than half this audience has any real familiarity.
But maybe if we dig into one case study, we'll all learn something. What can we learn from Informatica?
It's just so wild. So let me tell you just a few things about it. It started off as data integration software back in 1992. And it did pretty well for years, then went private in 2006. Came public again in 2021, did reasonably well, hit an all-time high in late 2021, then fell like everything else on AI worries. And now today, after more than 30 years, it's being acquired by Salesforce for almost $8 billion.
Wow. Just wow.
Let me take a step back. Salesforce's journey to where it is today, it was a bit different. They were founded way back in 1999 as an email service, became a CRM product, came public in 2004, and today they're a multibillion-dollar company growing at 20%. How much would your money be worth if you'd invested in Salesforce when it first went public? If you bought shares in that IPO back in 2004, you might feel pretty good about yourself right now because their stock price has gone up over 9,000 percent. At least on paper. That's the power of compounding.
From there, let's look at another great example: Datadog. Now you might say, "Wait a minute, isn't Datadog a cybersecurity company?" Well, yes, they are. But they also serve a related space called observability, which helps developers troubleshoot problems in their applications faster. And here's the interesting thing – they were able to combine these two markets to achieve impressive results. Their stock is trading near a record high. This week alone, Datadog rallied nearly 19%, marking its largest percentage gain in seven months.
Then there's ServiceTitan. Now this is really cool. It's a software platform designed specifically for home service contractors. Think electricians, plumbers, HVAC repair people, pest control professionals. The founders realized these businesses often struggle to keep track of scheduling, inventory management, payments, and customer communications, so they built a comprehensive toolset to address those pain points. And here's the kicker – it doesn't require a lot of technical expertise to use.

!

answer:
Hi everyone. I think we can all agree that content marketing works well for us,
as long as you do it right. And one thing I've learned over the years is there are many different types of content marketing. There's your blog. There's podcasting. We're going to be doing more podcasting at SaaStr this year than ever before because so many folks like it. There are webinars. You know some people love them. Some people hate them. But they work really well if you market them properly. And then there are videos on YouTube. Now, it turns out, when I first started my career as an investor and VP marketing, maybe eight or nine years ago now, I didn't even use social media much at all. Didn't tweet too often. Didn't put up any slides online until recently. So, I was pretty surprised how powerful video would become. If you go back just a few years, our top video had barely hit 100,000 views. It wasn't even close. Today, by contrast, our top video has almost 300,000 views. That's pretty cool. What does that mean? Why should you care? First off, with each view, we get paid a small amount of money. So, these views are monetized. More importantly though, it helps spread the word. This content gets shared again and again. It gets embedded into LinkedIn posts and tweets and everything else. So, if you create great content, don't worry if you don't have millions of followers yet. Don't worry if you don't have lots of subscribers. As long as you create great stuff, eventually those things will compound. Alright, let me take a look at what's been working best. Okay, so number ten here, which we'll get to in a minute, has 30,000 views. Number nine has 34,000 views.

answer:
So I’ve been doing this for a while now.  I started off helping sell Adobe Sign / EchoSign to our very first enterprise customers back in 2010-2011 (more on how those early days were here):
Then, when I got to my next startup, I was CRO at a time when every B2B company seemed to have just 1 or 2 reps.  So I didn’t really see any change there, per se.  But then I joined another startup later as CEO, and saw everything change:
The number of vendors went from 20 or so to hundreds
The sheer amount of data and tools grew dramatically.  As did the complexity of selling them
The number of people you needed to close deals grew from 2–3 folks on the buyer side to 100s
And by 2023, most B2B companies had an entire army of people managing your account.  From FDEs to Product Managers, from Solution Engineers to Technical Account Executives — everyone wanted a piece of you
All this stuff happened between 2010 and today.  And yet … it wasn’t really that much change.
But now?  Everything is changing again.  Not because of price increases, or even macro impacts.  No, something far bigger than that.
It’s because the products themselves are getting smarter.  That’s why everything is changing again in SaaS sales.  At least, if you want to stay ahead.
Why?
Because of the explosion of AI features across business applications.  More than ever before, they can do the work.  So why should you need an army of human professionals to manage your account?  Or help deploy it?  Or answer your questions?
This is why Salesforce Agentforce, Slack, HubSpot, ZoomInfo, and others are investing so heavily in agentic workflows.  Because their apps aren’t just going to get better.

So it does seem like some of the biggest changes to the human side of SaaS are now coming. I’ve talked with three CEOs at leading vendors in sales and post-sales at $200m+ in ARR the past few weeks and they’ve all reinforced these are some of the biggest changes in a generation. What we’ve seen in the first 15 years of SaaS:
Specialization in sales
. Segment reps, and have closers close. The rise of the SDR and productizing outbound and qualifying inbound with humans
. Outbound is nothing new, but the formal role of the SDR exploded in the past decade. The rise of customer success as a new, empowered function. Everyone has fully staffed CS over the past decade. We’ve all become NRR, GRR, and CSAT experts, and CS owned it all. Human support remained important, at least for paying customers
. Sometimes begrudgingly, but everyone has some level of human support, especially for larger customers. In fact, leaders from Intercom to Front to Gorgias to Zendesk exploded as this function, while not remotely new, became standardized. The reality is this is all now changing, for the first time. AI isn’t the only reason, the real drive is efficiency. But AI is the accelerant:
#1. There is a general sense among the leaders in sales software that we will end up with fewer, better SDRs, and that the majority of email and follow-up will be done with AI. Salesloft, Outreach, Gong and more radically changed the space. But we may be looking at far more radical change in the coming few years.
#2. Customer Success has in many cases morphed into part of the sales team.

AI isn’t the only reason, the real drive is efficiency. But AI is the accelerant:
#1. There is a general sense among the leaders in sales software that we will end up with fewer, better SDRs, and that the majority of email and follow-up will be done with AI. answer: Why Now Is the Biggest Change in SaaS Sales in 15+ Years If you’ve been doing B2B sales even just a little while — you know what the last 15-20 years have brought. - An explosion of roles. From SMB to enterprise, every traditional SaaS company started hiring: - A Head of Sales - SDRs (new) - Account Executives (not really new but more senior ones than ever before) - Customer Success Managers - Support Specialists - Solutions Engineers - Renewal Managers And so much more - The need for specialized human-based processes, especially in mid-market and larger deals. Outbound, Inbound, Qualification, etc. - All these folks had to work together as a true team. Even if they didn’t always like each other. - So this was the playbook for the past two decades or so. It’s worked well. But … now? That entire playbook seems poised to go into the bin. Not all at once, nor everywhere. But I think we’re on the cusp of change in how startups sell B2B products for real. And there are several factors behind this change. First, the rise of AI agents has opened our eyes to what can be automated in GTM. Second, many in GTM aren’t needed anymore. No one wants to meet in person anymore, no matter where they are. Third, most founders want to do it themselves again. At least some of it. This isn’t just about cost savings, although that matters too. This is also about wanting to get back closer to customers

answer:
I was at this event called the SaaStr Annual. It's an annual conference for SaaS founders. And I had the chance to catch up with a number of folks there. One of them was a VP of Sales who had been running his own company. He'd sold it for $500 million. But he wasn't doing anything since then. He said, "Jason, what do you think about these new age of AI tools?" And I said, "Well, they're exciting." And he goes, "Yeah, but how much is going to change?"
And I looked at him and I said, "This is probably the biggest change in sales in 20 years."
He said, "Really? What are you talking about?"
I said, "The whole way we work today, the whole way we sell, the whole way we work together. If you look at just the last two weeks, everything's different." Even if your headcount hasn't changed yet, things have already fundamentally changed in sales. Let me tell you why.
Let's take a few examples of changes we've seen in the last couple of months. First one, SDRs. In the early days of SaaS, when we started selling Salesforce.com back in the day, we didn't even know what an SDR was. But by around 2010-2011, everyone knew what an SDR was. And the job became very productized. You could buy a tool like SalesLoft, which later became Outreach. Or you could hire someone to manage those people and make sure they were qualified. These roles grew rapidly from '08 to 2020. So did human support. That really didn't exist until late in the game. Early on, support was always handled by engineering or by someone else outside the organization. Later, companies figured out how to create a separate function for support and added it to their org chart. Then came customer success.

So it does seem like some of the biggest changes to the human side of SaaS are now coming. I’ve talked with three CEOs at leading vendors in sales and post-sales at $200m+ in ARR the past few weeks and they’ve all reinforced these are some of the biggest changes in a generation. What we’ve seen in the first 15 years of SaaS:
Specialization in sales
. Segment reps, and have closers close. The rise of the SDR and productizing outbound and qualifying inbound with humans
. Outbound is nothing new, but the formal role of the SDR exploded in the past decade. The rise of customer success as a new, empowered function. Everyone has fully staffed CS over the past decade. We’ve all become NRR, GRR, and CSAT experts, and CS owned it all. Human support remained important, at least for paying customers
. Sometimes begrudgingly, but everyone has some level of human support, especially for larger customers. In fact, leaders from Intercom to Front to Gorgias to Zendesk exploded as this function, while not remotely new, became standardized. The reality is this is all now changing, for the first time. AI isn’t the only reason, the real drive is efficiency. But AI is the accelerant:
#1. There is a general sense among the leaders in sales software that we will end up with fewer, better SDRs, and that the majority of email and follow-up will be done with AI. Salesloft, Outreach, Gong and more radically changed the space. But we may be looking at far more radical change in the coming few years.
#2. Customer Success has in many cases morphed into part of the sales team.

answer:
So there’s been a lot of worry among VCs lately that public multiples have fallen so far — and will fall even further.  That startups are overvalued, that they need to raise at crazy valuations just to get funded, etc.  The point being raised here is that for a VC to make money on an investment … he has to sell those shares later at least 5x-10x what he paid in.
At current IPO prices, this won’t happen often enough:
The average SaaS IPO price-to-sales multiple today is around 7.6x. If you take out the outliers (like Snowflake), it drops to ~4.8x. And if you’re looking at private companies with similar revenue profiles, their multiples are half again lower—around 3-3.5x sales.
In 2019, that same group averaged 14x. In 2018? They hit 25x. And back when Datadog went public in 2019, they were trading at roughly 40x forward revenues.
That means your Series C might be worth $100 million instead of $300 million, depending how fast you grow. It means founders who could’ve taken money off the table now aren’t able to because every round feels like a necessity rather than an option. It means if you don’t go public by Year 15, you’ll probably miss your best exit opportunity entirely. The math works against the “just keep going” strategy. But that doesn’t mean it’s wrong. Even if your next funding round costs more because of market conditions, you still need to fund yourself through the inevitable downturns. At some point, markets cycle back up. IPO windows open again. Growth rates matter more than ever. The company that keeps running while everyone else freezes becomes the obvious acquisition target—and sometimes, as we saw with Salesforce acquiring Slack at peak valuation, that’s exactly what happens.
So do these worries matter?
Yes.
For one thing, the concern that venture capitalists can’t invest unless they believe they can easily double their money isn’t baseless.

answer: Your VCs Are Worried About Public Multiples. Do You Need To Worry, Too? We recently spoke with two successful SaaS founders who were each asked by their board to share what worries them most about the business right now. Both shared they worried that public multiples had dropped too low for acquisitions. But how much should you worry if your VCs are worried about public multiples? It depends on whether they will actually impact M&A activity. If there's no real impact -- then just tell them you'll see where things go. They probably don't care as much as it seems. And if they do have an impact -- then talk through together why this might be good news for you. Why would lower acquisition offers be such good news? In general, I'd say the vast majority of startups aren't going to get acquired. So a few less offers isn't really bad. A few more offers often comes out of nowhere. The best ones do. Even when times seem tougher. Just make sure any change in strategy doesn't hurt the odds here.

answer:
So you've heard this conversation before, I'm sure. It's one that we hear again and again as part of every single board meeting now for a while. "I know this company has some issues. But it does have great fundamentals. And if multiples were back to what they used to be when I invested, well then it would still work out."
And your investors are right. We're all worried. In fact, there was an interesting survey done by Carta with PwC that showed almost half of venture capital firms are less likely to invest today than they were even just six months ago because of fear of losing money on their investments. Fear of losing money. Because public market multiples aren't where they once were. So if I could share some advice here, my number one piece of advice is don't obsess over what you think your VC might be thinking. If your investors want to buy more stock, they will. They'll figure out how much. But it really doesn't matter so long as you're building a real business, which you clearly are. You guys are doing fine. The reality is, no investor can do anything that meaningfully impacts your equity. No investor can sell any material amount of shares until the next round comes up at least. This isn't something that happens quickly enough. Even if you see a lot of activity around secondary markets these days, those deals take time to close and then another 12-18 months after that to get sold into the public markets. A few years later, maybe, you can find someone who wants to sell their stock. But you won't need them to help you survive the short term.

answer:
So we’ve taken a look at many SaaS leaders over the years on our New New Podcast and Live Wednesday series.  But one I think we haven’t done enough is Atlassian.  Because they’re so interesting.  They started off as a developer tool and got pretty big (and then even bigger).  It took them a while to really go enterprise, but when they did … wow.
$2.7 billion in ARR
Growing 21%, with
37% Subscription Growth
That’s just incredible efficiency for an enterprise play!
25% Free Cash Flow Margins (!)
And importantly — it gets better:
100% NRR
Not bad for a product that doesn’t have sales reps!  More on this below
110% GRR / Net Retention Rate
A related metric, but higher than NRR because it includes upsells, etc.  And again, without traditional sales support.  Wow.
Incredibly Efficient Hiring
Only 230 employees to serve 300,000 customers!  A stunning ratio.
What’s more impressive?  This was all during Covid.
Let’s take a look at some learnings:

#1.  60% of its Business Customers Are Outside Tech
While half their users are techies, 60% of their customers outside tech, and 40% of those are “non-technical” departments like HR and finance.  So don’t worry too much if your early leads aren’t technically savvy.  Just make sure you can get them into production quickly.  And keep the product simple enough to deploy there.
#2.  100% NRR, With 50% of Revenue From Self-Serve + Freemium Editions
Atlassian does have sales, but a lot less than most of us.  Most of its top partners are solution providers.  That means Atlassian has gotten almost 100% NRR out of self-service and freemium editions alone!  That’s what it takes to scale efficiently.

retrieval_query: 5 Interesting Learnings from Atlassian at Almost $3 Billion in ARR

retrieval_hits.text: New!!  5 Nonobvious Learnings from Atlassian’s Path to The First $10B in ARR With Ex-CRO Cameron Deatsch

So Atlassian has cruised past $4 Billion in ARR, still growing a steady 21% in a very efficient fashion.  It’s raining cash, with 27% free-cash flow margins.
The markets like this combination.  Even with a few bumps, Atlassian is still trading at a $55 Billion market cap, so over 12x ARR.  That’s twice the average of 6x ARR for public SaaS companies.
Efficient, steady, profitable growth at scale.  The markets say Yes to Atlassian.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  300,000 Total Paying Customers, With 43,000 Paying $10k or More
The vast majority of Atlassian’s customers pay less than $10k a year, but the $10k+ ones make up the bulk of the revenue.  A reminder that the long tail really does work in collaboration.  And also how important it is to go a smidge upmarket if you sell to SMBs and smaller customers.

So Atlassian is bucking the trend. At almost $5B ARR, subscription growth is up a stunning 33%, and revenue overall up 21% The markets loved it, driving the stock up +29% the past month Is SaaS Back? 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. Raising Guidance and Growth Rate for Cloud Revenue That’s pretty darn impressive growth at almost $5B in ARR, and just as importantly, they’re raising their prediction here. Atlassian is bullish on maintain and accelerating Cloud growth over the next year. #2. 500 $1M+ Customers Atlassian is going more and more enterprise, which has become key to maintaining growth. It now has 500 $1M+ customers. #3. 51% of Revenue From Outside North America A reminder to go global as early as practical. #4. 50% of Users on "Business Side”, 50% Technical An interesting breakdown across their core products. Yes, Atlassian’s roots are selling to developers. But as you go more upmarket, and more enterprise, the business users become critical stakeholders and users, too. It’s split 50/50 at Atlassian. #5. Seat Expansion Driving Growth, Along with Cross-Sell of New Products Long live per-seat models and pricing! Atlassian, HubSpot, GitLab and more are seeing growth fueled by classic account expansion of more seats. _______ The Atlassian engine just keeps on running!! Even at almost $5 Billion in ARR. Pretty impressive. Pretty, pretty impressive.

#5.  Planning to Hit $10B ARR in 5 Years
The beauty of recurring revenue and 100%+ NRR — that is, if you are also growing net new customer count too.  Which is Atlassian is.  You can predict long-term growth with fairly high confidence.
And a few other interesting learnings:

#6.  Continuing to See Pressures on Seat Counts — And Plan to Continue to Increase Prices
Atlassian isn’t immune from customers’ desires to cut and minimize seat count.  It just hasn’t seen the dramatic impact there
Salesforce
and others have.   They also plan to offset this with more price increases.
#7.  12,000 Employees, So About $370,000 in Revenue Per Employee
You don’t need to be here in the start-up phase.  But the leaders in SaaS and Cloud all seem to be
skating toward $400k in revenue per employee
to hit Wall Street’s profitability expectations.
Pretty cool, Atlassian.  Pretty cool.

retrieval_hits.text: New!!  5 Nonobvious Learnings from Atlassian’s Path to The First $10B in ARR With Ex-CRO Cameron Deatsch

So Atlassian has cruised past $4 Billion in ARR, still growing a steady 21% in a very efficient fashion.  It’s raining cash, with 27% free-cash flow margins.
The markets like this combination.  Even with a few bumps, Atlassian is still trading at a $55 Billion market cap, so over 12x ARR.  That’s twice the average of 6x ARR for public SaaS companies.
Efficient, steady, profitable growth at scale.  The markets say Yes to Atlassian.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  300,000 Total Paying Customers, With 43,000 Paying $10k or More
The vast majority of Atlassian’s customers pay less than $10k a year, but the $10k+ ones make up the bulk of the revenue.  A reminder that the long tail really does work in collaboration.  And also how important it is to go a smidge upmarket if you sell to SMBs and smaller customers.

So Atlassian is bucking the trend. At almost $5B ARR, subscription growth is up a stunning 33%, and revenue overall up 21% The markets loved it, driving the stock up +29% the past month Is SaaS Back? 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. Raising Guidance and Growth Rate for Cloud Revenue That’s pretty darn impressive growth at almost $5B in ARR, and just as importantly, they’re raising their prediction here. Atlassian is bullish on maintain and accelerating Cloud growth over the next year. #2. 500 $1M+ Customers Atlassian is going more and more enterprise, which has become key to maintaining growth. It now has 500 $1M+ customers. #3. 51% of Revenue From Outside North America A reminder to go global as early as practical. #4. 50% of Users on "Business Side”, 50% Technical An interesting breakdown across their core products. Yes, Atlassian’s roots are selling to developers. But as you go more upmarket, and more enterprise, the business users become critical stakeholders and users, too. It’s split 50/50 at Atlassian. #5. Seat Expansion Driving Growth, Along with Cross-Sell of New Products Long live per-seat models and pricing! Atlassian, HubSpot, GitLab and more are seeing growth fueled by classic account expansion of more seats. _______ The Atlassian engine just keeps on running!! Even at almost $5 Billion in ARR. Pretty impressive. Pretty, pretty impressive.

#5.  Planning to Hit $10B ARR in 5 Years
The beauty of recurring revenue and 100%+ NRR — that is, if you are also growing net new customer count too.  Which is Atlassian is.  You can predict long-term growth with fairly high confidence.
And a few other interesting learnings:

#6.  Continuing to See Pressures on Seat Counts — And Plan to Continue to Increase Prices
Atlassian isn’t immune from customers’ desires to cut and minimize seat count.  It just hasn’t seen the dramatic impact there
Salesforce
and others have.   They also plan to offset this with more price increases.
#7.  12,000 Employees, So About $370,000 in Revenue Per Employee
You don’t need to be here in the start-up phase.  But the leaders in SaaS and Cloud all seem to be
skating toward $400k in revenue per employee
to hit Wall Street’s profitability expectations.
Pretty cool, Atlassian.  Pretty cool.

Q:  I’m an SaaS founder who’s seen his NRR go from ~130% to <80%. My customers complain that my product isn’t as good as before. They say that it’s too complicated now and that there aren’t enough humans on staff to help them with any issues. The churn rate has been very high this quarter. In fact, our revenue growth is just 10%. How do I turn things around? It sounds like you’ve become one of those “NRR Zombies” we see so often these days. A classic example:
Your NRR has dropped below 90%, which means your existing customer base won’t grow organically anymore
. And when that happens, no amount of new logo sales will save you. Your new bookings have to be significantly higher than your existing business just to keep up — let alone grow faster. As soon as you fall behind here, all hope fades quickly. We’ll talk about what to do after this, but first, let me share some examples of how bad it gets once you hit this state. For example, RingCentral fell into this trap, going from epic hypergrowth (50%-60%) … to zombie mode. At $600m+ ARR, its NRR had fallen to 95%. That meant it could only get so much out of its massive installed base. And so growth slowed dramatically to single digits. And then Slack went through something similar. Its NRR stayed at 98% but the stock was crushed because its growth stalled. Even though their net retention remained strong, Wall Street lost faith. Why did this happen? Because they couldn’t deliver the same level of value to their core customers anymore. This happened again and again across many Cloud leaders during the last downturn in 2019-2020. So here’s what I’d suggest. First,
don’t blame anyone but yourself. The market didn’t change overnight
. Second, make sure you really know why your NRR dropped. Did you raise prices without adding enough value?

answer:
So we've talked before on SaaStr about how I call this the age of AI. And that really started last year when AI exploded into business software. But now we're entering the Age of Atonement, because all these companies that didn't keep up with change have fallen off the edge of the earth. This is happening right now. So many leaders just aren't keeping up with the new pace of change in B2B and SaaS. They are falling behind so fast today, that their customers are leaving them faster than ever. And one simple way to measure this is net revenue retention. Net Revenue Retention. We'll get to what it means, why it matters and why you should care later. But first let me tell you some stories about folks who haven't kept up. Because there are two types of founders out there today. There are zombies and non-zombies. Non-Zombies are still getting better. Their NRR is above 110%. Even as things get harder, they're finding a way to grow at least 10 points higher than NRR. The Zombies though... they're dead. No matter what anyone says. The Zombies' NRR has been below 90% for quite a while. Maybe even below 80%. And no matter how hard they try, no matter how much marketing budget they put into it, no matter how many salespeople they hire — nothing seems to work. At all. Now some will say well, maybe I'm doing fine at $30 million in ARR and 85% NRR. Or whatever it might be. Well, here's my rule:
Don't settle for less growth than Your NRR + 20%.
That's your floor, period. It doesn't mean you won't struggle. It doesn't mean you won't face challenges. It doesn't mean you won't have upsells fail sometimes. Of course it does. That's life. But once you fall below that line, you become a zombie. And after that, everyone knows it. Everyone knows you just aren't growing anymore. And no one wants to buy another seat. No one wants to increase their spend. And the ones you do have? They churn anyway.

answer:
Dear SaaStr: Our CFO Sounds Very Polished But Are We Going to Miss Another Burn Budget This Month?
Polish sounds good.  And polish always sounds good coming out of finance.
But if you’re missing the monthly burn plan again … well, that’s just too many excuses.
In my experience, if a startup misses its monthly cash burn goals even once,
it never gets back on track after that
. It’s easy to miss one or two months when things get tough, or when the model was off — especially early-ish in the journey.
But then folks sort of stop paying attention to it.
Then, next thing you know, you’ve missed another month. Then another. They all blend together at some point.
And before you know it, you don’t have enough money anymore. Or rather, you’ll find out you do eventually …
So what should you do?
First, start building a real, dynamic model yourself:
Everyone needs to understand how much we have (Cash Balance) and how quickly it changes (Burn Rate). You need to build this simple model yourself. Not trust someone else here.
Second, you really have to set a realistic goal, and challenge everyone to hit it
. If you aren’t sure what your “burn” goal is for the week/month/quarter/year, then you aren’t going to hit it. Period. So make sure everyone knows exactly what they have to hit each period. Each month. Make them own their piece of it. Everyone has to work to the same goal as CEO and founder.
Third, no matter what, put aside $500k-$750k in case of a rough patch. That usually covers most startups’ bumps
. Even if you think you won’t run out of money until late ’25, still take out an extra $600k today.
Fourth, maybe just move on
.

But you can’t cut your way to growth. So what should a CEO do? A few simple thoughts: #1. Let go of your bottom 10%-15% of sales reps, concentrate leads in the best reps. This always gives you both a top-line boost (the top reps close more per lead), and gives you room to hire more reps at the same budget. #2. Have a firm, management-team wide burn rate budget. And stick to it. Pick a fixed amount of cash you can burn each month, period. And make all your VPs accountable to it. Just move on from any VP that isn’t getting it done They almost always overspend compared to the VPs that overperform. They hire mediocre folks on their team. And they overspend to try to make their plan. #4. Spend more time with existing customers. And go save the ones on the fence I know this is a broken record on SaaStr, but it works. Relatively speaking, the easiest sales are from your existing customers. So go spend more time with them. And go save the ones on the fence. #5. Build an L4M Model, and update it every month. Religiously.

4. Set a burn-rate budget for each and every month
.
This will focus your team and de-stress your life.  Most of us come up with a rough budget for the year, but not a
burn-rate budget
for
each month
.  This will force everyone on the team, starting Monday, to collaborate on hiring and other trade-offs.  If you go over the budget, now everyone will know.  In close to real time.  This will almost immediately improve the efficiency of your limited budgets, and improve teamwork.  And you will make better decisions on where to deploy your limited resources.  Which will not just manage your burn rate — but increase your revenues.  Starting Monday.  More
here
.

answer:
Dear SaaStr: Our CFO Sounds Very Polished but We are Missing the Burn Rate Plan Almost Every Month. What Should I Do?
Burn rate planning isn’t rocket science — it’s just accounting. Here's how you fix this:

First, stop relying on your CFO to do everything. That "polished" presentation? It might actually hide problems rather than solve them.

Second, understand that burn rate planning needs to happen at least once per quarter. Not monthly, unless you're in hypergrowth mode (which seems unlikely given your CFO issues).

Third, don't wait until the end of the month to figure out if you'll hit your targets. That's like flying without navigation. You need regular check-ins throughout the month.

Fourth, get your CFO into the rhythm of the business faster

answer:
Dear SaaStr: Our CFO Sounds Very Polished But We Are Missing the Monthly Cash Planning Almost Every Month. What Should I Do?
Your CFO probably has done this before as a public company or at least, multiple times, as a senior finance person.
But they haven't done it before as a founder-led start-up.
So here's what you have to do:

First, just ask them why this hasn't happened yet.
I bet it's because there isn't one core leader accountable.
There almost always isn't in start-ups that don't get this right.

Second, challenge her/him to create a real plan — a real monthly cash planning model. Not a spreadsheet.
And tell them if she/he doesn't deliver a working model by next week (or whatever timeline) that you'll need to find someone else to do it.

Third, give him/her a clear deadline and KPIs to hit.
And also set up weekly/monthly progress checks. And remind them to follow up when those check-ins happen.

Fourth, explain how much stress it takes off everyone if you know exactly where we stand at all times.

Fifth, force yourselves to understand, as founders, where the money is going. That's really the job of the CEO. Make sure you know. This is key.
It makes the whole exercise worth it.

Sixth, push hard to figure out the root cause of why folks aren't following up on tracking this.
Is it lack of training? Lack of interest? Lack of buy-in? Whatever it is, fix it.

Seventh, use the fact that the most successful startups never miss their monthly burn rate plans against your CFO.

answer:
Dear SaaStr: How long does it take to deploy an AI SDR?
The key here is that you don’t need to buy another product.  If you have Salesforce / HubSpot / etc., then for now at least, just start using what’s already there.
For example,
Qualified
has seen customers go live in under two weeks — sometimes as fast as one day!
In fact, their fastest deployment was less than a week:
Another AI GTM leader saw companies going live in “just days” and generating hundreds of thousands of dollars in pipeline per month within the first few months of deployment. One company reported $200K+ in closed-won revenue attributed directly to their AI SDR within its first six weeks. That’s not theoretical ROI—it’s real money coming out of qualified opportunities generated by an AI system running on top of existing CRM data. And
Agentforce
from Salesforce says they see similar results. They claim that Agent Force has been used more than 100 million times since its launch. So how quickly should we expect to get this up and running? In general, most B2B leaders recommend allowing around four to eight weeks for initial training before expecting meaningful output. But if you’re deploying a tool like Qualified or AgentForce that runs natively inside your CRM, the timeline might be significantly shorter—think two weeks max. The actual deployment process usually breaks down into three phases: setup (a couple hours), daily monitoring/tuning (30-60 minutes), and ongoing optimization over time. For many users, the biggest challenge is learning the tools themselves—not necessarily the technology itself, which is increasingly user-friendly, but understanding how to train them effectively.

Dear SaaStr: I Want to Roll Out an AI SDR. How Do I Start? First, get clear on what you’re actually buying — and what it actually does. We’ve now been running AI SDRs at SaaStr for over a year. Multiple platforms. Real data. Real pipeline. And the honest answer is: it works. But it works very differently than most vendors will tell you, and the gap between a good deployment and a wasted one comes down almost entirely to how you set it up. Here’s what we actually learned. The Single Best Use Case to Start With: The Leads Your Team Is Ignoring
This is the insight that changed how we think about AI SDRs entirely. Your human SDRs are force-ranking in their heads every single day. They’re chasing the big deals, the warm inbound, the accounts that feel like they could close this quarter. The leads they consider “not worth it” — return event attendees, old website visitors, ghosted CRM contacts — those get nothing. Not bad follow-up. Nothing. That’s where AI SDRs absolutely shine. When we deployed AI on the leads our human team refused to work — people who had engaged with SaaStr but never got follow-up — we got a
72% open rate
on Agentforce and generated
15% of our London event revenue
from a segment that would have produced zero without AI. Not 15% incremental lift. 15% of total revenue from leads that were producing $0. So before you start thinking about AI SDRs as a way to scale your best motion, ask yourself: what’s the motion your team isn’t running at all? Start there.

The real implementation involves:
ICP and messaging work:
2–4 weeks of your best sales brain. Don’t rush this. Integration and setup:
1–2 weeks of technical lift depending on your CRM and stack. Ongoing tuning:
30–45 minutes per day, minimum, for the first 60–90 days. Then 20–30 minutes daily after that. This is not set-it-and-forget-it. The vendors will tell you it takes an afternoon to set up. You can turn it on in an afternoon. That’s very different from having it work. The Honest Expectation
A well-deployed AI SDR in 2026 will do the work your human team isn’t doing — the segments they consider too small, the leads they consider too cold, the follow-ups they keep meaning to send. That’s where the ROI is clearest and fastest. It will also scale your warm outbound to volumes no human team can match. We went from 285 emails per rep per month to 3,221 per month on a single platform, with equivalent or better response rates. What it won’t do is replace a great enterprise SDR who navigates complex organizations and handles nuanced objections in real-time. That’s still a human job — at least for now. Use AI SDRs to cover the motions where speed and volume matter most. Redeploy your human SDRs to the work where judgment and relationships matter most. That’s not a downgrade for your team. That’s a better use of everyone’s time — and more pipeline from leads that would have otherwise produced nothing. Have a question for SaaStr? We answer the real ones at
SaaStr.ai
.

SDR turnover is the highest of any go-to-market role. The best SDRs want to be AEs within six months. Get above the quality bar, and 99% of people are happy to interact with your AI agent. The 1% who get frustrated are a rounding error, and about half of those are just people trying to prompt-inject your bot for fun. The AI SDR is not a magic bullet. It requires real setup time, real ongoing maintenance, and real human judgment to run well. But if you do the work, the results are better than what most human SDR teams deliver, at a fraction of the cost and at genuinely infinite scale.

answer: So there's so much confusion around deploying an AI SDR. So I wanted to just give you some learnings on this because we've deployed three different AI agents now at SaaStr itself, two of them are outbound, one inbound. And we also use one for our content review, which was really important for us. But what we found out was that if done right, you don't have to deploy an AI agent over weeks. You can get going almost overnight. Now let me tell you why. First, most humans aren't even checking their email anymore anyway. Email open rates are down to like 0.5%. They're terrible. Nobody checks email the way they used to. So if nobody's reading it, who cares how long it takes to put in an AI agent? Second, we tested all these AI SDRs ourselves before we bought any of them. We tried five different ones and asked them to sell tickets to SaaStr London. And guess what? Three of them were pretty good. Two of them worked great. One had a weird bug where it wouldn't take credit cards, but otherwise they worked fine. What did we find out? Inbound, you want to set up an agent fast because folks are already coming to your website. If you're getting a thousand leads a month, you probably shouldn't wait six months to deploy an AI agent. That's too slow. Because those folks could be meeting with sales reps today. Outbound though, here's my learning. You can train an AI agent to send emails tonight. You don't need to spend weeks training it. Here's why. If you look at our data with Artisan, when we first started, it took maybe half a day to deploy the AI agent, not more than that. And then it took 30 days to tune it. Why? Because once the agent starts sending emails and booking meetings, you start seeing results. You'll see it book a meeting and you'll think, "Oh man, this works." Then you'll go back and adjust the parameters.

answer:
Dear SaaStr: Should I Use an AI SDR Before I Have a Working Human SDR motion?
I’d say yes. Here’s why:
First,
95% of human SDRs don’t really understand what they are selling
. If you think your SDR team does — well that’s great! But if most humans on sales teams don’t truly get how their own products work … then it’s pretty easy to see why AI can be better here. And we’ve all seen this in practice at so many start-ups:
The first few AEs will sell whatever they want. The VP of Sales will push out crazy quotas, even when no one understands how anyone would hit them …
And by the time the first AE leaves (or gets fired), everyone sort of just gives up. It takes too long to train new folks, anyway. So nothing really ever scales beyond the early days.
So the odds your SDR team knows enough about your product to close deals is low. Low enough that AI often already wins before you deploy it.
Second, 95% of human SDRs can’t answer any real questions
. This might sound harsh, but it’s true. They’re good at sequences, at sending emails, at reaching out to people in their CRM. But ask them anything more nuanced than that, especially around complex enterprise software, and most won’t know how to respond. And the ones that try to figure it out? Well, they’ll take weeks.
Third, 95% of human SDRs need help with everything. They need scripts, training, coaching, check-ins every day. They struggle to onboard quickly. And once they finally get going, they plateau fast because they run out of ideas and energy.
Fourth, AI SDRs already win at almost every startup today, even with mediocre human SDRs. In fact, 90%+ of our AI Agents >win< against our mediocre human SDRs
.

answer: Dear SaaStr: Should I Use an AI SDR Before I Have a Working Human SDR motion? Probably. We’ve seen this pattern play out with founders across every stage: They hire their first “SDR” — who’s really just doing outbound research, scheduling meetings, or sending generic emails that don’t actually sell anything. Then they realize: This isn’t working. The results are terrible. It’s sucking up time and resources without delivering real pipeline. And honestly? Most human SDRs aren’t great at sales anyway. So here’s my honest take: If you’re still figuring out your outbound strategy, if you haven’t cracked the code on what works yet, deploying an AI SDR before you have a human one in place can be brilliant. But only if you deploy it right. Here’s why: AI SDRs don’t make excuses. They don’t need training (or pretend they do). They don’t miss follow-ups because they forgot. They work 24/7. They send perfect outreach sequences. They never get tired of calling back. They never forget to send the follow-up email. What they CAN’T do: They won’t truly understand your prospects like a human would. They’ll struggle with complex conversations or nuanced objections. You still need humans to qualify leads, build relationships, and close deals. But for the 80-90% of your prospecting that ISN’T about relationship building, an AI SDR can absolutely crush it while you figure out the rest. Just remember: Deployment matters more than technology itself. Train it well,

answer:
Dear SaaStr: Should I Use an AI SDR Before I Have a Working Human SDR Motion?
Yes.  This is almost always correct, even if you're early days.
The reality today is that 95% of humans don't know the products they sell (E1) and can't answer tough questions (E2). And they often need help getting back to customers quickly (E3).
We've seen this at SaaStr itself. Our own sales team uses Artisan as their primary tool, sending millions of messages per year and achieving an average open rate of 5-6%, which is roughly double what most companies see with outbound emails.
And here's the thing—these results aren't unique to our setup. Other organizations we work with achieve similar performance on their AI SDR tools, including Qualified, Apollo Inbound, and Agentforce.

Dear SaaStr: We’re At $8m ARR Growing 90% But Can’t Get a VC To Give Us a Term Sheet. What Should I Do?
This is an issue with many founders that think too much about their own metrics.  First, let me give you some real advice:
First, understand this — 90% YoY Growth May Not Be Enough Today to Really Excite VCs (But That Doesn’t Mean No One Will Want to Fund You)
Let’s look at what it takes to get funded these days.  And remember, 95% of start-ups fail.  So if nothing else, fundraise enough so that you don’t run out of money before then 🙂
VCs want to see a clear path to Initial Scale ($20-$50m) ARR in most cases. Even for seed deals,
most VCs aren’t going to put up capital without a clear way to get there
— i.e., high NRR, strong market traction, etc. The math has to work.
At ~$8M ARR growing 80%, you might have to show how you’ll grow into something like this within 12-18 months
. This could include adding another revenue stream, expanding into adjacent markets, hiring experienced leadership to help drive growth, etc.
If you can demonstrate a clear plan and timeline for reaching Initial Scale, investors will likely be interested.
However, if you’re simply “hitting the wall” and struggling to scale due to internal or external factors, it may be tougher to secure funding until you’ve figured things out.

Dear SaaStr: We are at $10MM ARR and it’s … hell.  We can’t seem to breakthrough and we are short on cash. Do we sell? Push through? Last year we grew 40% so growth is slow but we’re still growing.
We all get burnt out in a scenario like this.  Many years in, real ARR, but not at true scale.  Cash being tight only makes it harder.
First, 40% growth at $10M ARR isn’t a rocketship.  But it’s still real growth.  You can still get to $100m+ ARR.
It’s not hypergrowth, but it’s respectable, especially in the enterprise, where sales cycles can be long and complex. This tells me the business isn’t broken—it’s just stuck in the grind of scaling. And scaling from $10M to $20M ARR is often the hardest phase. It’s where you feel like you’re running uphill with a boulder strapped to your back, especially since you just don’t have much redundancy on the team.
The cash crunch is the real issue here.
When you’re short on cash, you’re forced to underinvest, and underinvestment kills momentum. I’ve seen this play out too many times. At $10M ARR, you need at least $5M on your balance sheet to scale properly. Without it, every decision feels like triage, and you can’t make the bold moves that drive growth.
So, should you sell or push through? Here’s how I’d think about it:

1. Do You Believe in the Business?
If you still believe this is a $100M ARR business in the making, then you push through. But you need to be honest with yourself. Is the TAM big enough? Are your unit economics solid? If the answer is yes, then it’s worth fighting for.

Dear SaaStr: Who Drafts the Term Sheet, The Entrepreneurs or the VC?
It depends who is selling and who is buying.
In the old days, and still mostly commonly today, term sheets only came from VCs. Founders were almost always selling. Well,
almost
always.
But even in the Old Days, the hottest of start-ups made up the terms. Microsoft took one venture investor, sold them only 5%, and named the terms:
The Venture Capitalist Microsoft Allowed To Invest Early
Today, it’s still the case. In almost all “standard” VC financings, the VC drafts and issues a fairly standard term sheet.
But if you are very hot, it’s different. At the seed stage, for example, Ycombinator SAFE notes have evolved essentially into a form of term sheet issued by founders. Originally, SAFEs were designed to save legal fees. But today, what they really serve as is a very simple, founder-friendly, founder-generated term sheet. The valuation is set by the founders, and the terms are the SAFE itself — again set by the founders, in essence.
In any stage of investing, if you get 4–5+ offers and demand for every 1 share available, the founders will set the terms, even if they don’t literally issue the term sheet.
But if you aren’t super hot — let the VCs take the lead there. It’s their money, and you are the one selling.

Dear SaaStr: We are at $10MM ARR and it’s … hell.  We can’t seem to breakthrough and we are short on cash. Do we sell? Push through? Last year we grew 40% so growth is slow but we’re still growing.
We all get burnt out in a scenario like this.  Many years in, real ARR, but not at true scale.  Cash being tight only makes it harder.
First, 40% growth at $10M ARR isn’t a rocketship.  But it’s still real growth.  You can still get to $100m+ ARR.
It’s not hypergrowth, but it’s respectable, especially in the enterprise, where sales cycles can be long and complex. This tells me the business isn’t broken—it’s just stuck in the grind of scaling. And scaling from $10M to $20M ARR is often the hardest phase. It’s where you feel like you’re running uphill with a boulder strapped to your back, especially since you just don’t have much redundancy on the team.
The cash crunch is the real issue here.
When you’re short on cash, you’re forced to underinvest, and underinvestment kills momentum. I’ve seen this play out too many times. At $10M ARR, you need at least $5M on your balance sheet to scale properly. Without it, every decision feels like triage, and you can’t make the bold moves that drive growth.
So, should you sell or push through? Here’s how I’d think about it:

1. Do You Believe in the Business?
If you still believe this is a $100M ARR business in the making, then you push through. But you need to be honest with yourself. Is the TAM big enough? Are your unit economics solid? If the answer is yes, then it’s worth fighting for.

Dear SaaStr: Who Drafts the Term Sheet, The Entrepreneurs or the VC?
It depends who is selling and who is buying.
In the old days, and still mostly commonly today, term sheets only came from VCs. Founders were almost always selling. Well,
almost
always.

The Venture Capitalist Microsoft Allowed To Invest Early

answer:
Dear SaaStr: We’re At $8m ARR Growing 90% But Can’t Get a VC To Give Us a Term Sheet
This question comes up all the time. Folks grow nicely at $20k, $50k, $80k ACV, maybe have some upsells, sometimes a bit more enterprise … and they start to see the venture capital doors close. “Why? I’m growing 70%, 80%, 90%. That should be enough.”
Well let me tell you why it might not be enough. Let me break this down into two categories, because there are two answers here. And one answer is that if you don’t like the answer — change something. Because you’re not going to be able to change how VCs think about startups quite yet. So first, let’s do what VCs are looking for these days, especially in seed stage and early stage investing. What are folks looking for now? Well I’ll give you my list. First, if you want to invest in AI today, that’s great. Go fund an agent. Or a B2B startup with insane growth and an incredible founder. But if you want to go fund a company growing at 60-80% at $10m ARR, then you better believe you’ve got to be in a hot space. A lot of them aren’t as hot right now. Second, in many cases, VCs would rather wait until later to invest in any given category where they know there will be success. Especially if they already invested earlier. Third, you have to have a strong brand and track record behind you. Fourth, most importantly, you have to be self-sufficient. If you raise less than $5 million, you’re probably not gonna be able to hire enough people to get to say $30m-$50m ARR, and beyond. Now if you’re $5m ARR growing 100%, you’ve raised a big round. You’re self sufficient. You’re going to make it. That’s cool. The next thing is that if you haven’t proven product-market fit by $2m-$3m ARR, it’s hard to convince someone that you will. Even if you have, it can still be tough. And so finally, and most importantly, when we were last doing this stuff regularly, no one wanted to invest unless they could control the outcome.

And scaling from $10M to $20M ARR is often the hardest phase. It’s where you feel like you’re running uphill with a boulder strapped to your back, especially since you just don’t have much redundancy on the team.

When you’re short on cash, you’re forced to underinvest, and underinvestment kills momentum. I’ve seen this play out too many times. Dear SaaStr: How long does it take to negotiate a term sheet? Who should open the negotiation on valuation – VC or entrepreneur? What are the top tips for entrepreneurs preparing for a term sheet negotiation? It shouldn’t take more than a week, or even just a few days, to negotiate a term sheet. That is — once a VC decides they truly want to do a deal. There really aren’t many variables these days for seed to Series A deals, really just
price
and
how much you are raising/selling. Most of the rest of the terms are much lower drama than they used to be. Most VCs aren’t trying to control your board and your company in the early days anymore. (If they do, that may take longer to work out). So what are the tips to get the
best deal
— but
also
to ensure the deal closes? A few learnings and insights:
It doesn’t really matter “who goes first”
. Many founders will expect a VC to “go first” and make an offer. They may also think it gives them some leverage. Perhaps it does, in later stage and oversubscribed deals, and in general at the margin. But going first also might have advantages, in letting you anchor high. I am just not sure it much matters in earlier stage investing. Personally, I just
ask
. “What is your ask? How much are you raising? What valuation are you looking for?” It’s not a game for me, at least. I just want to know. I just want to know if I can do it, if I can meet the ask. But what really gives you leverage, if you want it, are multiple offers
. Going first, last, in the middle doesn’t matter nearly so much as having other
options
.

[train_3128]
Dear SaaStr: We are at $10MM ARR and it’s … hell.  We can’t seem to breakthrough and we are short on cash. Do we sell? Push through? Last year we grew 40% so growth is slow but we’re still growing.
We all get burnt out in a scenario like this.  Many years in, real ARR, but not at true scale.  Cash being tight only makes it harder.
First, 40% growth at $10M ARR isn’t a rocketship.  But it’s still real growth.  You can still get to $100m+ ARR.
It’s not hypergrowth, but it’s respectable, especially in the enterprise, where sales cycles can be long and complex. This tells me the business isn’t broken—it’s just stuck in the grind of scaling. And scaling from $10M to $20M ARR is often the hardest phase. It’s where you feel like you’re running uphill with a boulder strapped to your back, especially since you just don’t have much redundancy on the team.
The cash crunch is the real issue here.
When you’re short on cash, you’re forced to underinvest, and underinvestment kills momentum. I’ve seen this play out too many times. At $10M ARR, you need at least $5M on your balance sheet to scale properly. Without it, every decision feels like triage, and you can’t make the bold moves that drive growth.
So, should you sell or push through? Here’s how I’d think about it:

1. Do You Believe in the Business?
If you still believe this is a $100M ARR business in the making, then you push through. But you need to be honest with yourself. Is the TAM big enough? Are your unit economics solid? If the answer is yes, then it’s worth fighting for.

[train_7249]
Dear SaaStr: Who Drafts the Term Sheet, The Entrepreneurs or the VC?
It depends who is selling and who is buying.
In the old days, and still mostly commonly today, term sheets only came from VCs. Founders were almost always selling. Well,
almost
always.
But even in the Old Days, the hottest of start-ups made up the terms. Microsoft took one venture investor, sold them only 5%, and named the terms:
The Venture Capitalist Microsoft Allowed To Invest Early
Today, it’s still the case. In almost all “standard” VC financings, the VC drafts and issues a fairly standard term sheet.
But if you are very hot, it’s different. At the seed stage, for example, Ycombinator SAFE notes have evolved essentially into a form of term sheet issued by founders. Originally, SAFEs were designed to save legal fees. But today, what they really serve as is a very simple, founder-friendly, founder-generated term sheet. The valuation is set by the founders, and the terms are the SAFE itself — again set by the founders, in essence.
In any stage of investing, if you get 4–5+ offers and demand for every 1 share available, the founders will set the terms, even if they don’t literally issue the term sheet.
But if you aren’t super hot — let the VCs take the lead there. It’s their money, and you are the one selling.

answer:
So there’s a fairly common objection I hear from traditional SaaS folks when someone suggests deploying an AI agent:
“Customers won’t trust an AI.”
And often, the next part is “especially if something goes wrong.  They’ll just blame us.”
But let me tell you what I saw this week at SaaStr AI London (we had thousands of people attend, record attendance):
I asked our team — which included two of our best salespeople who’d never worked with AI before —
if they would trust an AI salesperson.  It was unanimous.  Yes, they said.  They trusted our AI sales reps more than humans.
The reasons were simple:
availability
— our AI reps could work 24/7, answer questions instantly
knowledge depth
— our AI knew everything about SaaStr’s products cold, no research needed
no BS or lies
— unlike some human reps, our AI didn’t make stuff up to close deals
No excuses. No games. Just help. Why We Built Our Own Agent First
Before anyone asks: yes, we built our own internal AI agent first because we couldn’t find anything good off-the-shelf. Here’s what we learned:
Our internal tool isn’t perfect yet. It has bugs, it can hallucinate sometimes, and it requires daily management. But it works. And that experience made everything else click into place. We went from zero to deployment-ready faster than any vendor promised. What Works Today
Here’s where we’re actually at right now, based entirely on real data and usage patterns:
New!!  Most people that say “buyers won’t trust an AI” haven’t bought software in years, or tried to deploy an AI agent.  If they did, they’d see it’s mostly fine.
Many customers already interact with AI systems regularly. When something breaks or doesn’t go as expected, they complain to whoever is closest — usually their point of contact.
