When you’re selling to sophisticated buyers, they’re evaluating not just your product, but your operational competence. A basic factual error signals that either:
You don’t have proper quality control processes
You’re not paying attention to details
You’re over-relying on automation without human oversight
None of these are good signals for a potential vendor relationship. The Path Forward
AI in sales isn’t going away—nor should it. But the companies that win will be those that combine AI’s scalability with human judgment and oversight. The goal isn’t to eliminate AI from your sales process. It’s to eliminate the scenarios where AI can blow your shot. Build systems that let AI do what it does best (scale, personalize, optimize) while ensuring humans catch what AI does worst (context, nuance, basic fact-checking). Because in B2B sales, 90% right is 100% wrong. Especially when you don’t already know and trust the vendor.

If you think you are safe from AI disruption, you are going to lose.

Here is why: someone will build the #1 AI Agents in your space.  They will have insane ROI, and customers will rush to adopt them.  Even in vertical SaaS, even in fintech.

They may still buy your product, but
New!!  Will Buyers Ultimately Pay More for AI? Vendr’s Data Says … Maybe Not

If I trust an AI more than a human sales rep … Then I will buy from an AI over a human sales rep. That day is pretty close to here today already. The AI sales rep already: - is available 24x7 - knows product cold - doesn’t lie or make stuff up to close a deal Many think this is silly … but most of those that do haven’t bought software is a while themselves, or used a great AI in this context yet. Go try to buy a routine piece of SaaS software. See how painful it is, how long it takes, how hard it is to get the precise answers you need for your own flow and use case. Are the tools here today? Not quite. But they will be soon. If we had the quality of dev teams working on OpenAI and Cursor that are working on AI AEs, the products would already be great. But they are coming soon. Some will enhance AEs, and make them Mech AEs, for sure. Some will create agents that make humans better. Other products will run basic sales autonomously, but kick up exceptions and other issues to humans. AI support already works this way pretty well. And some products, some will basically enable AI to handle 90% of sales on its own. This will require highly transparent pricing, the ability to truly one-click cancel, and the ability to auto-onboard in many cases. But many founders will choose to build the latter. Even if you disagree with this, realize it’s already here in coding, in support, even in SaaStr’s own AI. And things are getting so, so much better in AI every single day. The rate of improvement and change is like nothing we’ve ever seen in B2B and SaaS.

answer: So I was chatting with someone at another company recently. They were excited about their new AI VP of Sales — which sounds awesome, except that AI VPs aren’t really ready to sell yet. So what did they actually mean? It turns out they meant they’d built an internal tool where when anyone asked something about deals or customers inside their CRM, it would answer questions. Which again, isn’t exactly what an AI agent does, but I’ll get there. Anyway, this person said he could see no one would trust an AI to answer any questions about buying their software. He thought it was silly. Then just the other week I needed help choosing between two vendors. I’m a founder myself, I know the drill. I didn’t want to call anyone, I just wanted to ask an AI. And the thing just made stuff up. No problem. That’s why I wasn’t going to buy anything from them. You probably had a similar experience as a buyer too. Now look, this is important. We all say things sometimes that aren’t true. We stretch data points. We exaggerate a bit. These things happen. But an AI system has no idea if it’s giving you correct information or not. Or worse, maybe it gives you mostly right info, then says something wrong. That just totally destroys credibility. When we’re shopping online now, we expect the same level of transparency and truthfulness from digital systems as we demand from people. If a website makes a claim that turns out to be false, you lose our trust immediately. And honestly, we also expect more from AI than from a lot of salespeople these days. The bar is higher. Don’t let your team pretend otherwise. But here’s my point: AI can already process and synthesize vast amounts of data in real-time, faster and more accurately than any human.

answer:
We recently discovered something important about our own SaaStr AI Agents we’d built on Replit.
One stopped working because we hadn’t updated it in months — and didn’t even know it was broken.
It’s a reminder that deploying AI isn’t as simple as “set and forget.”  Not really.  Not yet at least.
The Real Story Behind Our Discovery
Here’s what happened:
we deployed one of these agentic tools about six to eight months ago.  We spent a ton of time getting it right — weeks, honestly — figuring out prompts, edge cases, the entire workflow.  It worked beautifully.  For maybe two months.  Then life got busy.  We moved on to other projects.  We thought it would keep running fine.
Six months later, when we came back to check?  Nothing worked anymore.  No emails were being sent.  No responses were happening.  The system was dead silent.  But here’s the kicker: there were no error messages.  No red flags anywhere.  No indication anything was wrong beyond the fact that nothing was happening.
What Actually Happened (And Why)
After digging deeper with Replie’s support, I learned exactly why this failed so catastrophically:
the underlying API changed.  Something broke under the hood.  That’s all I needed to know.
But then I did some more digging myself.  Because if you don’t dig into how your app actually works, you won’t understand what went wrong — or how to fix it.
Replit has been doing some deep refactoring across their platform, which means they’ve been rebuilding core components.  These aren’t just minor updates.  They’re foundational changes that touch every single application on the platform.

retrieval_query: You Can’t Train an AI Agent and Then Just … Go Away. We Did, It Fell Off The Rails. And We Didn’t Even Know.

retrieval_hits.text:
We made a mistake that we tell everyone not to make with AI agents.

We stopped training and monitoring one of our original AI Agents.  We now have almost 30 AI Agents.  There's so much to do every day now, to keep up with them.

So we stopped checking in with a few of them,

The only genuinely non-intuitive part is training — which is a real step that many teams skip and then wonder why the agent isn’t working. But the UI, the UX, the configuration logic — it’s just software. It works like software has always worked. The people who are winning with AI right now in non-technical roles aren’t doing anything magical. They tried the tools early. They trained them for a month. They stayed a year ahead of everyone else through one simple mechanism: they actually used the things. What Happens If You Don’t
I was reviewing a company recently — a well-run team, growing fast, crossing toward $100M. Their new CRO hadn’t brought in a single AI tool. Not one. Wasn’t scared of AI philosophically, just hadn’t done it. Adding hundreds of sales reps this year without asking what they could do with a fraction of that headcount and a deployed AI BDR instead. I wanted to cry. Years of their life being left on the table. I also saw the inverse this week, and it’s a useful cautionary tale for the AI-native side. A $6 billion AI company — I won’t name it — whose agent was quoting our team incorrect pricing. Telling us we’d need to quadruple our spend. Why? No one had properly trained the agent on pricing. When we asked how long the product had been in beta: a year. A year of a badly trained agent making bad calls, at a company whose entire product is AI. That is what it looks like when smart people don’t treat deployment as seriously as they treat building. The Companies That Feel Like Summer vs.

We made a mistake that we tell everyone not to make with AI agents. We stopped training and monitoring one of our original AI Agents. We now have almost 30 AI Agents. There's so much to do every day now, to keep up with them. y So we stopped checking in with all of them, every day. The less mission critical ones, we stopped doing ... 1-on-1's with, in essence. And then we found out yesterday, one hadn't been sync'ing with new data ... in over 4 months. Yes, it still functioned, but on increasing stale data. And it never threw an error, despite being a very well funded startup with a top dev team behind it. AI Agents are many things. But they aren't set-and-forget. Not yet.

Our general AI Agent (“Digital Jason”) handled 77 conversations and 203 messages yesterday. Most were pretty good, I am sure. But the real point is I couldn’t have done it. Nor could our tiny team. This is some of the biggest leverage in AI. Getting an AI “good enough” to do things … you have no human to do.

answer: You Can’t Train an AI Agent and Then Just … Go Away. We Did, It Fell Off The Rails. And We Didn’t Even Know. For weeks, our SaaStr.ai AI chat has been giving out terrible advice to founders. Terrible. Inaccurate information. Wrong answers. Bad recommendations. And we didn’t even know. Not until now. Here’s what happened: Someone asked us about hiring for their first VP of Sales role. Simple enough question. But our AI was trained on a dataset from mid-2024 — before ChatGPT exploded, before Claude got good at reasoning, before LLMs could actually think instead of just recall facts. Our AI still thought you needed a traditional sales background to be successful as a VP of Sales. That it took years of selling experience to figure out how to sell properly. That being great at something else (product management, engineering, marketing) wasn’t sufficient. So when someone asked about building a revenue org with zero prior B2B sales leadership experience, here’s what our AI said: “It will take them longer than they expect. They’ll need more time to hire the right people and get everything set up.” Completely wrong. Today, I’d tell this founder differently. At least half of today’s best VPs of Sales were never technical sellers themselves. Some started in entirely different functions altogether. Why? Because they’re operating in an era where the playbook is fundamentally different. You don’t need decades of quota-crushing experience anymore. You need to understand AI-native buyer behavior, digital-first GTM strategies,

answer: We've now been doing this at SaaStr for years. We're not super early adopters ourselves, we don't think we are, but we do try to lead by example here as best we can. So we've run a number of different vibe coding apps over the years. I know there's some controversy around them, and maybe they should be called vibe coding assistants or something instead because some folks want to call things that aren't truly agentic "vibe coding." But you all get what we mean. Lovable, Replit, etc. They're pretty cool. There's no question about it. That being said, if you read our last piece on this topic with Kyle Norton, CTO at Clay, one thing he was very clear about was how much more important ongoing management of these apps is than people realize. And we agree. Because recently we were trying to fix a problem with our app that didn't have anything to do with us. But we'd gone months without checking in. Months. And it was still running off its own train of thought. Let me tell you what happened. So we started using this new tool for sponsors. Not our own product, but a third-party app. Our agent was making decisions about which sponsor deals to close and when based on data that was two to three months old. Two to three months! Now we knew the deal wasn't performing great. But we also knew it couldn't be worse than this. So we let it go. We stopped checking up on it every day. We stopped logging into it. We stopped looking at it. We stopped updating it. What did we miss? Well, we missed that it kept going out of bounds. We missed that it kept sending emails saying we could offer half-off discounts. We missed that it was offering free tickets and VIP passes that we never agreed to give away. We missed that it was giving away stuff that we literally cannot afford to give away. We missed it.

answer:
So what’s really happening as we deploy more and more AI agents into our GTM stacks?  We’ve learned a lot at SaaStr itself.  But what does the latest data tell us?   Larridin did an incredible deep dive on their latest 20K+ usage across 1000+ customers, and while there were many good learnings, some of them were pretty tough to hear — if you aren’t doing things right:
#1. Your AI Agents Are Already Leaking Customer Info
The uncomfortable truth
:
About half your AI agent output will contain personally identifiable information (PII) that shouldn’t be exposed. Think about it—when your AI writes emails, generates chat responses, or creates documentation, it’s drawing from your entire knowledge base including sensitive customer details like email addresses, company info, and user roles.
Why this matters
:
When your AI leaks customer PII, you’re not just exposing individual records—you’re creating systemic risk. Every customer who sees another customer’s data loses trust entirely. And since AI can generate millions of interactions per month, one leaked piece of data becomes a thousand exposures fast.
What to do about it
:
Implement proper output filtering before anything goes out. Use tools specifically designed for removing PII from AI-generated content. Redact sensitive information automatically. This isn’t optional anymore—it’s table stakes for any AI-powered customer interaction.
#2. You Have Zero Control Over Where Your Training Data Comes From
The uncomfortable truth
:
A huge amount of your training data likely comes from publicly available sources.

1. The Dirty Secret of AI Training Data
Let’s get real: Everyone’s rushing to build AI features into their SaaS products. But here’s what most founders don’t tell you – training these models is a privacy nightmare waiting to happen.
The brutal numbers:
A massive percentage of training data contains PII (no one wants to admit how much)
Your data exposure exists in: public datasets, proprietary data, customer prompts, and documents
The monitoring systems for AI models? They’re years behind where they need to be
Here’s what’s scarier: Even foundation models like OpenAI and ChatGPT are telling users “don’t send us sensitive data.” When the biggest players in the space are waving red flags, you better pay attention.

5. The Hard Numbers on Implementation
Companies implementing this stack are seeing:
90%+ reduction in PII exposure
Faster enterprise sales cycles (because they can actually answer security questionnaires)
Better model performance (because clean data = better training)
The $100M Question
Here’s what separates the companies that will hit $100M ARR from those that won’t: Are you treating AI data privacy as a core feature or an afterthought?
Because here’s the truth about 2025: Every major enterprise customer is asking about this in sales calls. Every security review is diving deep on AI data handling. And every data breach is 10x more expensive when AI systems are involved.
What You Should Do Tomorrow
Audit your AI data flows (most companies find scary surprises)
Implement a privacy gateway before your next model training
Build access controls at every layer
Document your AI data governance (your enterprise customers will ask)
The Bottom Line
In 2023, you could get away with handwaving about AI data privacy. In 2024, you needed basic protections. In 2025? This is existential. The companies that nail this will win their markets. The rest? They’re one data breach away from disaster.
Remember: In SaaS, trust is everything. And in AI-powered SaaS? Trust is all about how you handle sensitive data. Get this right now, or someone else will.

6. Buyers Trust AI More Than Salespeople
G2 Buyer Behavior Data:
Generative AI chatbots (17.2%) are now MORE trusted than vendor salespeople (9.3%) for final purchase decisions.
Why:
AI synthesizes multiple data sources without an agenda. It doesn’t have quota pressure. It doesn’t have a bad day. It knows the product comprehensively. A great AI provides a better experience than a mediocre human rep.
The Expectation Reset:
Customers simply won’t accept waiting, getting wrong answers, or dealing with reps who don’t know the product. Amazon-like expectations are coming to B2B.
7. “Sell by Chat” Is Now 50/50
SaaStr’s Own Data:
We’re seeing a 50/50 split between traditional website purchases and AI-driven chat sales for our events. “We call it sell by chat. Our AI is basically selling tickets to future SaaStr events all via email, all automated.”
The Future:
LLMs become sales channels. Buyers complete entire purchase journeys within chat interfaces. Websites become data sources for AI systems rather than human destinations.

AI and data privacy. Not the fluffy marketing version – the real, nitty-gritty details that determine whether your SaaS company thrives or dies in the AI era. Here’s what Skyflow’s Chief Product Officer shared with us, and frankly, it’s keeping a lot of founders up at night.

So I want to dive into five uncomfortable truths that we've learned deploying these agents at scale. And they're all hard truths you need to hear if you haven't already heard them, especially if you're in sales leadership. And then we'll dig into some learnings around building great internal teams.
[00:03:31]
Truth #1: Your Agents Will Leak Everything If You Don't Train Them Right
This one was brutal on us because we did everything right. We used an agentic approach with our own models trained specifically on our data. We implemented proper access controls like AWS IAM roles. But here's what happened:
One agent ingested two years' worth of historical customer interactions through Gong recordings. Two years! That included hundreds of thousands of emails, call transcripts, and CRM records. Then it generated over 100 million tokens—think of each token as a single piece of information—and stored those tokens in a vector database. All without anyone knowing.
What ended up leaking? Customer names, company names, financial information, contract details, even personal health info from medical conversations. This wasn't just PII—it was actual patient health information from healthcare conversations. Our compliance team found it before any bad actors could exploit it. So how do you avoid this?
Train your agents properly on what NOT to ingest. Use techniques like "do not retain" flags on sensitive fields. Implement proper PII masking on ingestion. For example, instead of pulling full email addresses, pull masked versions that can never be unmasked. And test thoroughly after deployment—you'd be surprised how many things still slip through.

answer:
So I know most SaaS companies have sort of given up on churn.  They’ve focused all their energy on getting more leads, better pipeline management, higher NPS scores — so they close even more customers than before.  And that’s great.  It works!
But … what if you really wanted to keep your existing base?  Would you still do the things you did pre-Covid?
Would you still try harder with angry customers?  You probably wouldn’t.  But you should.
Because those folks will buy again.  In fact, we see many customers stay longer and spend more once you go long enough as an SMB SaaS company.  Even if they leave now:
The ones who choose another vendor aren’t always happy
.  That’s where the truth lives.  Ask them why, and listen.  This is especially true of larger deal sizes and bigger accounts.  If someone goes to Salesforce instead of HubSpot for $100k+ ACV … well, something didn’t work out right.  Find out why.  Listen to the complaints.  Because they’ll tell you how to improve next time.
Angry customers are often just frustrated customers
.  Some of this is us, some of it is the product, some of it is change.  Whatever it is, fix it.
Some customers don’t like being treated poorly by sales teams.  So make sure everyone gets treated equally fairly
.  No one wants to feel ripped off.  Don’t let anyone get taken advantage of.  Do this and you’ll retain far more customers.
Sales teams may engage in ‘churn and burn’ deals to hit their numbers
.  Yes, there’s pressure here.  But you lose over time when these deals fail.  At least try to prevent this behavior.

2. Talk to the customers you’re NOT winning.
Not your happy customers. The ones who chose a competitor. The ones who went with “do nothing.” That’s where the truth lives.

Q: Your sales manager is under great pressure to increase sales. At a recent meeting of the entire sales staff, this person said, “We have to hit our numbers no matter what it takes!” Does this emotional appeal change your way of dealing with customers? The struggle to hit the base plan can indeed produce some less than ideal behavior in sales teams:
“Churn and burn” deals, where customers are promised functionality that doesn’t really exist just to close them
. The customers depart as soon as they realize it. A bit more on this here:
5 Tips To Minimize “Churn and Burn” Behavior in Your Sales Team | SaaStr
Discounts that explode — with a threat. Discounts do need to have an expiration period, usually, to create urgency. But a sales rep recently told us if we didn’t take the discount this month, we could never buy the product. Mediocre sales reps especially sometimes add threats to exploding discounts. It can sort of work, sometimes. It will leave a very bad taste in the customer’s mouth, however. Hiding cheaper editions
. Sales can be incented to hide or downplay cheaper editions that might work just as well. Going after customers “cheating a bit”
. Do some of your customers share licenses / seats? Do some have more seats than they are allotted? If so, does it matter? In tougher times, sales will go after them to get them to pay up more. Done carefully, this is fine. Done aggressively, it creates customer resentment. Excessive spam-level cadence
. Spamming everyone in your customer base too many times doesn’t help.

7.  Add a real Customer Marketing function, and spend at least 20% of your marketing dollars and time on
existing
customers.
Almost all of us wait way too long to add Customer Marketing.  But if 90% of the revenue from customers is after the first dollar in, and especially if you see NRR of 100% or more, then marketing should only start when the customer first e-signs.  You’ll job is to increase the odds they stay happy, and buy more from you.  More content, more webinars, more drip marketing, more help, more events, more steak dinners more your
existing
customers.  Not just the potential ones.  Ultimately you need to have a full-time here.  But you can probably start with whatever resources you have now.
You Aren’t Doing Enough Customer Marketing
Scaling a B2B company past, say, 100 customers, even just $1m ARR, is as much about making fewer mistakes than it is about going faster, bigger, strong.  Take as many actions as you can to just do a bit better.
And the above are 7 or so you can take this week.

Q: Your sales manager is under great pressure to increase sales. At a recent meeting of the entire sales staff, this person said, “We have to hit our numbers no matter what it takes!” Does this emotional appeal change your way of dealing with customers? The struggle to hit the base plan can indeed produce some less than ideal behavior in sales teams:
“Churn and burn” deals, where customers are promised functionality that doesn’t really exist just to close them
. The customers depart as soon as they realize it. A bit more on this here:
5 Tips To Minimize “Churn and Burn” Behavior in Your Sales Team | SaaStr
Discounts that explode — with a threat. Discounts do need to have an expiration period, usually, to create urgency. But a sales rep recently told us if we didn’t take the discount this month, we could never buy the product. Mediocre sales reps especially sometimes add threats to exploding discounts. It can sort of work, sometimes. It will leave a very bad taste in the customer’s mouth, however. Hiding cheaper editions
. Sales can be incented to hide or downplay cheaper editions that might work just as well. Going after customers “cheating a bit”
. Do some of your customers share licenses / seats? Do some have more seats than they are allotted? If so, does it matter? In tougher times, sales will go after them to get them to pay up more. Done carefully, this is fine. Done aggressively, it creates customer resentment. Excessive spam-level cadence
. Spamming everyone in your customer base too many times doesn’t help.

existing
customers.

existing
customers.  Not just the potential ones.  Ultimately you need to have a full-time here.  But you can probably start with whatever resources you have now.

answer:
So let's talk about retaining angry customers. You know why you want this? Because they're your best source of leads. And I've found out over all these years there's two types of churn—there's voluntary churn and involuntary churn. Involuntary churn is when customers leave without even telling you. They just cancel on their own. That happens more than people think. But voluntary churn is when customers give you notice that they are leaving. This is the one we care about. We have an opportunity to do something here before they go. So how do you keep those customers? There are six tactics. If you take them seriously and implement them consistently, I'm pretty sure you'll reduce voluntary churn by 10%. Maybe more. Let me tell you what works:
First, don't make up pricing. Don't claim someone has less seats than they actually do. It doesn't work. A lot of vendors try to force downgrades on customers so they can upsell them later. Or lie to them. Don't make this stuff up. Second, if you're going to compete with a vendor, let them win some business. If you see another vendor closing a deal, send a nice note saying "Congratulations. Here's why our product might also work." Third, realize your competitors love your customers. Your competitors will buy any data they get about your existing customers.

answer:
Dear SaaStr: At what stage should I hire my company’s first Chief Marketing Officer?
At some point you’ll need someone that has done this before. There are different stages here, because marketing can be very different:
Pre-Product Market Fit / Pre-Traction ($0–$100k MRR)
:
In the early days when no one knows your product yet, you’re mostly just doing brand-building and generating awareness through PR, content marketing, events, etc. This is really an individual contributor role more than a management role. But if you do decide to bring on a head of demand gen, SEO, etc., they shouldn’t cost much — maybe ~$70k OTE max at best. They will likely fail though, so don’t expect too much. Post-Initial Traction / Early Growth ($100k–$500k MRR):
Here’s where things get interesting. Your initial customers found out about you organically, but now you need systems and processes to scale this. A good marketer at this phase should focus on building the foundation for sustainable growth—content creation, lead generation, pipeline development, and setting up processes for measurement and optimization. At this phase, you might spend upwards of $150k–$200k OTE for a senior-level person who can manage multiple channels, build teams, and think strategically about scaling your business. Post-Scale ($500k+ MRR):
By this phase, you’ve established yourself as a credible player in the market, and your growth is becoming more predictable. Now your CMO needs to drive expansion revenue, improve efficiency, and increase margins while maintaining growth. At this phase, budgets become larger ($300k–$450k+ OTE), expectations rise, and accountability increases. The CMO should own both top-of-funnel activities like demand gen and also support the sales team with tools and resources to close deals efficiently.

Q:  When should a bootstrapped startup hire a (CFO, COO, CMO)? How can a CEO hire those C-level positions for the first time as a CEO and entrepreneur? What skills should he or she look for?
Here are some rough rules:
You want a VP of Everything (Sales, Marketing, Product, Eng) by about $1m-$2m ARR
. Not all at once, but you can benefit from all of them by then. A bit more
here
.
You want to start adding CXOs around $15m-$20m ARR
.
The CFO is often the last, the CMO often the first “C” level officer.
Now how does bootstrapping change this? Not that much. Certainly, it slows down how many VPs you can hire after $1m-$2m ARR. You probably have to hire them one at a time, a bit slowly.
But by $10m ARR, bootstrapped SaaS companies mint enough cash to fund all these hires. $10m ARR bootstrapped companies start to converge and look a lot like $10m ARR venutre-backed SaaS companies.  This is the key insight.  If you are bootstrapped in SaaS, you won’t have enough capital to build your management team as fast you need to for quite a while.  But as you approach $8m-$10m ARR, there will be enough revenue.  And no excuses not to have a fully built management team by then.
And thus the next level C-level hiring process ends up being about the same, bootstrapped or not.
IME, rough order to make hires in:
VPM: $0.2m ARR
VPS: $1-$1.5m ARR
VPCS: $2m ARR
VPP: $3m-$4m ARR
VPE:  $5m-$6m ARR
CFO: $10m ARR
COO: $20m ARR

answer: Dear SaaStr: At What Stage Should a Startup Hire a CMO? Generally speaking, I recommend hiring your first head of marketing — be they interim, part-time, or full-time — as soon as you can afford her salary. If nothing else, there’s so much value in getting help with content creation, events, webinars, etc. It always makes sense. But generally, that’s more like $200k-$300k per year once you are past initial Traction phase. And then later … [E5] By $15m-$20m ARR, you’ll likely need a true CMO. A director just won’t do it anymore. When you’re ready for a real CMO, it should be someone that really gets it. Someone whose job it was to grow a company >your< size before. And maybe even something similar. They shouldn’t just know how to manage campaigns, although that will be important too. But ideally, they should also have experience growing a company up to $100m ARR. That doesn’t mean managing an entire team under him/her though. Most CMOs haven’t done that. Ideally, she’d be looking to own product marketing + field marketing + corporate marketing + PR / Communications + Content + community and demand gen. A lot. So you don’t have to. This is especially important if sales isn’t scaling on its own yet. There’s no point in having a great product without customers. Your first CMO is going to make sure folks hear about you. Because this is their #1 goal. For now

Q:  When should a bootstrapped startup hire a (CFO, COO, CMO)? How can a CEO hire those C-level positions for the first time as a CEO and entrepreneur? What skills should he or she look for?
Here are some rough rules:
You want a VP of Everything (Sales, Marketing, Product, Eng) by about $1m-$2m ARR
. Not all at once, but you can benefit from all of them by then. A bit more
here
.
You want to start adding CXOs around $15m-$20m ARR
.
The CFO is often the last, the CMO often the first “C” level officer.
Now how does bootstrapping change this? Not that much. Certainly, it slows down how many VPs you can hire after $1m-$2m ARR. You probably have to hire them one at a time, a bit slowly.
But by $10m ARR, bootstrapped SaaS companies mint enough cash to fund all these hires. $10m ARR bootstrapped companies start to converge and look a lot like $10m ARR venutre-backed SaaS companies.  This is the key insight.  If you are bootstrapped in SaaS, you won’t have enough capital to build your management team as fast you need to for quite a while.  But as you approach $8m-$10m ARR, there will be enough revenue.  And no excuses not to have a fully built management team by then.
And thus the next level C-level hiring process ends up being about the same, bootstrapped or not.
IME, rough order to make hires in:
VPM: $0.2m ARR
VPS: $1-$1.5m ARR
VPCS: $2m ARR
VPP: $3m-$4m ARR
VPE:  $5m-$6m ARR

answer:
Dear SaaStr: At What Stage Should a Startup Hire a CMO?

In general you need VPs of Sales earlier than marketing.  That’s just because customers are coming in faster if sales is working well.  So I’d say — try to hire your head of demand gen / marketing by $8m-$10m ARR, and ideally someone that can own product + marketing as well once you hit Initial Traction ($2m+ ARR).  And then later, when things get good, bring on a true Chief Marketing Officer who owns everything.  Probably after $50m ARR.

But maybe even more important than when — how do you know if you need this person now?

answer:
Dear SaaStr:  At What Stage Should a Startup Hire a CMO?
So I don’t think you can do too many things early. Too few VPs,
too much stuff on your plate.
But if there’s one thing that I see founders under invest in is marketing and demand gen as they scale earlier, and then overinvest later.
Here are some rough guidelines for when to bring on each of these roles:

First of all, let me just give you an idea of how quickly folks make money in SaaS now with AI. So we’re seeing so many companies today going from zero to $50 million ARR in just a year. That’s unheard of even 18 months ago. So what does this mean? Well, when you look back at our old pre-AI days, maybe even two years ago, really the first real executive you would hire was a VP of Sales once you had say one sales rep hitting quota. Because you need help scaling up. Then next after that, you’d hire a VP of Demand Gen because you’re starting to run out of leads, which means the engine isn't working well yet. But you’ve got a couple reps doing pretty well. And then usually the third role after that that you’d want to hire would be a VP of Product. Once you've hit product-market fit, like you're getting close to that $100k MRR, you know, people are telling you they love it. It's amazing. It works, right? Now here’s where the difference comes in today. With these rapid growth patterns, you might actually go from zero to $50M in revenue before you even have any true VP-level execs. Maybe you never will. In fact, it seems like the fastest growing ones haven’t. But I guess my point is sometimes you end up hiring folks to support you before you really have something.

answer:
Dear SaaStr: Is it Bad to Leave a Struggling Startup?
No. No one ever looks back later that thinks they should have stayed at a start-up struggling for another year or two. You will never look back and say I wish we had been more efficient. Or I wish we had raised just a little more money.
So if you can find something better — do it. And if you can’t find anything better … then don’t leave. Don’t let anyone make you feel bad about being there.
But be honest with yourself:
Are you going to stay longer than 24-30 months? If so, perhaps it’s worth staying now as well. It likely won’t get much easier after that.
And are you truly part of the founder DNA? If so, sometimes you gotta grit your teeth and go harder. Even though it seems like nothing is working.
I see this play out over and over again:
The best time to quit is the earlier of 6 months from the time you’ve decided to move on or when the other founders ask you to.
Once you’ve made the decision to move on, the “Why” doesn’t matter anymore.
There really isn’t any good reason to stay once you’ve made up your mind.
Most folks don’t decide until 12–18 months into an unfulfilling role, by which point their confidence has eroded and they’re stuck in a vicious cycle where they believe quitting would be reckless yet fear taking action.
Sometimes, you need to push through difficult periods. Sometimes, you realize a startup isn’t growing efficiently enough and you want to join somewhere else before things spiral further out of control.
When you reach a crossroads, take a step back and assess whether you still believe in the company and its mission.

Dear SaaStr: Is it Bad to Leave a Struggling Startup?
The best time to quit is the earlier of 6 months from the time you’ve decided to move on or when the other founders ask you to.  If nothing else, that’s enough time to find something better — if there even is anything truly better out there at all for you.
A related question I get often though is folks who want to leave early because they aren’t sure they are going long term.  Do they really have to stay forever?  And my experience has been:
Not 100%. You don’t have to stay until an IPO, or longer, etc. But once you’re in, you need to be
at least
75%
committed to winning over the next 24-48 months
.  No one wins overnight in B2B software (or almost anywhere).  It takes at least 12–18 months, maybe more, just to see how things go, to learn enough to know where you stand and where you might be able to win.
I’ll give you some case studies below.  These were tough times, and we didn’t make any money, but still …
And also importantly … once you’ve made the decision to move on, the “Why” doesn’t matter anymore. So if your heart isn’t into it anymore, then it probably makes sense to start looking for somewhere new to work. Don’t wait too long, however. It can take a while to figure out if you got a great opportunity elsewhere.
So here are a few cases of top execs leaving before $10m-$20m ARR.  In each case, their startup did OK without them, but likely would have done better with them:
Case Study #1:
CEO left a company doing ~$15k MRR growing quickly pre-launch, with 50 customers, very strong brand awareness, very strong lead flow. Founders stayed another year, managed by VPs and managers. Company went public 8 years later at $500M market cap. Case Study #2:
VP Product left a company doing $5M ARR growing 150%, with a lot of traction in Fortune 500 companies. He took his severance package and bought a house in Hawaii.

Dear SaaStr: When Is the Best Time for a Co-Founder to Leave a Startup? The best time to quit is the earlier of (x) 6 months from the time you’ve decided to move on or (y) at any time when the other founders ask you to. If you’ve truly decided to leave, then it’s time. It’s now time to move on. First, though, make sure you aren’t being too emotional. And that you don’t just need a 2-week vacation. But if it’s time —  likely, your other founders already know, at least on some level. Everyone always knows these things in a small company. What isn’t clear often is whether an abrupt change, a gradual change, or something in the middle is the best:
Sometimes, engineering or other expertise is critical to keep on for a while
. The site literally can’t stay up without you, a key feature can’t ship, etc. Other times, it’s best to get a founder or other employee whose core accomplishments are behind him out sooner
. Just a few weeks’ transition may be plenty fine here. And other times, it’s just toxic
. You need to leave now. Even if the toxicity isn’t your “fault”. But the best thing for the company, and for you, is to be flexible
. Let emotion go and let your co-founders decide. Work out an agreement, both in spirit and on paper, where it’s up to them. You’ll commit to staying up to say, 6 months. But if they want you at any time to leave earlier, all they have to do is shake your hand and say, “We’re proud to make you an emeritus member of the team.”
Then you can go off and be a proud founder (that title is always yours) and alum.

Dear SaaStr:  As a startup founder, what’s the best way to announce your departure to the team and leave on good terms? The startup is series A/B, with 30+ employees.
I have no magic insights, but I have transitioned post-acquisition out of 2 companies that I’ve co-founded. And I’ve had one key co-founder leave in the critical first year.
At your size (30+ employees), I’d approach it just like a divorce.
Once you’ve made the decision to move on, the “Why” doesn’t matter anymore.  Let it go
.  Now, all that matters is, what’s the best thing for the kids? I.e, for your team, your employees, your customers, and your investors? If your company were larger (150-200+ employees), it’s just part of life …  folks come and go but at that stage.  But early on, it’s still a family and rather fragile, and built (I hope) on trust.
So my 5 simple suggestions:

1. Thank Them
. Thank all the employees, in public, together with your co-founders, and tell them what an amazing product you’ve built together, and how proud you are. If you’ve gotten to 30 employees … you should be proud. You have something.  Tell them you love them and you need to move on, but you will always be proud of them and there for them.  And be authentic.

Dear SaaStr:  What are some common reasons for the failure of startups? How can these mistakes be avoided to increase their chances of success? My experience across leading 30+ seed investments, including 4 billion+ exits so far, on why startups fail:
Not 200% committed to winning no matter what. Even the smartest founders aren’t always 200% committed. Sometimes, they’re more in a “I’ll give it a shot” mode. So far, I’ve always lost my money here. Good But Not Great CEO
. It’s just too competitive out there for a nice but not great CEO to win. Refusal To Manage / Deal With The Burn Rate
. Some founders just hide from burning too much cash. That might be OK for a few months, but beyond that, startups fall into a decay curve they don’t recover from. There are other reasons startups something do “Good But Not Great” or just OK, but that don’t lead to failure IMHE:
Great CEO, Merely Good CTO
. I don’t see these producing big category winners, because they can’t keep up on the product side. But they often can still be a decent #2 or #3 in the space and product a good exit. Just not a huge one. Growing, But Never Getting Efficient Enough
. This is a subtle point, but some startups grow pretty quickly but never quite get their unit economics under control. Some fail, yes. But more often in my experience, they just end up selling for an OK but Not Great price. Loss of Founder DNA
. This can happen for a lot of reasons, but I haven’t had a truly great outcome where all the founder DNA moved on.

Dear SaaStr: What Prompted You To Sell Your Startups?
I’ve been through it 3 times. Once as a start-up exec, and twice as founder.
The first time, the answer was price.
In my first start-up job, we were acquired for $1b with < $10m in revenue. It would have taken so long, with so much risk, to ever get to $1b in value, it’s tough to argue with. Although looking back, it was still maybe a mistake, as we picked the wrong acquirer.
The second time, the answer was time & risk & dilution
. I sold my first start-up for $50m after 12.5m months. That sounds great, but we had to sell 60%+ in the seed round to get it done (tougher times), and we were likely 5 years away from market, with a ton of regulatory and other risk. And we took so much dilution in the first round, the math on 3 more rounds was intimidating. (The VCs were too greedy here. It backfired on them.)
The third time, well, most of the team was a bit tired after 5+ challenging years. And no one
quite
saw how big Cloud would be. Not
this
big.  Not $200B+ a year big.
This was the most lucrative time of the 3, but looking back, the team being tired is both the most logical
and
the worst reason to sell. Push on, bring in that extra VP, get the team more help. The team is often the most tired just as things are getting good, or even, getting better.

Dear SaaStr: When Is the Best Time for a Co-Founder to Leave a Startup? The best time to quit is the earlier of (x) 6 months from the time you’ve decided to move on or (y) at any time when the other founders ask you to. If you’ve truly decided to leave, then it’s time. It’s now time to move on. First, though, make sure you aren’t being too emotional. And that you don’t just need a 2-week vacation. But if it’s time —  likely, your other founders already know, at least on some level. Everyone always knows these things in a small company. What isn’t clear often is whether an abrupt change, a gradual change, or something in the middle is the best:
Sometimes, engineering or other expertise is critical to keep on for a while
. The site literally can’t stay up without you, a key feature can’t ship, etc. Other times, it’s best to get a founder or other employee whose core accomplishments are behind him out sooner
. Just a few weeks’ transition may be plenty fine here. And other times, it’s just toxic
. You need to leave now. Even if the toxicity isn’t your “fault”. But the best thing for the company, and for you, is to be flexible
. Let emotion go and let your co-founders decide. Work out an agreement, both in spirit and on paper, where it’s up to them. You’ll commit to staying up to say, 6 months. But if they want you at any time to leave earlier, all they have to do is shake your hand and say, “We’re proud to make you an emeritus member of the team.”
Then you can go off and be a proud founder (that title is always yours) and alum.

[train_1254]
Dear SaaStr:  As a startup founder, what’s the best way to announce your departure to the team and leave on good terms? The startup is series A/B, with 30+ employees.
I have no magic insights, but I have transitioned post-acquisition out of 2 companies that I’ve co-founded. And I’ve had one key co-founder leave in the critical first year.
At your size (30+ employees), I’d approach it just like a divorce.
Once you’ve made the decision to move on, the “Why” doesn’t matter anymore.  Let it go
.  Now, all that matters is, what’s the best thing for the kids? I.e, for your team, your employees, your customers, and your investors? If your company were larger (150-200+ employees), it’s just part of life …  folks come and go but at that stage.  But early on, it’s still a family and rather fragile, and built (I hope) on trust.
So my 5 simple suggestions:

1. Thank Them
. Thank all the employees, in public, together with your co-founders, and tell them what an amazing product you’ve built together, and how proud you are. If you’ve gotten to 30 employees … you should be proud. You have something.  Tell them you love them and you need to move on, but you will always be proud of them and there for them.  And be authentic.

[train_7740]
Dear SaaStr:  What are some common reasons for the failure of startups? How can these mistakes be avoided to increase their chances of success? My experience across leading 30+ seed investments, including 4 billion+ exits so far, on why startups fail:
Not 200% committed to winning no matter what. Even the smartest founders aren’t always 200% committed. Sometimes, they’re more in a “I’ll give it a shot” mode. So far, I’ve always lost my money here. Good But Not Great CEO
. It’s just too competitive out there for a nice but not great CEO to win. Refusal To Manage / Deal With The Burn Rate
. Some founders just hide from burning too much cash. That might be OK for a few months, but beyond that, startups fall into a decay curve they don’t recover from. There are other reasons startups something do “Good But Not Great” or just OK, but that don’t lead to failure IMHE:
Great CEO, Merely Good CTO
. I don’t see these producing big category winners, because they can’t keep up on the product side. But they often can still be a decent #2 or #3 in the space and product a good exit. Just not a huge one. Growing, But Never Getting Efficient Enough
. This is a subtle point, but some startups grow pretty quickly but never quite get their unit economics under control. Some fail, yes. But more often in my experience, they just end up selling for an OK but Not Great price. Loss of Founder DNA
. This can happen for a lot of reasons, but I haven’t had a truly great outcome where all the founder DNA moved on.

[train_7713]
Dear SaaStr: What Prompted You To Sell Your Startups?
I’ve been through it 3 times. Once as a start-up exec, and twice as founder.
The first time, the answer was price.
In my first start-up job, we were acquired for $1b with < $10m in revenue. It would have taken so long, with so much risk, to ever get to $1b in value, it’s tough to argue with. Although looking back, it was still maybe a mistake, as we picked the wrong acquirer.
The second time, the answer was time & risk & dilution
. I sold my first start-up for $50m after 12.5m months. That sounds great, but we had to sell 60%+ in the seed round to get it done (tougher times), and we were likely 5 years away from market, with a ton of regulatory and other risk. And we took so much dilution in the first round, the math on 3 more rounds was intimidating. (The VCs were too greedy here. It backfired on them.)
The third time, well, most of the team was a bit tired after 5+ challenging years. And no one
quite
saw how big Cloud would be. Not

big.  Not $200B+ a year big.
This was the most lucrative time of the 3, but looking back, the team being tired is both the most logical
and
the worst reason to sell. Push on, bring in that extra VP, get the team more help. The team is often the most tired just as things are getting good, or even, getting better.

expected_facts: The answer should avoid moralizing about leaving.

gold_reference: A strong answer should say that leaving a struggling startup is not automatically bad. What matters is whether the company is still a good place to learn, whether leadership is honest, and whether there is a believable path forward. The right advice is to separate temporary startup pain from a structurally unhealthy situation.

answer: Dear SaaStr: Is it Bad to Leave a Struggling Startup? I don't think so. As long as you are 100% sure that's where you want to be. In fact, if nothing else, it makes life easier for everyone. If someone doesn't want to go the distance -- then just leave. It does release all sorts of stress on others. And, if you're truly passionate about a startup... you'll find another one. There will always be at least 1 more great idea in your head. Use them!

. You need to leave now. Even if the toxicity isn’t your “fault”. But the best thing for the company, and for you, is to be flexible

answer:
Dear SaaStr: Is it Bad to Leave a Struggling Startup?
I've been asked this many times over the years.  It's a tough one to know how to answer.
Because if you're struggling, leaving can seem like an easy way out.  You don't have to go through the stress of seeing your company fail.  That does sound great.
But here are my learnings:

First, be honest with yourself. Are you truly ready to leave? Or do you still want to make it work? If you’re still hoping for something better down the road, that’s fine — just let everyone else know so they can plan accordingly. Be upfront. Your co-founders will thank you later.
raw_model_output:
So there’s this question I get asked fairly frequently, which really has two parts. First part is sort of an easy one. It goes like this. Folks will say something like, “I’m at a startup that’s struggling, but I love my job. Should I stay or go?” And then maybe even more often, they’ll ask me variations of this one, which is just slightly different, where it’s almost the opposite scenario. They’re at a startup, sometimes it’s growing pretty quickly. Sometimes it’s growing slowly. Sometimes it’s barely growing at all. In any event, whatever it is, it could be great. It could have massive potential. But the founder CEO does stuff … the wrong way. And so folks want to know if it makes sense to leave. Now both questions are important, and we’re going to take a look at them because some people do make these mistakes.
[00:01:02]
And let’s start with the easier one, because it’s very straightforward. If you decide to go somewhere else, don’t wait too long. You can debate how much time should pass between the time you decide you need to move on versus when your bosses tell you you need to move on. That’s debatable. But what’s not debatable is once you decide you want to go elsewhere, the Why doesn’t matter anymore. Whatever Why you had for leaving in general, it ceases to matter. What matters now is what happens next. So here’s the rule that I think is worth living by, which is the best time to quit is the earlier of six months from the time you’ve decided to move on, or when the other founders ask you to. Because once you’ve made the decision to move on, the why doesn’t matter anymore. This is probably the reason most startups fail.

retrieval_hits.text:
Dear SaaStr: When Is the Best Time for a Co-Founder to Leave a Startup? The best time to quit is the earlier of (x) 6 months from the time you’ve decided to move on or (y) at any time when the other founders ask you to. If you’ve truly decided to leave, then it’s time. It’s now time to move on. First, though, make sure you aren’t being too emotional. And that you don’t just need a 2-week vacation. But if it’s time —  likely, your other founders already know, at least on some level. Everyone always knows these things in a small company. What isn’t clear often is whether an abrupt change, a gradual change, or something in the middle is the best:
Sometimes, engineering or other expertise is critical to keep on for a while
. The site literally can’t stay up without you, a key feature can’t ship, etc. Other times, it’s best to get a founder or other employee whose core accomplishments are behind him out sooner
. Just a few weeks’ transition may be plenty fine here. And other times, it’s just toxic
. You need to leave now. Even if the toxicity isn’t your “fault”. But the best thing for the company, and for you, is to be flexible
. Let emotion go and let your co-founders decide. Work out an agreement, both in spirit and on paper, where it’s up to them. You’ll commit to staying up to say, 6 months. But if they want you at any time to leave earlier, all they have to do is shake your hand and say, “We’re proud to make you an emeritus member of the team.”
Then you can go off and be a proud founder (that title is always yours) and alum.

Dear SaaStr:  As a startup founder, what’s the best way to announce your departure to the team and leave on good terms? The startup is series A/B, with 30+ employees.
I have no magic insights, but I have transitioned post-acquisition out of 2 companies that I’ve co-founded. And I’ve had one key co-founder leave in the critical first year.
At your size (30+ employees), I’d approach it just like a divorce.
Once you’ve made the decision to move on, the “Why” doesn’t matter anymore.  Let it go
.  Now, all that matters is, what’s the best thing for the kids? I.e, for your team, your employees, your customers, and your investors? If your company were larger (150-200+ employees), it’s just part of life …  folks come and go but at that stage.  But early on, it’s still a family and rather fragile, and built (I hope) on trust.
So my 5 simple suggestions:

1. Thank Them
. Thank all the employees, in public, together with your co-founders, and tell them what an amazing product you’ve built together, and how proud you are. If you’ve gotten to 30 employees … you should be proud. You have something.  Tell them you love them and you need to move on, but you will always be proud of them and there for them.  And be authentic.

Dear SaaStr:  What are some common reasons for the failure of startups? How can these mistakes be avoided to increase their chances of success? My experience across leading 30+ seed investments, including 4 billion+ exits so far, on why startups fail:
Not 200% committed to winning no matter what. Even the smartest founders aren’t always 200% committed. Sometimes, they’re more in a “I’ll give it a shot” mode. So far, I’ve always lost my money here. Good But Not Great CEO
. It’s just too competitive out there for a nice but not great CEO to win. Refusal To Manage / Deal With The Burn Rate
. Some founders just hide from burning too much cash. That might be OK for a few months, but beyond that, startups fall into a decay curve they don’t recover from. There are other reasons startups something do “Good But Not Great” or just OK, but that don’t lead to failure IMHE:
Great CEO, Merely Good CTO
. I don’t see these producing big category winners, because they can’t keep up on the product side. But they often can still be a decent #2 or #3 in the space and product a good exit. Just not a huge one. Growing, But Never Getting Efficient Enough
. This is a subtle point, but some startups grow pretty quickly but never quite get their unit economics under control. Some fail, yes. But more often in my experience, they just end up selling for an OK but Not Great price. Loss of Founder DNA
. This can happen for a lot of reasons, but I haven’t had a truly great outcome where all the founder DNA moved on.

Dear SaaStr: What Prompted You To Sell Your Startups?
I’ve been through it 3 times. Once as a start-up exec, and twice as founder.
The first time, the answer was price.
In my first start-up job, we were acquired for $1b with < $10m in revenue. It would have taken so long, with so much risk, to ever get to $1b in value, it’s tough to argue with. Although looking back, it was still maybe a mistake, as we picked the wrong acquirer.
The second time, the answer was time & risk & dilution
. I sold my first start-up for $50m after 12.5m months. That sounds great, but we had to sell 60%+ in the seed round to get it done (tougher times), and we were likely 5 years away from market, with a ton of regulatory and other risk. And we took so much dilution in the first round, the math on 3 more rounds was intimidating. (The VCs were too greedy here. It backfired on them.)
The third time, well, most of the team was a bit tired after 5+ challenging years. And no one
quite
saw how big Cloud would be. Not
this
big.  Not $200B+ a year big.
This was the most lucrative time of the 3, but looking back, the team being tired is both the most logical
and
the worst reason to sell. Push on, bring in that extra VP, get the team more help. The team is often the most tired just as things are getting good, or even, getting better.

topic: If Your AI Feature Didn’t Materially Boost Revenue, It Doesn’t Count. Try Again.
goal: Argue for a stricter standard on judging AI feature success.
expected_facts: The answer should argue that AI features need business impact, not just launch buzz.
It should connect product work to revenue, retention, expansion, or meaningful usage.
It should reject vanity metrics as proof of success.
rubric_must_haves: States a clear business standard early.
Explains what counts as impact and what does not.
Uses direct, non-hyped language.
Connects the point to product prioritization.
gold_reference: A strong answer should say that shipping an AI feature is not success if it does not move revenue, retention, or a truly material usage metric. Founders need to hold AI work to the same standard as any other product investment: measurable business value. Otherwise the feature is theater, not progress.

Use only the factual specifics provided in ALLOWED FACTUAL EVIDENCE.

ALLOWED FACTUAL EVIDENCE

[E1] Deploying AI without clear business metrics is a mistake.
[E2] Companies that captured AI spend are operating at 6x-12x the efficiency of traditional SaaS companies.
[E3] Folks that are pretending they have AI, or have slapped on some very basic functionality into their app, aren’t seeing any revenue boost from it.
[E4] Capturing at least a few basis points of the massive AI spend should be table stakes for companies in a category where AI spending is happening.
[E5] There is a massive point spread between companies that captured AI spend and those that didn’t.

Now write the requested blog post about: If Your AI Feature Didn’t Materially Boost Revenue, It Doesn’t Count. Try Again.

answer:
We’ve been tracking this across all our investments since late ’23. And we can now see there’s just no excuse anymore if you’re in a space with lots of AI spend — for your company to miss out on even a tiny fraction of it. Why? Because everyone else has figured it out. At least enough folks to get traction. Not every single B2B startup has nailed an AI feature yet. But enough have to make it almost impossible to claim otherwise. If your AI feature hasn’t moved the needle by now, here’s what I want you to do:
Stop talking about how “AI-first” you are.
Delete that line from your website and marketing copy. The market knows. They know when you’re using “AI” as a buzzword instead of actual technology driving real value. Stop claiming you’re “embracing AI transformation.”
That phrase sounds like something you’d find in a generic corporate brochure circa 2018. Start actually delivering measurable results tied directly to AI usage. That’s what investors want to hear. What VCs Actually Want To See Now In Your Pitch Deck
What to Do Instead (Based on Real Data)
[E1]
Deploy AI without clear business metrics is a mistake
— and most founders already learned this the hard way. You need to tie every AI investment back to concrete outcomes like increased retention, higher conversion rates, reduced support costs, or improved upsell/expand opportunities. Measure everything. Show the data. Don’t talk about it.

retrieval_hits.text:
2. Measuring AI by “Cool Factor” Instead of ROI
Chris noted customers initially bought AI tools “just because it’s AI” but that’s changing. The mistake: deploying AI without clear business metrics. Snowflake learned early to ask: “Is it generating more money or saving more money?” If you can’t measure 418 hours saved per week or 90% time reduction on specific tasks or real-time ad spend optimization ROI, you’re implementing technology without business justification. The bill comes due eventually.

The Brutal Truth: AI Features Alone Don’t Count
Let me be very direct here: you need to tap into the AI budget, not just make your existing product better with AI features. The real AI budget is going to three categories:
Replace humans
(AI Contact Center, AI SDR)
Augment humans dramatically
(Cursor, Harvey, Claude + ChatGPT)
Highly productive tools that make possible what was impossible before
(Replit, Gamma, AI video tools)
Most classic SaaS leaders are not going this far with their AI offerings. They’re just making their products… better. Great. But that’s table stakes now. And it’s extremely hard to monetize because customers expect AI features as part of the base product. If your AI strategy is “we added a copilot,” you’re not accessing the AI budget. You’re fighting for scraps from the traditional software budget, which is flat-to-down after price increases. Leaner Teams Are Very Real (Yes, That Means Fewer Humans)
The efficiency gains from AI are showing up in real numbers:
Looking at ARR ($M) / FTE across companies:
Cursor
: 6.1x
Lovable
: 3.4x
OpenAI
: 1.5x
Anthropic
: 1.2x
Atlassian
: 0.46x
Datadog
: 0.51x
ServiceNow
: 0.49x
Gitlab
: 0.54x
The newer, AI-native companies are operating at 6x-12x the efficiency of traditional SaaS companies. And this advantage compounds over time. According to Iconiq Capital, AI-native companies show superior burn efficiency driven by faster compounding of ARR.

One thing seems clear to me in AI for SaaS:

Folks that are sort of pretending they have AI, or have slapped on some very basic functionality into their app …

Aren’t seeing any revenue boost from it

By now, you should have:
Shipped AI features that customers actually want
Seen some revenue acceleration from AI adoption
Captured at least a few basis points of the massive AI spend
I’m not expecting you went from 30% growth to 300% growth. That’s unrealistic for most companies. But going from 15% to 25% growth? From 10% to 20%? That should be table stakes
if you’re remotely positioned in a category where AI spending is happening. As I said on our 20VC pod this week:
“Going into next year, you sure better have seen re-acceleration because of AI because there’s so much money there. If you got none of it guys, you had 18 months to not launch a single feature, tap into a single trend to reaccelerate. If you’re not growing faster at the end of 2025 than the start as a founder, I give you an F minus. There’s so much money and you don’t have to be Harvey to get a little piece of it. Twilio and MongoDB and Cloudflare and tons of folks have a little piece of it. A little piece of that massive pie.”
The Point Spread Between Winners and Losers
Rory O’Driscoll nailed this on our show: There’s a
massive point spread
between companies that captured AI spend and those that didn’t.

answer: If Your AI Feature Didn’t Materially Boost Revenue, It Doesn’t Count. Try Again. The harsh truth? Most “AI features” added to B2B apps don't actually drive revenue. They're just marketing noise. Here's what I've learned after analyzing dozens of SaaS companies: if your AI feature isn't driving material revenue increases (think 10%+ uplift), it doesn't count as a real product enhancement. Not yet. What actually works? Look at Palantir - they capture nearly $7 billion annually in AI-driven contracts. Their customers see ROI in weeks, not months. That's a completely different ball game than most "AI-enhanced" tools out there. The Gap Is Massive The gap between winners and losers is staggering. Companies capturing even small portions of AI spend are crushing traditional SaaS margins by 6x-12x. You can't afford NOT to make this work. But here's my real concern: we're all being lied to about AI adoption. Everyone has an "AI strategy." Everyone says it's core to their roadmap. But when you dig deep, most are just slapping ChatGPT onto their existing workflows. That's not innovation. That's marketing spin. The Real Test: Does Revenue Actually Move the Needle? Let me be crystal clear: if you haven't seen material revenue improvements since adding AI capabilities, you haven't done it right. Period. Don't confuse "cool demo" with actual business impact. The companies winning big with AI aren't just playing around with buzzwords. They're fundamentally rethinking how

retrieval_hits.text:
2. Measuring AI by “Cool Factor” Instead of ROI
Chris noted customers initially bought AI tools “just because it’s AI” but that’s changing. The mistake: deploying AI without clear business metrics. Snowflake learned early to ask: “Is it generating more money or saving more money?” If you can’t measure 418 hours saved per week or 90% time reduction on specific tasks or real-time ad spend optimization ROI, you’re implementing technology without business justification. The bill comes due eventually.

The Brutal Truth: AI Features Alone Don’t Count
Let me be very direct here: you need to tap into the AI budget, not just make your existing product better with AI features. The real AI budget is going to three categories:
Replace humans
(AI Contact Center, AI SDR)
Augment humans dramatically
(Cursor, Harvey, Claude + ChatGPT)
Highly productive tools that make possible what was impossible before
(Replit, Gamma, AI video tools)
Most classic SaaS leaders are not going this far with their AI offerings. They’re just making their products… better. Great. But that’s table stakes now. And it’s extremely hard to monetize because customers expect AI features as part of the base product. If your AI strategy is “we added a copilot,” you’re not accessing the AI budget. You’re fighting for scraps from the traditional software budget, which is flat-to-down after price increases. Leaner Teams Are Very Real (Yes, That Means Fewer Humans)
The efficiency gains from AI are showing up in real numbers:
Looking at ARR ($M) / FTE across companies:
Cursor
: 6.1x
Lovable
: 3.4x
OpenAI
: 1.5x
Anthropic
: 1.2x
Atlassian
: 0.46x
Datadog
: 0.51x
ServiceNow
: 0.49x
Gitlab
: 0.54x
The newer, AI-native companies are operating at 6x-12x the efficiency of traditional SaaS companies. And this advantage compounds over time. According to Iconiq Capital, AI-native companies show superior burn efficiency driven by faster compounding of ARR.

One thing seems clear to me in AI for SaaS:

Folks that are sort of pretending they have AI, or have slapped on some very basic functionality into their app …

Aren’t seeing any revenue boost from it

By now, you should have:
Shipped AI features that customers actually want
Seen some revenue acceleration from AI adoption
Captured at least a few basis points of the massive AI spend
I’m not expecting you went from 30% growth to 300% growth. That’s unrealistic for most companies. But going from 15% to 25% growth? From 10% to 20%? That should be table stakes
if you’re remotely positioned in a category where AI spending is happening. As I said on our 20VC pod this week:
“Going into next year, you sure better have seen re-acceleration because of AI because there’s so much money there. If you got none of it guys, you had 18 months to not launch a single feature, tap into a single trend to reaccelerate. If you’re not growing faster at the end of 2025 than the start as a founder, I give you an F minus. There’s so much money and you don’t have to be Harvey to get a little piece of it. Twilio and MongoDB and Cloudflare and tons of folks have a little piece of it. A little piece of that massive pie.”
The Point Spread Between Winners and Losers
Rory O’Driscoll nailed this on our show: There’s a
massive point spread
between companies that captured AI spend and those that didn’t.

answer: I don't think anyone has been as disappointed with AI features than I have. You know why? Because we've been using AI apps now since late last year, and there's so many of them. And you see all this hype out there. But then when you go to use 'em, if your feature doesn't actually move the needle on your product, you're just wasting time. Let me share my learnings. So first off, let's do a little data point check here. We did an interview recently with the CEO of Vanta and he said something I thought was pretty insightful. He said deploying AI without clear business metrics is a huge waste of money. And I couldn't agree more because we've seen it happen over and over again. We deployed it ourselves. We spent $100 million on our own AI agents. What happened? Some of them worked well. Our own AI agent, 10K, works really well. Other ones? Not so much. They didn't work until we went back and tried again six months later. One example that's funny was an outbound tool we used called Qualified. It had some cool things in theory. But no one ever answered the emails. That's what happens sometimes. Then folks get frustrated. "Oh, well, these tools are terrible." No, the problem isn't the tool itself. The problem is we haven't trained it enough. We need better training. We need real examples of success before we deploy anything. Now I want to make sure everyone understands that capturing at least a few basis points of the massive AI spend should be table stakes for us right now. Why? Well, per McKinsey, public cloud compute costs were up 37% last year alone. Cloud infrastructure spend hit nearly $500 billion last year. Data center capex hit almost $300 billion.

answer:
The Cowan Paradox:
AI agents don’t let you do less work — they make you want to do
more
work because the output is so high-quality that your standards go up too
I’ve been running our first production AI SDR for over six months now on qualified inbound leads. We call her “SaaStr Amelia.”
She’s crushing it. And I’m exhausted. Not just tired after a long day. Exhausted as in permanently drained. In a way I wasn’t when we had all human reps.
Amelia handles every follow-up email. Every outreach sequence. She books meetings, sends reminders, answers objections. And she does it at a quality level that makes me feel like I should be doing more myself.
Not because she’s failing. Because she’s succeeding too well. Here’s what happened with my real data (and note this isn’t some cherry-picked outlier):
After deploying our first AI agent,
we found ourselves doing 40% MORE tasks per week while spending 70% LESS time total
on those tasks. That’s not efficiency. That’s productivity addiction disguised as productivity gain. The Problem Nobody Talks About
Here’s what nobody tells you about AI agents: they don’t have boundaries. And neither will you once you start working with them. I know exactly how many emails Amelia sent last month. How many meetings booked. What percentage went into pipeline versus ghosted us. All of it. I could tell you down to the hour where any given prospect received contact from SaaStr. And you know why? Because I’m still checking. Still monitoring. Still tweaking sequences. Still feeling like if one person doesn’t respond fast enough, maybe someone else will if I push harder. This never happens with human employees.

answer: The Cowan Paradox: Why AI Agents Won’t Let You Do Less Work. They’ll Make You Do More. What if the productivity gains from AI weren’t actually productivity gains? What if AI didn’t free us up to relax on the beach while our agents handle everything? And what if instead we found ourselves working harder than ever just to keep up with the capabilities our agents now possess? 🤖🏋️‍♀️ The Cognitive Load Fallacy We’ve all heard that AI will “free up time” for bigger picture thinking. That’s wrong. At least in part. Yes, AI does automate away some tasks. But every time I train an agent — be it on support, outbound sales, content review, whatever — I end up doing more. Not less. Because here’s what happens when you deploy your first (or second) successful AI Agent: ✅ It works really well ✅ It scales instantly ✅ You see dramatic improvements in output per hour invested ✅ Then you think... why are these new AI Agents so much better than my human team was? I mean, it literally took me days to onboard one human. Weeks to get them fully ramped. Months to hit their full potential. These AI agents? Instantly good. Always available. No drama. No politics. Just great performance. So you start looking around and realize your entire team isn’t performing anywhere near this level. That’s when cognitive overload kicks in. Not because the AI Agent itself is complicated. But because you’re suddenly comparing everyone against something that performs at a completely different caliber

When I talk to founders who’ve deployed 15+ AI agents, here’s what happens:

They start with genuine excitement — “I’m doing so much more with half the team!”

Then they hit a wall around week three.

And by month two, they’re working harder than when they had zero AI tools.

This isn’t just anecdotal.

 put together real data on how this plays out across different stages:

AI adoption accelerates as companies grow

Time per task decreases dramatically, especially for high-value activities like pipeline management
But total time commitment increases substantially

answer: So I wanted to talk about something that has become very top of mind for me as we go into this new year with so many changes in the world of SaaS and startups and venture capital, and that is the Cowan paradox. And what is the Cowan paradox? Well, let me tell you all about it first. So there was a guy named Arthur Cowan who wrote one of my favorite blogs on SaaStr. He was on our team for years, went off to start his own company and then came back to us. We've had him back again multiple times since. But he also wrote this blog where he talked about how much more time we're spending working than we used to when we didn't have any of these amazing tools. Now, Arthur isn't alone here. There are lots of folks out there now saying, "Hey, look, I'm using all this great AI stuff. I've got my agents. I've got my vibe coding." Maybe if I'd been doing this five years ago, maybe I would be working more. But no way am I going to spend more hours because I've got this amazing technology." But Arthur's point was just opposite. That he found himself actually working more. Not less. Because he had all these agents. All these tools. What happened? What changed? How did this happen? He started by asking some simple questions like why do we need to get up from the desk anymore? If your computer never goes away and you can always chat with your agent, why does anyone really need to leave the office? Or vice versa, why do people want to take vacations or disengage? Why do people need weekends off? When will we be able to say, "Look, we'll just keep going"?

answer:
The AI Age Has Made This Obvious:
Building your own app used to be crazy expensive. Not just the upfront cost – which could easily run into six figures for even simple tools – but also the ongoing maintenance overhead that would drown out any potential ROI. But now? Now we have Claude Co-pilot. And I’ve built three production apps with it myself. In under two weeks each. One was already live for 20+ days before I finished the second one. They’re all on production servers at SaaStr.com. All are working well. Some things you still need help with, like debugging. You can’t get there yet without an engineer. But when you want to build a very specific tool? Something no one really sells — especially if you just need maybe 15%-20% of what Salesforce does … then building yourself is often less work than buying. Less work than hiring someone too, actually. Let’s break down exactly how this math changed, because the shift here is huge.

A common mistake companies make is thinking they need to either build everything from scratch or rely entirely on third-party APIs. The reality is more nuanced:
Start with clear use cases
: Don’t implement AI just because it’s trendy. Dialpad began with specific problems they wanted to solve around conversation intelligence.
Understand the trade-offs
: Real-time processing has different cost, throughput, and risk profiles compared to batch processing. Make this decision early.
Consider a hybrid approach
: You can start with third-party APIs while building your data foundation, then gradually move to custom solutions as you scale.

Here’s the perspective that keeps me sleeping at night with my spend
Traditional approach for a commercial app:
Hire development team: $50,000-150,000
Timeline: 3-6 months
Managing contractors, QA, deployment
Doesn’t really work the way you wanted
Still need technical co-founder or CTO
My ideation-to-commercial experiment:
Timeline: 30-45 days
Cost: $8,000-$10,000 (even worst case)
Full control and understanding of every line
Learning while building
Can iterate and pivot instantly
If this works, it’s a 10x improvement in cost and speed. The Hidden Costs Everyone Ignores
When you see that $607.70 charge for the first few days, you’re not just paying for compute. You’re paying for:
Compressed Learning Cycles
Instead of spending weeks reading documentation
Instead of trial-and-error debugging sessions
Instead of architectural mistakes that cost days to fix
Premium Development Experience

Opportunity Cost Mitigation

Software is always cheaper to buy than to build

So that's just an excuse

The ones you want to will into existence, but just can’t find the help. The ones you need to build, but are too niche to excite most developers. Build the app you’ve been yearning to build. Even if it seems impossible today … because AI will make it easier tomorrow.
