retrieval_hits.text:
1. The Build vs. Buy Decision Isn’t Binary
A common mistake companies make is thinking they need to either build everything from scratch or rely entirely on third-party APIs. The reality is more nuanced:
Start with clear use cases
: Don’t implement AI just because it’s trendy. Dialpad began with specific problems they wanted to solve around conversation intelligence.
Understand the trade-offs
: Real-time processing has different cost, throughput, and risk profiles compared to batch processing. Make this decision early.
Consider a hybrid approach
: You can start with third-party APIs while building your data foundation, then gradually move to custom solutions as you scale.

The Future May Not Be Here, But If Not, It’s Close
Here’s the perspective that keeps me sleeping at night with my spend
Traditional approach for a commercial app:
Hire development team: $50,000-150,000
Timeline: 3-6 months
Managing contractors, QA, deployment
Doesn’t really work the way you wanted
Still need technical co-founder or CTO
My ideation-to-commercial experiment:
Timeline: 30-45 days
Cost: $8,000-$10,000 (even worst case)
Full control and understanding of every line
Learning while building
Can iterate and pivot instantly
If this works, it’s a 10x improvement in cost and speed. The Hidden Costs Everyone Ignores
When you see that $607.70 charge for the first few days, you’re not just paying for compute. You’re paying for:
Compressed Learning Cycles
Instead of spending weeks reading documentation
Instead of trial-and-error debugging sessions
Instead of architectural mistakes that cost days to fix
Premium Development Experience
Instant code reviews and suggestions
Architecture guidance from a AI
Debugging partner that never gets tired
Opportunity Cost Mitigation
Shipping in hours instead of days
Getting to market faster — possibly. Possibly. Learning while building instead of building while learning
The Scenarios You Should Budget For
Based on my experience and others I’ve talked to, there are a lot of play apps you can build for the base $20-$25 a month. But you can’t go that far.

Software is always cheaper to buy than to build

So that's just an excuse

So I’ve spent over 200 hours vibe coding the last 100 or so days. And I really don’t have a spare 200 hours. Why? One reason was to learn. But not really. The real reason was to build things I needed to build, I wanted to build, that … I just couldn’t get built otherwise. One app that I’d been waiting 10 years to build. Build those ones. The ones you want to will into existence, but just can’t find the help. The ones you need to build, but are too niche to excite most developers. Build the app you’ve been yearning to build. That’s what will push you through the learning curve, the screenshots, the iterates, the 100s of releases, the rough patches, the regressions, and more.

answer:
The rise of "n=1" apps—custom software built by individuals for their own needs—is transforming how we think about technology adoption. These aren’t just prototypes anymore; they’re production-ready tools that are fundamentally changing our relationship with software. And the data shows this trend isn’t slowing down—it’s accelerating. Let's explore what makes these n=1 apps so powerful, why they're becoming increasingly popular, and what implications this shift has for both individual users and businesses alike. What Are We Talking About Here? When I say "n=1 app," I'm talking about custom-built software designed specifically for one person or organization. This could be anything from internal operational tools at SaaStr like our AI-powered content review system, to personal productivity assistants, or even simple utilities you use every day without realizing it was built by someone else. Think of them as bespoke solutions that solve very specific problems that off-the-shelf software either can't address or forces you into awkward workarounds for. Why Custom-Built Apps Are Suddenly Cool Again
Custom-built applications have been around since the dawn of software, but there's something different happening now. In the old days, building your own software meant hiring a team of developers, setting up servers, managing databases, and dealing with all the complexity most people want to avoid when trying new products. That barrier was significant enough that even though everyone had ideas for better ways to do things, actually turning those ideas into working software required serious resources. Today, that equation changed dramatically.

So Cloudflare is that quiet Cloud leader that just keeps … killing it.  We last checked in on them
at $500m in ARR, growing 50%
.
Today, they are at just about $1B in ARR … and growing even faster at 54% year-over-year than they were at $500m in ARR!  Wow.
And while everyone has taken a hit in public market valuations, Cloudflare has outperformed.  Its stock roared up 27% after its last earnings release.
Today is the Best of Times for Cloudflare.  No downturn, no slow down.  Even with some sales cycles indeed getting a bit more challenging, especially for deals in the $500k-$1m range.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  $100k+ Customers are Now 50% of Revenue — At $1B in ARR
.  Cloudflare has marched upmarket, but slowly for a product still with a free base.  Its $100k+ customers are now the fastest growing segment, and more than half its revenue is from these bigger customers.  Still, its big customers are barely 1% of its customer base of 151,000.

So B2B SaaS has been up and down but security hasn’t missed a beat. Cloudflare has been one of biggest beneficiaries: •$1.7B+ ARR •28% growth (!) •15% non-GAAP profit •39 Billion market cap 👉 Cloudflare is what 20x ARR looks like at scale. 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. 221,000 Total Paying Customers, But 65% of Revenue From 3,200 Large Customers This is what you should see when a “long tail” engine is really working at scale. 100k+ paying customers, but in the end, at scale your largest customers are likely making up 50%+ of your revenue. Don’t neglect the small ones. They grow up into big ones! #2. $400,000 in Revenue Per Employee Cloudflare grew from $300k in revenue per employee at $1B ARR to $400k at $1.5B ARR or so and that seems to be its target to balance growth and efficiency. #3. 50% of Revenue Outside the U.S. Our weekly reminder to Go Global as early as you can! #4. Self-Serve for Customers Of All Sizes — Not Just Small Ones Cloudflare is committed to building a self-serve product that enterprises can try and buy on their own if they choose. It can be done! 🙂 #5. NRR Has Come Down a Bit, But Still Strong at 110%. Clouldflare’s growth remains top tier, but it has come down a bit, and a dip in NRR is one of the reasons. 110% is still world-class. But it’s down from 115% a year ago. That makes net new ARR growth just that much harder than before.

So times are tougher for some, but for the most part, not in leaders in Cloud security.  Cloudflare is a great example.
While it saw some slowdown last year, it’s now accelerating again with 2 record quarters of new bookings in a row.
At ~ $1.5 Billion in ARR, it’s still growing 32% and it’s gotten pretty darn efficient, with 14% free cash flow margins now.
And the markets really like Cloudflare.  Really, really like it.  It’s trading at a stunning $36 Billion market cap, or 24x ARR!
The key?  They are seeing no slowdown at all in revenue growth from $100k+ customers.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  $100k+ Customers Are Key To Growth at Scale.  Revenue There Growing a Stunning 64% (!).
Cloudflare is getting more and more enterprise, but bear in mind that’s at $1.5 Billion in ARR.  It hasn’t left its free and smaller customers behind.  But the big ones are growing fast faster by revenue at scale.  They’ve also now crossed 2,750 $100k+ customers and 100 $1m+ customers.
#2.   3,063 Employees — So About $400,000 in Revenue Per Employee
This is the age of New Efficiency.  Public SaaS and Cloud companies now average $300,000 in revenue per employee, and many of the most efficient leaders are at $400,000 or higher.  Add Cloudflare to that club.

So Cloud and SaaS have had a bit of a rollercoaster the past 4 years, from the boom times of 2020-2021, to the tougher times overall of 2023, to the AI boom of 2024+.  But one thing has done well through all of it: security.  We always need it, and the threats keep coming.
And Cloudflare has been one of the biggest beneficiaries.  It just keeps on going:
$1.7B+ ARR
28% growth (!)
15% non-GAAP operating profit, and 11% free-cash flow margins … and ..
a $39 Billion market cap (!!), up 45% in past 12 months (!!!)
Cloudflare is what 20x ARR looks like at scale, post-IPO.  Top-tier growth, cash-flow positive, and very durable revenue.  The last point is key.  Wall Street wants revenue that is durable.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  221,000 Total Paying Customers, But 65% of Revenue From 3,200 Large Customers
This is what you should see when a “long tail” engine is just working at scale.  100k+ paying customers, maybe even 1m+ free, but in the end, at scale your largest customers are likely making up 50%+ of your revenue.  Just don’t neglect the small ones.  They grow up into big ones!
#2.  $400,000 in Revenue Per Employee
Cloudflare grew from $300k in revenue per employee at $1B ARR to $400k at $1.5B ARR or so and that seems to be its target to balance growth and efficiency.
#3.  50% of Revenue Outside the U.S.
Our reminder to Go Global as early as you can.

at $500m in ARR, growing 50%
.

#1.  $100k+ Customers are Now 50% of Revenue — At $1B in ARR
.  Cloudflare has marched upmarket, but slowly for a product still with a free base.  Its $100k+ customers are now the fastest growing segment, and more than half its revenue is from these bigger customers.  Still, its big customers are barely 1% of its customer base of 151,000.

[train_12125]
So B2B SaaS has been up and down but security hasn’t missed a beat. Cloudflare has been one of biggest beneficiaries: •$1.7B+ ARR •28% growth (!) •15% non-GAAP profit •39 Billion market cap 👉 Cloudflare is what 20x ARR looks like at scale. 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. 221,000 Total Paying Customers, But 65% of Revenue From 3,200 Large Customers This is what you should see when a “long tail” engine is really working at scale. 100k+ paying customers, but in the end, at scale your largest customers are likely making up 50%+ of your revenue. Don’t neglect the small ones. They grow up into big ones! #2. $400,000 in Revenue Per Employee Cloudflare grew from $300k in revenue per employee at $1B ARR to $400k at $1.5B ARR or so and that seems to be its target to balance growth and efficiency. #3. 50% of Revenue Outside the U.S. Our weekly reminder to Go Global as early as you can! #4. Clouldflare’s growth remains top tier, but it has come down a bit, and a dip in NRR is one of the reasons. 110% is still world-class. But it’s down from 115% a year ago. That makes net new ARR growth just that much harder than before.

[train_7696]
So times are tougher for some, but for the most part, not in leaders in Cloud security.  Cloudflare is a great example.
While it saw some slowdown last year, it’s now accelerating again with 2 record quarters of new bookings in a row.
At ~ $1.5 Billion in ARR, it’s still growing 32% and it’s gotten pretty darn efficient, with 14% free cash flow margins now.
And the markets really like Cloudflare.  Really, really like it.  It’s trading at a stunning $36 Billion market cap, or 24x ARR!
The key?  They are seeing no slowdown at all in revenue growth from $100k+ customers.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  $100k+ Customers Are Key To Growth at Scale.  Revenue There Growing a Stunning 64% (!).

#2.   3,063 Employees — So About $400,000 in Revenue Per Employee

$1.7B+ ARR
28% growth (!)
15% non-GAAP operating profit, and 11% free-cash flow margins … and ..
a $39 Billion market cap (!!), up 45% in past 12 months (!!!)

5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  221,000 Total Paying Customers, But 65% of Revenue From 3,200 Large Customers
This is what you should see when a “long tail” engine is just working at scale.  100k+ paying customers, maybe even 1m+ free, but in the end, at scale your largest customers are likely making up 50%+ of your revenue.  Just don’t neglect the small ones.  They grow up into big ones!
#2.  $400,000 in Revenue Per Employee
Cloudflare grew from $300k in revenue per employee at $1B ARR to $400k at $1.5B ARR or so and that seems to be its target to balance growth and efficiency.
#3.  50% of Revenue Outside the U.S.
Our reminder to Go Global as early as you can.

#2.  $400,000 in Revenue Per Employee
Cloudflare grew from $300k in revenue per employee at $1B ARR to $400k at $1.5B ARR or so and that seems to be its target to balance growth and efficiency.

Our reminder to Go Global as early as you can.

answer:
Cloudflare is one of those companies that never seems to get any easier. But for some reason, they just keep on firing.
They're now approaching $2 Billion in ARR -- up from $1 billion just a little while ago!  And importantly, unlike most public SaaS companies today... they are still growing a stunning 28%.  They've also crossed 220,000 total paid customers (up from 180,000), so we can look at this as a true SMB leader too, with 10x more customers than ZoomInfo / Demandbase.
And yet even with all these incredible metrics, Wall Street doesn't totally love them. Their P/E multiple is only around 20-25x ARR.  Now I'm no expert here, but 20-25x sounds pretty good right there to me!
Why? Because they are actually executing at an elite level.  At scale.
Let's break down what makes Cloudflare special — because founders should study this company if you want to understand how to build something truly durable.

Number One:
$1.7B In ARR Growing 28%, With 30% Non-GAAP Profitability
This is where the magic happens. Cloudflare hit $1.7B ARR growing 28%, with non-GAAP operating margins hitting 29%.
The math here tells the entire story. If you're building a $500M ARR business growing 40%, your net new ARR each quarter is $150M. To get to $1B ARR, you need eight quarters of consistent execution at that rate. The problem? By quarter four or five, growth starts decelerating. You're probably doing 35%, then 33%, maybe 31% when you finally hit the number.
That's why Cloudflare's 28% at $1.7B is genuinely impressive. They're maintaining high-growth velocity at massive scale.
For context, HubSpot got to $800M ARR growing roughly 48% before slowing meaningfully.

retrieval_query: While Most B2B Companies Are Decelerating, Cloudflare Just Had Its Best Quarter Since 2021. 10 Numbers That Explain Why

retrieval_hits.text:
So Cloudflare is that quiet Cloud leader that just keeps … killing it.  We last checked in on them
at $500m in ARR, growing 50%
.
Today, they are at just about $1B in ARR … and growing even faster at 54% year-over-year than they were at $500m in ARR!  Wow.
And while everyone has taken a hit in public market valuations, Cloudflare has outperformed.  Its stock roared up 27% after its last earnings release.
Today is the Best of Times for Cloudflare.  No downturn, no slow down.  Even with some sales cycles indeed getting a bit more challenging, especially for deals in the $500k-$1m range.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  $100k+ Customers are Now 50% of Revenue — At $1B in ARR
.  Cloudflare has marched upmarket, but slowly for a product still with a free base.  Its $100k+ customers are now the fastest growing segment, and more than half its revenue is from these bigger customers.  Still, its big customers are barely 1% of its customer base of 151,000.

So B2B SaaS has been up and down but security hasn’t missed a beat. Cloudflare has been one of biggest beneficiaries: •$1.7B+ ARR •28% growth (!) •15% non-GAAP profit •39 Billion market cap 👉 Cloudflare is what 20x ARR looks like at scale. 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. 221,000 Total Paying Customers, But 65% of Revenue From 3,200 Large Customers This is what you should see when a “long tail” engine is really working at scale. 100k+ paying customers, but in the end, at scale your largest customers are likely making up 50%+ of your revenue. Don’t neglect the small ones. They grow up into big ones! #2. $400,000 in Revenue Per Employee Cloudflare grew from $300k in revenue per employee at $1B ARR to $400k at $1.5B ARR or so and that seems to be its target to balance growth and efficiency. #3. 50% of Revenue Outside the U.S. Our weekly reminder to Go Global as early as you can! #4. Self-Serve for Customers Of All Sizes — Not Just Small Ones Cloudflare is committed to building a self-serve product that enterprises can try and buy on their own if they choose. It can be done! 🙂 #5. NRR Has Come Down a Bit, But Still Strong at 110%. Clouldflare’s growth remains top tier, but it has come down a bit, and a dip in NRR is one of the reasons. 110% is still world-class. But it’s down from 115% a year ago. That makes net new ARR growth just that much harder than before.

So times are tougher for some, but for the most part, not in leaders in Cloud security.  Cloudflare is a great example.
While it saw some slowdown last year, it’s now accelerating again with 2 record quarters of new bookings in a row.
At ~ $1.5 Billion in ARR, it’s still growing 32% and it’s gotten pretty darn efficient, with 14% free cash flow margins now.
And the markets really like Cloudflare.  Really, really like it.  It’s trading at a stunning $36 Billion market cap, or 24x ARR!
The key?  They are seeing no slowdown at all in revenue growth from $100k+ customers.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  $100k+ Customers Are Key To Growth at Scale.  Revenue There Growing a Stunning 64% (!).
Cloudflare is getting more and more enterprise, but bear in mind that’s at $1.5 Billion in ARR.  It hasn’t left its free and smaller customers behind.  But the big ones are growing fast faster by revenue at scale.  They’ve also now crossed 2,750 $100k+ customers and 100 $1m+ customers.
#2.   3,063 Employees — So About $400,000 in Revenue Per Employee
This is the age of New Efficiency.  Public SaaS and Cloud companies now average $300,000 in revenue per employee, and many of the most efficient leaders are at $400,000 or higher.  Add Cloudflare to that club.

So Cloud and SaaS have had a bit of a rollercoaster the past 4 years, from the boom times of 2020-2021, to the tougher times overall of 2023, to the AI boom of 2024+.  But one thing has done well through all of it: security.  We always need it, and the threats keep coming.
And Cloudflare has been one of the biggest beneficiaries.  It just keeps on going:
$1.7B+ ARR
28% growth (!)
15% non-GAAP operating profit, and 11% free-cash flow margins … and ..
a $39 Billion market cap (!!), up 45% in past 12 months (!!!)
Cloudflare is what 20x ARR looks like at scale, post-IPO.  Top-tier growth, cash-flow positive, and very durable revenue.  The last point is key.  Wall Street wants revenue that is durable.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  221,000 Total Paying Customers, But 65% of Revenue From 3,200 Large Customers
This is what you should see when a “long tail” engine is just working at scale.  100k+ paying customers, maybe even 1m+ free, but in the end, at scale your largest customers are likely making up 50%+ of your revenue.  Just don’t neglect the small ones.  They grow up into big ones!
#2.  $400,000 in Revenue Per Employee
Cloudflare grew from $300k in revenue per employee at $1B ARR to $400k at $1.5B ARR or so and that seems to be its target to balance growth and efficiency.
#3.  50% of Revenue Outside the U.S.
Our reminder to Go Global as early as you can.

answer:
So there are two playbooks out right now for how much of a “traditional” sales team you really need at an AI B2B startup.  They aren’t mutually exclusive — most startups end up blending both approaches.  But the question is which playbook you should start with.
Playbook #1: Zero Humans Needed Here At All
The pitch here is that so long as your product is truly great, easy to deploy, and has strong word-of-mouth, you shouldn’t need any human salespeople at all. Not one. This is the pure PLG (product-led growth) approach, where customers discover your app through social media, try it themselves, and buy directly online when they see value.
And it’s working well enough for some hot new leaders.  We’ve already seen this play out at Cursor and Replit. Both Cursor and Replit let users self-deploy. Yes, they still have support and community teams.  But no real sales team. And both are worth billions and growing incredibly quickly.
In fact, Replit actually had zero sales reps until recently, despite hitting $200 million in revenue. Their founder, Amjad Masad, was literally handling every single customer call himself—including enterprise deals worth hundreds of thousands of dollars. Only after reaching $150M did they bring in their first sales hires. That’s not a typo—zero salespeople for over a year while generating eight-figure revenue.
This model requires extreme product-market fit, minimal complexity in deployment, and customers who can onboard autonomously. For high-demand products with viral components, it can be surprisingly effective.

retrieval_hits.text: So how big of a sales team do you need with a hot AI B2B startup? I think there are roughly two playbooks being run: Playbook #1: Just focusing on servicing massive in-bound demand. Many AI B2B leaders are doing this and often end up with quotas as high as $4m per AE. That sounds high and it is high, but … imagine a rep can close 2x as many deals, since they are such high intent leads. And the deal size is say $50k. So you can close 10 $50k deals a month = $500k a month bookings. $6m a year. That’s very doable at the hottest AI companies. It’s not that hard when they often have more demand than they can service. Con is you often leave a lot of prospects and leads behind. Org tends to focus mainly on top leads, as that’s plenty to hit plan. And with a small team, you can literally only do so many demos, calls, etc. These vendors are often hard to even book a call with. Playbook #2: Service every lead, go hard. I see this a lot when a hot AI B2B startup starts to hit scale, say $50m+ ARR or more. And then hire a CRO from the pre-AI world. They come in and see to hit plan … they need 100 reps. Like tomorrow. Using “old” math, let’s say the CRO brings in $700k quotas. And needs to add $150m in bookings next year, or more. You need 200 reps. Tomorrow. This ends up creating some chaos as there aren’t enough FDEs or others to support all these AEs. But it does ensure every lead gets called back, gets a demo, etc. Net net which is better? The Mega Quota? Or the Traditional Quota? I think as founders we prefer the former.

AI B2B companies do need sales teams. Almost all of them. The question is just … how large of a sales team? It’s a question no one fully questioned until recently. But now founders & CEOs are asking: - is some of the headcount better put into FDEs? We’re already seeing this - are human SDRs worth it when market demand is strong? - if AI Native B2B leaders have close rates 50% higher, does that mean they can get by with 50% fewer AEs? - many VPs of Sales and CROs now want leaner teams Net net, I’m seeing sales teams often half the size of 24 months ago They may or may not be leaving money on the table. But they are also far, far more efficient.

The 2026 Sales Org Structure
Here’s what I’m seeing work at AI-first companies:
Gone or drastically reduced:
Traditional email-based outbound SDRs (replaced by AI + 1-2 humans managing)
Inbound BDRs doing basic qualification (replaced by AI chat/voice)
CSMs who just do QBRs and don’t solve problems
Expanded:
Solutions Engineers running technical deep-dives before contracts
Forward Deployed Engineers / Implementation Specialists
GTM Engineers orchestrating AI agents
“Super SDRs” managing fleets of AI agents
Account Executives focused on complex deal navigation
New hybrid roles:
Field Data Engineers assessing integration requirements
Solutions Architects designing implementations with prospects
AI Trainers who spend 30+ days per agent getting them into production
The Bottom Line for 2026
Many AI-first B2B startups can scale to $10M, $50M, even $100M+ without a traditional sales team. But that doesn’t mean it will work for you if you have a sales-driven motion. And it doesn’t mean having humans won’t help. Maybe they are FDEs, maybe it’s a few reps. But even the hottest AI B2B startups will benefit from humans assisting PLG and managing their AI Agents. The 2026 sales team isn’t “no humans.” It’s different humans doing different things. But honestly, probably fewer humans in a traditional sales function at least.

An AI sales rep that knows the product cold 24×7 is better than struggling to hire anyone at all you trust to add to the team. The Top 10% of Sales Reps Today Close 65% of All Deals. Will We Need The Rest? Once you think about it this way, you may agree we just won’t need as many sales execs for routine deals. Even today, the top 10% of reps close 65% of deals. If AI lets you focus the human-driven deals into your Top 10% reps … you may not need all that many of the rest. Clari: The Top 10% of Reps Close 65% of Revenue. And The Bottom 50%? Just 7.6%
Enterprise Will Lag, But Change Still Coming
Enterprise sales still generally needs a quarterback to close deals. A quarterback that can manage a team and plays over many, many months. And that will require account management by humans. But also ask yourself — how many sales processes have you been through that weere great? Not that many. There will be plenty of change coming in enterprise sales with AI. But for now, it won’t be to 50/50 Human/AI ratios. We’ll see where it goes over time. You can see Windsurf’s built a massive enterprise sales team overnight. One that is AI infused, but with humans still the quarterbacks:
The Future is Already Here. Just Look. Organizations clinging to traditional sales structures especially in SMB and mid-marklet will find themselves rapidly outpaced by competitors embracing this hybrid approach. The 50/50 sales team isn’t a far-future concept—it’s the reality innovative companies are building right now.

Topic: How Big of a Sales Team Do You Really Need at a Hot AI B2B Startup? The Two Playbooks.

Source passages:
[train_11587]
So how big of a sales team do you need with a hot AI B2B startup? I think there are roughly two playbooks being run: Playbook #1: Just focusing on servicing massive in-bound demand. Many AI B2B leaders are doing this and often end up with quotas as high as $4m per AE. That sounds high and it is high, but … imagine a rep can close 2x as many deals, since they are such high intent leads. And the deal size is say $50k. So you can close 10 $50k deals a month = $500k a month bookings. $6m a year. That’s very doable at the hottest AI companies. It’s not that hard when they often have more demand than they can service. Con is you often leave a lot of prospects and leads behind. Org tends to focus mainly on top leads, as that’s plenty to hit plan. And with a small team, you can literally only do so many demos, calls, etc. These vendors are often hard to even book a call with. Playbook #2: Service every lead, go hard. I see this a lot when a hot AI B2B startup starts to hit scale, say $50m+ ARR or more. And then hire a CRO from the pre-AI world. They come in and see to hit plan … they need 100 reps. Like tomorrow. Using “old” math, let’s say the CRO brings in $700k quotas. And needs to add $150m in bookings next year, or more. You need 200 reps. Tomorrow. This ends up creating some chaos as there aren’t enough FDEs or others to support all these AEs. But it does ensure every lead gets called back, gets a demo, etc. Net net which is better? The Mega Quota? Or the Traditional Quota? I think as founders we prefer the former.

[train_11725]
AI B2B companies do need sales teams. Almost all of them. The question is just … how large of a sales team? It’s a question no one fully questioned until recently. But now founders & CEOs are asking: - is some of the headcount better put into FDEs? We’re already seeing this - are human SDRs worth it when market demand is strong? - if AI Native B2B leaders have close rates 50% higher, does that mean they can get by with 50% fewer AEs? - many VPs of Sales and CROs now want leaner teams Net net, I’m seeing sales teams often half the size of 24 months ago They may or may not be leaving money on the table. But they are also far, far more efficient.

[train_665]
The 2026 Sales Org Structure
Here’s what I’m seeing work at AI-first companies:
Gone or drastically reduced:
Traditional email-based outbound SDRs (replaced by AI + 1-2 humans managing)
Inbound BDRs doing basic qualification (replaced by AI chat/voice)
CSMs who just do QBRs and don’t solve problems
Expanded:
Solutions Engineers running technical deep-dives before contracts
Forward Deployed Engineers / Implementation Specialists
GTM Engineers orchestrating AI agents
“Super SDRs” managing fleets of AI agents
Account Executives focused on complex deal navigation
New hybrid roles:
Field Data Engineers assessing integration requirements
Solutions Architects designing implementations with prospects
AI Trainers who spend 30+ days per agent getting them into production
The Bottom Line for 2026
Many AI-first B2B startups can scale to $10M, $50M, even $100M+ without a traditional sales team. But that doesn’t mean it will work for you if you have a sales-driven motion. And it doesn’t mean having humans won’t help. Maybe they are FDEs, maybe it’s a few reps. But even the hottest AI B2B startups will benefit from humans assisting PLG and managing their AI Agents. The 2026 sales team isn’t “no humans.” It’s different humans doing different things. But honestly, probably fewer humans in a traditional sales function at least.

[train_5401]
An AI sales rep that knows the product cold 24×7 is better than struggling to hire anyone at all you trust to add to the team. The Top 10% of Sales Reps Today Close 65% of All Deals. Will We Need The Rest? Once you think about it this way, you may agree we just won’t need as many sales execs for routine deals. Even today, the top 10% of reps close 65% of deals. If AI lets you focus the human-driven deals into your Top 10% reps … you may not need all that many of the rest. Clari: The Top 10% of Reps Close 65% of Revenue. And The Bottom 50%? Just 7.6%
Enterprise Will Lag, But Change Still Coming
Enterprise sales still generally needs a quarterback to close deals. A quarterback that can manage a team and plays over many, many months. And that will require account management by humans. But also ask yourself — how many sales processes have you been through that weere great? Not that many. There will be plenty of change coming in enterprise sales with AI. But for now, it won’t be to 50/50 Human/AI ratios. We’ll see where it goes over time. You can see Windsurf’s built a massive enterprise sales team overnight. One that is AI infused, but with humans still the quarterbacks:
The Future is Already Here. Just Look. Organizations clinging to traditional sales structures especially in SMB and mid-marklet will find themselves rapidly outpaced by competitors embracing this hybrid approach. The 50/50 sales team isn’t a far-future concept—it’s the reality innovative companies are building right now.

We’ve been tracking what’s really happening in go-to-market across hundreds of conversations with founders building AI products—and one question keeps coming up: how small can your sales team get while still scaling? Here’s my take after looking at where we’re actually ending up, especially at the fastest-growing AI companies. The Math Behind Minimalist Teams The math gets interesting when you look at what’s possible. If you can close 10 $50K deals a month—that’s $500K in bookings—many hot AI B2B start-ups could run with much smaller teams than most people assume. And yes, many are trying this. Some are succeeding spectacularly. Others are learning hard lessons about what works and what doesn’t. The Brutal Truth About Leaving Money On The Table The reality? Most successful AI-first companies aren’t running minimal sales teams because they want to save money—they’re running them because these models genuinely work. When your conversion rate is high enough, you can afford to let more deals sit rather than force-fit human sellers onto every opportunity. This isn’t about being lazy; it’s about economics. retrieval_hits.text: So how big of a sales team do you need with a hot AI B2B startup? I think there are roughly two playbooks being run: Playbook #1: Just focusing on servicing massive in-bound demand. Many AI B2B leaders are doing this and often end up with quotas as high as $4m per AE. That sounds high and it is high, but … imagine a rep can close 2x as many deals, since they are such high intent leads. And the deal size is say $50k. So you can close 10 $50k deals a month = $500k a month bookings. $6m a year. That’s very doable at the hottest AI companies. It’s not that hard when they often have more demand than they can service. Con is you often leave a lot of prospects and leads behind. Org tends to focus mainly on top leads, as that’s plenty to hit plan. And with a small team, you can literally only do so many demos, calls, etc. These vendors are often hard to even book a call with. Playbook #2: Service every lead, go hard. I see this a lot when a hot AI B2B startup starts to hit scale, say $50m+ ARR or more. And then hire a CRO from the pre-AI world. They come in and see to hit plan … they need 100 reps. Like tomorrow. Using “old” math, let’s say the CRO brings in $700k quotas. And needs to add $150m in bookings next year, or more. You need 200 reps. Tomorrow. This ends up creating some chaos as there aren’t enough FDEs or others to support all these AEs. But it does ensure every lead gets called back, gets a demo, etc. Net net which is better? The Mega Quota? Or the Traditional Quota? I think as founders we prefer the former.

AI B2B companies do need sales teams. Almost all of them. The question is just … how large of a sales team? It’s a question no one fully questioned until recently. But now founders & CEOs are asking: - is some of the headcount better put into FDEs? We’re already seeing this - are human SDRs worth it when market demand is strong? - if AI Native B2B leaders have close rates 50% higher, does that mean they can get by with 50% fewer AEs? - many VPs of Sales and CROs now want leaner teams Net net, I’m seeing sales teams often half the size of 24 months ago They may or may not be leaving money on the table. But they are also far, far more efficient.

The 2026 Sales Org Structure
Here’s what I’m seeing work at AI-first companies:
Gone or drastically reduced:
Traditional email-based outbound SDRs (replaced by AI + 1-2 humans managing)
Inbound BDRs doing basic qualification (replaced by AI chat/voice)
CSMs who just do QBRs and don’t solve problems
Expanded:
Solutions Engineers running technical deep-dives before contracts
Forward Deployed Engineers / Implementation Specialists
GTM Engineers orchestrating AI agents
“Super SDRs” managing fleets of AI agents
Account Executives focused on complex deal navigation
New hybrid roles:
Field Data Engineers assessing integration requirements
Solutions Architects designing implementations with prospects
AI Trainers who spend 30+ days per agent getting them into production
The Bottom Line for 2026
Many AI-first B2B startups can scale to $10M, $50M, even $100M+ without a traditional sales team. But that doesn’t mean it will work for you if you have a sales-driven motion. And it doesn’t mean having humans won’t help. Maybe they are FDEs, maybe it’s a few reps. But even the hottest AI B2B startups will benefit from humans assisting PLG and managing their AI Agents. The 2026 sales team isn’t “no humans.” It’s different humans doing different things. But honestly, probably fewer humans in a traditional sales function at least.

An AI sales rep that knows the product cold 24×7 is better than struggling to hire anyone at all you trust to add to the team. The Top 10% of Sales Reps Today Close 65% of All Deals. Will We Need The Rest? Once you think about it this way, you may agree we just won’t need as many sales execs for routine deals. Even today, the top 10% of reps close 65% of deals. If AI lets you focus the human-driven deals into your Top 10% reps … you may not need all that many of the rest. Clari: The Top 10% of Reps Close 65% of Revenue. And The Bottom 50%? Just 7.6%
Enterprise Will Lag, But Change Still Coming
Enterprise sales still generally needs a quarterback to close deals. A quarterback that can manage a team and plays over many, many months. And that will require account management by humans. But also ask yourself — how many sales processes have you been through that weere great? Not that many. There will be plenty of change coming in enterprise sales with AI. But for now, it won’t be to 50/50 Human/AI ratios. We’ll see where it goes over time. You can see Windsurf’s built a massive enterprise sales team overnight. One that is AI infused, but with humans still the quarterbacks:
The Future is Already Here. Just Look. Organizations clinging to traditional sales structures especially in SMB and mid-marklet will find themselves rapidly outpaced by competitors embracing this hybrid approach. The 50/50 sales team isn’t a far-future concept—it’s the reality innovative companies are building right now.

Topic: How Big of a Sales Team Do You Really Need at a Hot AI B2B Startup? The Two Playbooks.

Source passages:
[train_11587]
So how big of a sales team do you need with a hot AI B2B startup? I think there are roughly two playbooks being run: Playbook #1: Just focusing on servicing massive in-bound demand. Many AI B2B leaders are doing this and often end up with quotas as high as $4m per AE. That sounds high and it is high, but … imagine a rep can close 2x as many deals, since they are such high intent leads. And the deal size is say $50k. So you can close 10 $50k deals a month = $500k a month bookings. $6m a year. That’s very doable at the hottest AI companies. It’s not that hard when they often have more demand than they can service. Con is you often leave a lot of prospects and leads behind. Org tends to focus mainly on top leads, as that’s plenty to hit plan. And with a small team, you can literally only do so many demos, calls, etc. These vendors are often hard to even book a call with. Playbook #2: Service every lead, go hard. I see this a lot when a hot AI B2B startup starts to hit scale, say $50m+ ARR or more. And then hire a CRO from the pre-AI world. They come in and see to hit plan … they need 100 reps. Like tomorrow. Using “old” math, let’s say the CRO brings in $700k quotas. And needs to add $150m in bookings next year, or more. You need 200 reps. Tomorrow. This ends up creating some chaos as there aren’t enough FDEs or others to support all these AEs. But it does ensure every lead gets called back, gets a demo, etc. Net net which is better? The Mega Quota? Or the Traditional Quota? I think as founders we prefer the former.

[train_11725]
AI B2B companies do need sales teams. Almost all of them. The question is just … how large of a sales team? It’s a question no one fully questioned until recently. But now founders & CEOs are asking: - is some of the headcount better put into FDEs? We’re already seeing this - are human SDRs worth it when market demand is strong? - if AI Native B2B leaders have close rates 50% higher, does that mean they can get by with 50% fewer AEs? - many VPs of Sales and CROs now want leaner teams Net net, I’m seeing sales teams often half the size of 24 months ago They may or may not be leaving money on the table. But they are also far, far more efficient.

[train_665]
The 2026 Sales Org Structure
Here’s what I’m seeing work at AI-first companies:
Gone or drastically reduced:
Traditional email-based outbound SDRs (replaced by AI + 1-2 humans managing)
Inbound BDRs doing basic qualification (replaced by AI chat/voice)
CSMs who just do QBRs and don’t solve problems
Expanded:
Solutions Engineers running technical deep-dives before contracts
Forward Deployed Engineers / Implementation Specialists
GTM Engineers orchestrating AI agents
“Super SDRs” managing fleets of AI agents
Account Executives focused on complex deal navigation
New hybrid roles:
Field Data Engineers assessing integration requirements
Solutions Architects designing implementations with prospects
AI Trainers who spend 30+ days per agent getting them into production
The Bottom Line for 2026
Many AI-first B2B startups can scale to $10M, $50M, even $100M+ without a traditional sales team. But that doesn’t mean it will work for you if you have a sales-driven motion. And it doesn’t mean having humans won’t help. Maybe they are FDEs, maybe it’s a few reps. But even the hottest AI B2B startups will benefit from humans assisting PLG and managing their AI Agents. The 2026 sales team isn’t “no humans.” It’s different humans doing different things. But honestly, probably fewer humans in a traditional sales function at least.

[train_5401]
An AI sales rep that knows the product cold 24×7 is better than struggling to hire anyone at all you trust to add to the team. The Top 10% of Sales Reps Today Close 65% of All Deals. Will We Need The Rest? Once you think about it this way, you may agree we just won’t need as many sales execs for routine deals. Even today, the top 10% of reps close 65% of deals. If AI lets you focus the human-driven deals into your Top 10% reps … you may not need all that many of the rest. Clari: The Top 10% of Reps Close 65% of Revenue. And The Bottom 50%? Just 7.6%
Enterprise Will Lag, But Change Still Coming
Enterprise sales still generally needs a quarterback to close deals. A quarterback that can manage a team and plays over many, many months. And that will require account management by humans. But also ask yourself — how many sales processes have you been through that weere great? Not that many. There will be plenty of change coming in enterprise sales with AI. But for now, it won’t be to 50/50 Human/AI ratios. We’ll see where it goes over time. You can see Windsurf’s built a massive enterprise sales team overnight. One that is AI infused, but with humans still the quarterbacks:
The Future is Already Here. Just Look. Organizations clinging to traditional sales structures especially in SMB and mid-marklet will find themselves rapidly outpaced by competitors embracing this hybrid approach. The 50/50 sales team isn’t a far-future concept—it’s the reality innovative companies are building right now.

Source passages:
[train_11587]
So how big of a sales team do you need with a hot AI B2B startup? I think there are roughly two playbooks being run: Playbook #1: Just focusing on servicing massive in-bound demand. Many AI B2B leaders are doing this and often end up with quotas as high as $4m per AE. That sounds high and it is high, but … imagine a rep can close 2x as many deals, since they are such high intent leads. And the deal size is say $50k. So you can close 10 $50k deals a month = $500k a month bookings. $6m a year. That’s very doable at the hottest AI companies. It’s not that hard when they often have more demand than they can service. Con is you often leave a lot of prospects and leads behind. Org tends to focus mainly on top leads, as that’s plenty to hit plan. And with a small team, you can literally only do so many demos, calls, etc. These vendors are often hard to even book a call with. Playbook #2: Service every lead, go hard. I see this a lot when a hot AI B2B startup starts to hit scale, say $50m+ ARR or more. And then hire a CRO from the pre-AI world. They come in and see to hit plan … they need 100 reps. Like tomorrow. Using “old” math, let’s say the CRO brings in $700k quotas. And needs to add $150m in bookings next year, or more. You need 200 reps. Tomorrow. This ends up creating some chaos as there aren’t enough FDEs or others to support all these AEs. But it does ensure every lead gets called back, gets a demo, etc. Net net which is better? The Mega Quota? Or the Traditional Quota? I think as founders we prefer the former.

[train_11725]
AI B2B companies do need sales teams. Almost all of them. The question is just … how large of a sales team? It’s a question no one fully questioned until recently. But now founders & CEOs are asking: - is some of the headcount better put into FDEs? We’re already seeing this - are human SDRs worth it when market demand is strong? - if AI Native B2B leaders have close rates 50% higher, does that mean they can get by with 50% fewer AEs? - many VPs of Sales and CROs now want leaner teams Net net, I’m seeing sales teams often half the size of 24 months ago They may or may not be leaving money on the table. But they are also far, far more efficient.

Traditional email-based outbound SDRs (replaced by AI + 1-2 humans managing)

CSMs who just do QBRs and don’t solve problems
Expanded:
Solutions Engineers running technical deep-dives before contracts
Forward Deployed Engineers / Implementation Specialists
GTM Engineers orchestrating AI agents
“Super SDRs” managing fleets of AI agents
Account Executives focused on complex deal navigation
New hybrid roles:
Field Data Engineers assessing integration requirements
Solutions Architects designing implementations with prospects
AI Trainers who spend 30+ days per agent getting them into production

answer: So there's been a lot of conversation over the past year or two about how much sales teams are needed these days when you're hot. And the answer is complicated, and I'm going to break it down into two playbooks because it really depends what kind of company you are. So playbook number one is the high growth self-service playbook where your customers are paying monthly and they can try you out right then and there. If that's your company, you might be able to get away with zero human sales reps. Like Harvey, Replit, Lovable, etc. These guys are growing like crazy. Harvey is growing like crazy. They've got millions of users. They've got huge revenues. They've got hundreds of thousands of dollars paid up front. There's no reason to have any human sales team here at all. And yet, and yet... most of us aren't Harvey. Most of us sell something more complicated. We require some deployment time. We need someone to understand our use cases. We need someone to implement and deploy our software, which is why I see the second playbook being deployed far more widely. This is the enterprise-focused model. This is the one where you still need real people to help your customers succeed. And look, let me tell you, my experience is, yeah, I'd love to have 100 human AEs at SaaStr itself. I wish I could afford 'em. I wish I had enough money to pay them, to pay their salary. But realistically, I know I need folks to help me understand whether I should buy a piece of software or not. I'll take an agent, but I'm not sure I want to train an agent myself. I want somebody to help me figure it out.

retrieval_hits.text: So how big of a sales team do you need with a hot AI B2B startup? That sounds high and it is high, but … imagine a rep can close 2x as many deals, since they are such high intent leads. And the deal size is say $50k. So you can close 10 $50k deals a month = $500k a month bookings. $6m a year. That’s very doable at the hottest AI companies. It’s not that hard when they often have more demand than they can service. Con is you often leave a lot of prospects and leads behind. Org tends to focus mainly on top leads, as that’s plenty to hit plan. And with a small team, you can literally only do so many demos, calls, etc. These vendors are often hard to even book a call with. Playbook #2: Service every lead, go hard. I see this a lot when a hot AI B2B startup starts to hit scale, say $50m+ ARR or more. And then hire a CRO from the pre-AI world. They come in and see to hit plan … they need 100 reps. Like tomorrow. Using “old” math, let’s say the CRO brings in $700k quotas. And needs to add $150m in bookings next year, or more. You need 200 reps. Tomorrow. This ends up creating some chaos as there aren’t enough FDEs or others to support all these AEs. But it does ensure every lead gets called back, gets a demo, etc. Net net which is better? The Mega Quota? Or the Traditional Quota? I think as founders we prefer the former.

AI B2B companies do need sales teams. Almost all of them. The question is just … how large of a sales team? It’s a question no one fully questioned until recently. But now founders & CEOs are asking: - is some of the headcount better put into FDEs? CSMs who just do QBRs and don’t solve problems

Forward Deployed Engineers / Implementation Specialists
GTM Engineers orchestrating AI agents
“Super SDRs” managing fleets of AI agents
Account Executives focused on complex deal navigation

Solutions Architects designing implementations with prospects
AI Trainers who spend 30+ days per agent getting them into production

Topic: How Big of a Sales Team Do You Really Need at a Hot AI B2B Startup? The Two Playbooks.

Source passages:
[train_11587]
So how big of a sales team do you need with a hot AI B2B startup? I think there are roughly two playbooks being run: Playbook #1: Just focusing on servicing massive in-bound demand. Many AI B2B leaders are doing this and often end up with quotas as high as $4m per AE. That sounds high and it is high, but … imagine a rep can close 2x as many deals, since they are such high intent leads. And the deal size is say $50k. So you can close 10 $50k deals a month = $500k a month bookings. $6m a year. That’s very doable at the hottest AI companies. It’s not that hard when they often have more demand than they can service. Con is you often leave a lot of prospects and leads behind. Org tends to focus mainly on top leads, as that’s plenty to hit plan. And with a small team, you can literally only do so many demos, calls, etc. These vendors are often hard to even book a call with. Playbook #2: Service every lead, go hard. I see this a lot when a hot AI B2B startup starts to hit scale, say $50m+ ARR or more. And then hire a CRO from the pre-AI world. They come in and see to hit plan … they need 100 reps. Like tomorrow. Using “old” math, let’s say the CRO brings in $700k quotas. And needs to add $150m in bookings next year, or more. You need 200 reps. Tomorrow. This ends up creating some chaos as there aren’t enough FDEs or others to support all these AEs. But it does ensure every lead gets called back, gets a demo, etc. Net net which is better? The Mega Quota? Or the Traditional Quota? I think as founders we prefer the former.

[train_11725]
AI B2B companies do need sales teams. Almost all of them. The question is just … how large of a sales team? It’s a question no one fully questioned until recently. But now founders & CEOs are asking: - is some of the headcount better put into FDEs? We’re already seeing this - are human SDRs worth it when market demand is strong? - if AI Native B2B leaders have close rates 50% higher, does that mean they can get by with 50% fewer AEs? - many VPs of Sales and CROs now want leaner teams Net net, I’m seeing sales teams often half the size of 24 months ago They may or may not be leaving money on the table. But they are also far, far more efficient.

[train_665]
The 2026 Sales Org Structure
Here’s what I’m seeing work at AI-first companies:
Gone or drastically reduced:
Traditional email-based outbound SDRs (replaced by AI + 1-2 humans managing)
Inbound BDRs doing basic qualification (replaced by AI chat/voice)
CSMs who just do QBRs and don’t solve problems
Expanded:
Solutions Engineers running technical deep-dives before contracts
Forward Deployed Engineers / Implementation Specialists
GTM Engineers orchestrating AI agents
“Super SDRs” managing fleets of AI agents
Account Executives focused on complex deal navigation
New hybrid roles:
Field Data Engineers assessing integration requirements
Solutions Architects designing implementations with prospects
AI Trainers who spend 30+ days per agent getting them into production
The Bottom Line for 2026
Many AI-first B2B startups can scale to $10M, $50M, even $100M+ without a traditional sales team. But that doesn’t mean it will work for you if you have a sales-driven motion. And it doesn’t mean having humans won’t help. Maybe they are FDEs, maybe it’s a few reps. But even the hottest AI B2B startups will benefit from humans assisting PLG and managing their AI Agents. The 2026 sales team isn’t “no humans.” It’s different humans doing different things. But honestly, probably fewer humans in a traditional sales function at least.

[train_5401]
An AI sales rep that knows the product cold 24×7 is better than struggling to hire anyone at all you trust to add to the team. The Top 10% of Sales Reps Today Close 65% of All Deals. Will We Need The Rest? Once you think about it this way, you may agree we just won’t need as many sales execs for routine deals. Even today, the top 10% of reps close 65% of deals. If AI lets you focus the human-driven deals into your Top 10% reps … you may not need all that many of the rest. Clari: The Top 10% of Reps Close 65% of Revenue. And The Bottom 50%? Just 7.6%
Enterprise Will Lag, But Change Still Coming
Enterprise sales still generally needs a quarterback to close deals. A quarterback that can manage a team and plays over many, many months. And that will require account management by humans. But also ask yourself — how many sales processes have you been through that weere great? Not that many. There will be plenty of change coming in enterprise sales with AI. But for now, it won’t be to 50/50 Human/AI ratios. We’ll see where it goes over time. You can see Windsurf’s built a massive enterprise sales team overnight. One that is AI infused, but with humans still the quarterbacks:
The Future is Already Here. Just Look. Organizations clinging to traditional sales structures especially in SMB and mid-marklet will find themselves rapidly outpaced by competitors embracing this hybrid approach. The 50/50 sales team isn’t a far-future concept—it’s the reality innovative companies are building right now.

answer:
We’ve talked so much over the years on SaaStr about running out of cash. And we’ll keep talking about it until founders finally get it right:
It’s OK if you run out of money sometimes. But it’s really, really hard to recover once you do. You have to close all your biggest deals — now. Your team will leave. It takes forever to raise another round. Even if you raise another round, it rarely comes with enough money to carry you through even one year. So what can you do? Two things that always help:
Hire an amazing VP Finance/Controller/CFO ASAP
. If you don’t already have this role filled, go find her today. This person won’t just manage cash flow and the books. She’ll be a mentor to you. The best VPs of Finance become trusted advisors to CEOs. They know how many leads you need to hit the quarter. They understand when you’re chasing too many big opportunities. They know exactly which costs you can cut without hurting growth. More importantly, they’ll stop you before you make mistakes with the money. Because most founders aren’t naturally good financial managers. I’m still waiting for my first $100m check. Here’s what keeps me up at night. The #1 reason companies fail isn’t lack of demand—it’s poor planning and execution around capital management. A great CFO helps you avoid making those costly errors. Double Down On What Works
The second thing is to focus relentlessly on doubling down on what works. When you’re raising venture capital, investors want to see two things: traction and potential. Traction shows you’ve built something real. Potential shows there’s more to come. Focus on both simultaneously. For example, look at
Snowflake
—still the gold standard for SaaS finance.

2. On acquiring customers consistently
You may not have that magical sales person, but as a founder, you simply have to sell. Here’s the trick with founder lead sales: customers and prospects love to talk to the CEO. And then, there are your superpowers. In those early days, founders are good at one or two aspects— these are what work well for your company. These are what Jason calls your superpowers. For instance, when Algolia was trying to get off the ground, the co-founder Nicolas Dessaigne often got on the stage at events, which generated a lot of buzz and product interest. He would also attend developer networking events and man a booth. His consistent efforts paid off when Algolia became a known brand among developers. Julien Lemoine, Algolia’s other co-founder, wrote a data-rich blog article comparing Algolia with its top competitor at the time. It was an earnest piece that spoke about instances where the competitor was better than Algolia and vice versa. The article which was well-researched with supporting data brought in consistent leads for a very long time. This generated tons of leads and credibility — before content marketing was even a consideration. The idea is to identify your superpower(s) and double down on it. Most SaaS startup founders have shiny object syndrome— they want to try events, blog articles, partner programs, outbound outreach all at once.

.  The entire venture industry is under stress this year.  If you need a bridge round, discuss it — early.  Talk about it,  Talk about what to do if you have less than 18-24 months of runway.  Don’t just … run out of money.  You might laugh, but this is far too common.  Founders hide from running out of money, and/or plan way too optimistic financial plans that can’t realistically be hit.

answer: How To Not Run Out of Cash as a Founder: 2 Things That Really, Really Help Use ONLY allowed factual evidence (E1-E5) above. Let me share two things that really work well — if you do them consistently: First, use your precious time wisely. Don’t waste too much time selling yourself. The best founders don’t have a lot of downtime. They aren't all introverts. But they know how to make every minute count. This means you'll be more effective when speaking with potential clients because you've already prepared thoroughly before each conversation. You won't feel like an imposter anymore! Second, make sure your team knows what success looks like. A great sales rep will always be able to articulate exactly how many leads they need to hit their number. If they can't explain this clearly, then they're probably struggling with something deeper than just lead generation. It's often easy to see this in first-time managers. They struggle to tell you why they haven't met their goals. And why they think they still might meet those goals. Why? Because they don't understand yet themselves. Or at least not enough.

answer:
So I want to share two things that really help founders make sure they don't run out of cash. And there's just one caveat. The caveat is you have to do these two things before your start-up runs out of money. So let me share those with you.
The first thing we're going to talk about is how to get more leads and more customers without spending more dollars. Now this seems like something that would be obvious, but so many startups actually fail at this. And then the second point is why you need to make sure everyone has skin in the game. Why every single person working at your startup needs to have some personal financial risk if they lose all their money if the startup goes under. Those are the two points I wanted to talk about today. First up, getting more leads and more customers without burning through your capital base. There's an old adage that says if someone believes in you enough to pay for what you're doing, you shouldn't have to worry about money. If people believe in your product, they will buy it. They'll give you money for it. You won't even have to worry about running out of money. It's true. But here's the problem. In order to take advantage of that advice, you've got to know how to leverage your strengths to increase sales. Your strength is what makes your business unique. It might sound trite, but think back to when you were selling products as a kid. When you started off, maybe you sold lemonade at the corner store. Maybe you learned how to cut lemons perfectly. Maybe you learned how to slice oranges perfectly. Maybe you had the best lemonade stand in town because you knew how to cut the perfect lemon.

My list:
Slow it down if you don’t have a great co-founder
. Another idea will come, but it’s almost impossible to thrive without an amazing co-founder.  More
here
.
You always need about 25% more than your raise
. So always raise 25% more than you think you need, even in an angel round. But don’t spend that 25%. Maybe even put it in a different business bank account.  A bit more
here
.
You’ll lose a year to a truly terrible VP hire
. They’ll hire an entire terrible team, your revenue will slow, and they’ll spend a ton of money doing it. You are better off with No VP than a bad one.  More
here
.
Competition doesn’t kill you
. Not having a 10x feature kills you. Giving up kills you. But even the best competitors don’t try to win in every segment of the market. And even the best competitor doesn’t have 100% market share.  More
here
.

It’s OK to start in a small segment of a large market. Better to win there first, usually.  More
here
.

.  The entire venture industry is under stress this year.  If you need a bridge round, discuss it — early.  Talk about it,  Talk about what to do if you have less than 18-24 months of runway.  Don’t just … run out of money.  You might laugh, but this is far too common.  Founders hide from running out of money, and/or plan way too optimistic financial plans that can’t realistically be hit.

answer:
We’ve been running 20+ AI agents at SaaStr for months now — Artisan (our outbound agent), Qualified (inbound lead qualification), Clay (content generation), Gamma (meeting notes summarization), Fin (support ticketing), Agentforce (Salesforce’s new agent), Opus Pro (our internal knowledge base), and more.
The results have been genuinely transformative. Revenue has grown dramatically. Lead response times dropped from hours to seconds. Customer support tickets get answered instantly instead of “we’ll follow up Monday.”
But nobody talks about the real problems we’re solving every single day. The ones that aren’t in any sales deck or marketing presentation.
Here are the five things no one tells you when they pitch you on buying an AI agent:
Issue #1: Your Team Will Leave When You Deploy AI Agents
This is the most important one. It happened at SaaStr first. And then across our entire portfolio of investments. Not everyone leaves. But some do. And even those who stay … change. I had my head of content leave me because she said she could never work this way again after seeing our AI output. She was passionate about her craft. She wanted to create. And she felt like she’d lost control over something she cared deeply about.
I wasn’t upset. In fact, I told her go. Because I knew where this was going. This isn’t just about job insecurity. Many employees literally cannot handle their roles being augmented by machines. They’re trained to believe that human judgment matters. That expertise requires experience. That quality comes from people making decisions.
When your team member sees their role reduced to “review and edit” rather than “create and own,” they react. Some quit quietly. Others stage dramatic exits.

Here Are the Top 5 Issues No One Talks About The biggest surprises for us after launching 20+ AI agents at SaaStr weren’t technical—they were human dynamics. Most founders I talk to expect the technology to work (it does), then struggle with everything else that breaks when you introduce AI into your organization. After months of intense experimentation, here’s what we’ve learned about implementing AI agents successfully. #1: Budgeting Is Broken — And Everyone Knows It Nobody wants to spend $100K on an agent upfront when they’re used to paying Salesforce annual fees. But here’s reality check: If you want results, you need to pay up. Whether it’s Qualified ($80K/year), Artisan ($60K), or Agentforce ($25K-$40K per agent), these aren’t impulse buys. You’re essentially buying dedicated software plus a team member salary—just one that doesn’t quit and works 24/7. Your existing vendors know this too. They’ll just charge more because you have budget now. And honestly? This might all change once Lovable and Cursor become enterprise-grade products. Maybe by end-of-year we won’t need to buy anything from anyone if our own tools get good enough. Time will tell there. #2: Training Is More Work Than People Admit Think 10 minutes training = instant results. Think again. In my experience, training usually takes longer than expected and requires significant ongoing investment. For example, our AI support agent took weeks to train properly—a lot longer than the 15

#5. Launch Your First AI Agent That Actually Works.  And That You Can Really Sell.
Not an AI feature. Not a chatbot. A real AI agent that handles actual workflows end-to-end.
I’ve deployed 20+ AI agents across SaaStr’s operations. Support agents. Content agents. Sales qualification agents. Together they’ve generated over $1M in revenue while reducing our headcount needs.
Most founders are still debating whether to add AI to their product. That’s table stakes now. The real question is: are you using AI agents to fundamentally transform your own operations?
Because here’s what I’m seeing: companies deploying working AI agents are operating with 30-50% fewer humans in key functions. Customer support. Sales development. Content creation. Implementation. Legal review.
Those aren’t future capabilities. They’re working today. At scale. And if you’re not deploying them, your competitors are.
Launch one high value agent in Q1. Get it working. Learn. Then launch two more by end of year.
The companies that figure out AI agents first will have massive cost advantages and speed advantages over everyone else. Don’t wait.
How we manage 20+ AI Agents without them stepping all over each other ...

answer:
So we have 20 plus AI agents in production at SaaStr now,
and we've been using them for over six months, since our first one launched back in May of last year. And there's so much more stuff that people don't really talk about when they deploy their agents. So I'm gonna walk through five of those today because I think most folks aren't aware of these issues, even if they're on the way to getting some real value from an agent. Number one is security. Every single one of our agents has access to all your data. They all read everything. All right? This is a huge issue. Nobody wants to hear this. Everyone's worried about their data. But every single agent we use has full access to Salesforce, HubSpot, Outreach, Gmail, Slack, etc. Because they need it to work. Now, there is no solution here. There is just awareness. Be careful who you pick. If you're buying an AI sales rep, understand what data they're accessing. If you buy a customer success tool, make sure you know where its permissions are set up. It is better than trying to hack around it. The vendors get it now. You got to give them permission. They cannot function without it.

answer:
DigitalOcean is up 12% in 2026 while the rest of SaaS is down -24%
It’s hard to imagine anything more out of fashion than “on-prem” infrastructure for many public B2B companies right now.  Cloudflare’s core business has grown much faster since they went multi-product — by adding AI, security, etc. that customers can buy on top of their cloud.  And everyone seems to want to be “agentic”, even if just as hype today.
But … what about developers?
What do they need right now?
They still need compute.
AI is all consuming, but it doesn’t change the fundamental fact that apps run on servers. That data centers exist. That bandwidth matters. And that you need places where your agents actually run.
So here’s something really interesting:
The digital-native leaders are winning again. But this time, not because they’re replacing old things. Because they’re selling new ones that aren’t going away either.

answer:
So we've talked a lot on SaaStr over the years about how Cloud has changed and how things have evolved since we started back in 2012 with our first podcast talking to Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff and then with my first post on Quora, "What Are the Top Mistakes Founders Make When They Start?"
And I think one of them is thinking that your market will stay the same as when you start. And maybe for some categories, this is true. But more often than not, the markets change dramatically after you launch. And if you're just starting out today, boy, I got so many learnings for you.
I wanted to spend a little time doing an update on where public B2B and SaaS companies stand right now because most of us don't know what's going on beyond our own companies. We know how our company's doing, but do you really know where the rest of the market stands?
Well, let me take a step back here, and there's three big areas I want to focus on. Number one, the overall health of the entire tech stack. How much money is being spent on software and hardware these days. What's happening in AI, and why it matters. And finally, what's happening in infrastructure and DevOps, which is where I am at home. Where's all the spending in DevOps going?
Let's dig into each of those areas quickly.
First, the overall health of the entire tech stack. So according to Gartner, total IT spending worldwide was almost $8 trillion last year. That's up from about $7 trillion two years ago. A pretty good number, right? You're seeing nice growth across the board. But there's a catch. About half of that growth is coming from price increases. Not real demand.

And I think one of them is thinking that your market will stay the same as when you start. And maybe for some categories, this is true. But more often than not, the markets change dramatically after you launch. And if you're just starting out today, boy, I got so many learnings for you.
I wanted to spend a little time doing an update on where public B2B and SaaS companies stand right now because most of us don't know what's going on beyond our own companies. We know how our company's doing, but do you really know where the rest of the market stands?
Well, let me take a step back here, and there's three big areas I want to focus on. Number one, the overall health of the entire tech stack. How much money is being spent on software and hardware these days. What's happening in AI, and why it matters. And finally, what's happening in infrastructure and DevOps, which is where I am at home. Where's all the spending in DevOps going?
Let's dig into each of those areas quickly.
First, the overall health of the entire tech stack. So according to Gartner, total IT spending worldwide was almost $8 trillion last year. That's up from about $7 trillion two years ago. A pretty good number, right? You're seeing nice growth across the board. But there's a catch. About half of that growth is coming from price increases. Not real demand.

answer:
SaaS isn’t dead.  Not yet.  And even if it was … well, you can see folks like Salesforce doing better these days as well.  But what I do think is clear is there hasn’t been much change in how many of us sell software since 2010/2011:
The products got more powerful over time, and the teams grew bigger
But basically, they were still selling the same way for years
I’m not sure any of us truly adapted to the changes of the past few years.  We’re finally seeing some real adaptations in early 2024 though.  It’s starting to get exciting.  Here’s my take on where things stand today:
It used to be easy to win in SaaS with high NRR and happy customers
We’d close them in the early days, then raise prices every year because the product got better and better.  Today, NRR overall has fallen to 105%.   And in fact, in the public companies, their net retention has fallen below 100% on average.  Even ZoomInfo had negative NRR!  This means churn has gone up and up.  Folks aren’t staying as long anymore.  It’s harder to keep customers when competition gets hotter, especially in the age of AI.  So we’ve entered a new era where we don’t have 130%+ NRR and happy customers buying more and more seats each year.  Instead, we often struggle to retain our existing base, and lose them once they buy another app that does something similar.  It’s tough out there.  But the best are finding a way.
We used to use prototypes to try to get deals done quickly
A great tool!  In the Age of AI, now you can build prototypes almost instantly.  In fact, one of the most recent tools we tried here at SaaStr took less than 24 hours to deploy (!).

retrieval_query: SaaS Isn’t Dead. But the Way You Used to Win in B2B? That’s Gone.

retrieval_hits.text:
SaaS isn’t dead, even with the massive sell off this year (and really since July 2025)

But … what is dead is the classic pattern and way to scale:

- 1, maybe 2 players, take over a space by $20m ARR
- Massive sales & marketing spend gets you to $100m+ ARR, often takes years
- Product then mostly stagnant, quarterly releases,  big platform advance only every 5 years or so
- High NRR of 130%+ in enterprise, 110%+ in SMBs basically on autopilot
- Customers happily renew and keep spending more with you

That is dead

It’s been replaced with:

- Prototype built in days
- AI creating 100s of new competitors, many dramatically better at agentic functionality 
- Outliers get to $100m in 12 months, become budget magnets
- AI radically expanding functionality, obliterating prior pace software development 
- Massive reluctance to buy more products or seats from slow moving vendors they already pay for 
- High reluctance to contribute any budget that doesn’t show massive ROI almost immediately (from AI)
- Endless price increases since 2022 leading to frustration and even anger at existing leaders and brands

That is "SaaS" today.  If you want to win.

The Era of Slow SaaS Evolution is Dead
SaaS and B2B software is experiencing an unprecedented transformation. From 2011 to 2023, the SaaS world was … predictable. You’d build a product, add a couple features annually, make quarterly releases, and if you hit $10M ARR with 110-120% net retention, your ticket was pretty much punched to $100m+ ARR and beyond. But that playbook is now obsolete. Revenue is still recurring in SaaS, of course. But the rate of change, and the threats from AI, are making the model far tougher than it was just 12 months ago. The stable, predictable SaaS world we knew has been replaced by rapid AI-driven evolution that’s breaking all the old rules. What worked yesterday is aging out FAST. The truth is harsh but necessary:
if you’re still running your 2023 playbook in 2025, you’re already falling behind. The 4 Red Flags You’re Getting “Maimed” by AI-First Competitors
You might not see competitors taking all your business overnight, but the “death by a thousand cuts” has begun:
Deals are getting smaller
Net Retention is steadily declining
Win rates dropping by 10-15%
(from 90% to 78%)
Existing customers downgrading
This isn’t about total displacement (yet). It’s about getting “maimed” as innovative AI-first companies eat into your business—not by destroying you, but by steadily cutting away at your growth.

So it was just 8 months ago
we wrote “Is SaaS Dead?
” and the post not only took off, it summarized a zeitgeist, a malaise, a feeling across much of B2B at the start of 2024. That SaaS was Dead. A combination of AI and buyer retrenchment had killed it. What a difference 8 months makes. It’s not 2021 again, but so much has changed for the better as the year ends:
Many top SaaS and Cloud stocks are up +40%-60% or more in the back half of the yea
r. Not all of them, but so many. This makes everyone feel … richer. They are richer. Many top SaaS and Cloud leaders have seen growth re-accelerate
. This is a bigger deal. Shopify is growing far faster today at $9B ARR (a stunning 26%) than it was just a year before (21%). Even folks that were struggling to rebound from pandemic-fueled growth like Twilio have bounced back, to an extent at least. Twilio is now above 10% growth again. This isn’t 2020 levels of growth, but acceleration is acceleration. Many SaaS leaders are now benefitting from selling AI
. Salesforce has seen a boost. Dialpad has seen
stunning re-acceleration, from $200m ARR last year to $300m+ this year
. Not everyone has benefitted from selling AI to their base. But a number have. IPOs are restarting — and really good ones are coming
. There have only been 4 SaaS IPOs since 2021, but they’ve done well, and ServiceTitan had a big pop in its recent IPO. The pipeline looks strong for the back half of 2025 and into 2026, from Canva to Databricks to Stripe to Wiz to Snyk and on and on. More liquidity makes everyone feel better, for many reasons.
New!!  There Probably Is No Downturn in SaaS. It’s Time To Stop Waiting For It To End.

answer: SaaS Isn’t Dead. But the Way You Used to Win in B2B? That’s Gone. We’ve lost some of our best friends to the “AI downturn”. Some of them didn’t understand what happened. Others understood — they just couldn’t make any changes fast enough. And others still … they got there quickly. They adapted. Fast. In many cases, even much faster than their own management. I don’t think you can blame anyone for being confused right now. The entire playbook for building SaaS companies changed dramatically between 2020 and 2025—literally overnight—and most founders are still trying to figure out where the bodies went. Let me be clear on one thing: SaaS isn’t dying. Not yet. The public markets’ panic over the past two years tells a different story entirely—one of unprecedented disruption and evolutionary pressure that’s forcing every B2B company to fundamentally rethink how they build products, sell them, and grow. What we’re witnessing isn’t the death of software as a service—it’s the birth of something completely new. It’s messy. It’s painful. And if you’re leading a SaaS business, you need to get your head around it before your investors lose theirs. Here’s what actually happened: the classic playbook broke. The pattern of spending millions on enterprise sales teams, running complex six-month implementation cycles, pricing based on seat count, and expecting predictable quarterly results stopped working. For real. The New Rules Nobody Taught Us 🤖 AI created 100s of new competitors overnight. Products that used to take years
