SaaS isn’t dead, even with the massive sell off this year (and really since July 2025)

But … what is dead is the classic pattern and way to scale:

- 1, maybe 2 players, take over a space by $20m ARR
- Massive sales & marketing spend gets you to $100m+ ARR, often takes years
- Product then mostly stagnant, quarterly releases,  big platform advance only every 5 years or so
- High NRR of 130%+ in enterprise, 110%+ in SMBs basically on autopilot
- Customers happily renew and keep spending more with you

That is dead

It’s been replaced with:

- Prototype built in days
- AI creating 100s of new competitors, many dramatically better at agentic functionality 
- Outliers get to $100m in 12 months, become budget magnets
- AI radically expanding functionality, obliterating prior pace software development 
- Massive reluctance to buy more products or seats from slow moving vendors they already pay for 
- High reluctance to contribute any budget that doesn’t show massive ROI almost immediately (from AI)
- Endless price increases since 2022 leading to frustration and even anger at existing leaders and brands

That is "SaaS" today.  If you want to win.

The Era of Slow SaaS Evolution is Dead
SaaS and B2B software is experiencing an unprecedented transformation. From 2011 to 2023, the SaaS world was … predictable. You’d build a product, add a couple features annually, make quarterly releases, and if you hit $10M ARR with 110-120% net retention, your ticket was pretty much punched to $100m+ ARR and beyond. But that playbook is now obsolete. Revenue is still recurring in SaaS, of course. But the rate of change, and the threats from AI, are making the model far tougher than it was just 12 months ago. The stable, predictable SaaS world we knew has been replaced by rapid AI-driven evolution that’s breaking all the old rules. What worked yesterday is aging out FAST. The truth is harsh but necessary:
if you’re still running your 2023 playbook in 2025, you’re already falling behind. The 4 Red Flags You’re Getting “Maimed” by AI-First Competitors
You might not see competitors taking all your business overnight, but the “death by a thousand cuts” has begun:
Deals are getting smaller
Net Retention is steadily declining
Win rates dropping by 10-15%
(from 90% to 78%)
Existing customers downgrading
This isn’t about total displacement (yet). It’s about getting “maimed” as innovative AI-first companies eat into your business—not by destroying you, but by steadily cutting away at your growth.

we wrote “Is SaaS Dead?

Many top SaaS and Cloud stocks are up +40%-60% or more in the back half of the yea
r. Not all of them, but so many. This makes everyone feel … richer. They are richer. Many top SaaS and Cloud leaders have seen growth re-accelerate
. This is a bigger deal. Shopify is growing far faster today at $9B ARR (a stunning 26%) than it was just a year before (21%). Even folks that were struggling to rebound from pandemic-fueled growth like Twilio have bounced back, to an extent at least. Twilio is now above 10% growth again. This isn’t 2020 levels of growth, but acceleration is acceleration. Many SaaS leaders are now benefitting from selling AI
. Salesforce has seen a boost. Dialpad has seen
stunning re-acceleration, from $200m ARR last year to $300m+ this year
. Not everyone has benefitted from selling AI to their base. But a number have. IPOs are restarting — and really good ones are coming
. There have only been 4 SaaS IPOs since 2021, but they’ve done well, and ServiceTitan had a big pop in its recent IPO. The pipeline looks strong for the back half of 2025 and into 2026, from Canva to Databricks to Stripe to Wiz to Snyk and on and on. More liquidity makes everyone feel better, for many reasons.

answer:
So I know you've heard a lot of different things over the past few months, but let me give you my take on where we stand right now with SaaS.
And I want to start off with a couple quotes because they sum up what's going on for founders and CEOs in the public markets and more broadly across tech.
This first one comes from Peter Gassner, CEO of Veeva Systems, which is one of our favorite companies. And he said something incredibly insightful recently on LinkedIn. He said:
"We're seeing AI as a force multiplier and a threat."
I think most of us would agree with that. We're using AI as a force multiplier. It allows us to do so much more than ever before. But if your team doesn't understand how to use it effectively, if it's not embedded into every function of your company, then it will be a threat.
The second quote is from Drew Houston, co-founder and CEO of Dropbox. He made a similar point, although maybe less articulate, when he talked about the AI revolution being like the mobile internet transition all over again. This time, though, there are 700 open source LLMs out there competing with each other and others. So it's even more intense than back then.

retrieval_hits.text:
SaaS isn’t dead, even with the massive sell off this year (and really since July 2025)

But … what is dead is the classic pattern and way to scale:

- 1, maybe 2 players, take over a space by $20m ARR
- Massive sales & marketing spend gets you to $100m+ ARR, often takes years
- Product then mostly stagnant, quarterly releases,  big platform advance only every 5 years or so
- High NRR of 130%+ in enterprise, 110%+ in SMBs basically on autopilot
- Customers happily renew and keep spending more with you

That is dead

It’s been replaced with:

- Prototype built in days
- AI creating 100s of new competitors, many dramatically better at agentic functionality 
- Outliers get to $100m in 12 months, become budget magnets
- AI radically expanding functionality, obliterating prior pace software development 
- Massive reluctance to buy more products or seats from slow moving vendors they already pay for 
- High reluctance to contribute any budget that doesn’t show massive ROI almost immediately (from AI)
- Endless price increases since 2022 leading to frustration and even anger at existing leaders and brands

That is "SaaS" today.  If you want to win.

The Era of Slow SaaS Evolution is Dead
SaaS and B2B software is experiencing an unprecedented transformation. From 2011 to 2023, the SaaS world was … predictable. You’d build a product, add a couple features annually, make quarterly releases, and if you hit $10M ARR with 110-120% net retention, your ticket was pretty much punched to $100m+ ARR and beyond. But that playbook is now obsolete. Revenue is still recurring in SaaS, of course. But the rate of change, and the threats from AI, are making the model far tougher than it was just 12 months ago. The stable, predictable SaaS world we knew has been replaced by rapid AI-driven evolution that’s breaking all the old rules. What worked yesterday is aging out FAST. The truth is harsh but necessary:
if you’re still running your 2023 playbook in 2025, you’re already falling behind. The 4 Red Flags You’re Getting “Maimed” by AI-First Competitors
You might not see competitors taking all your business overnight, but the “death by a thousand cuts” has begun:
Deals are getting smaller
Net Retention is steadily declining
Win rates dropping by 10-15%
(from 90% to 78%)
Existing customers downgrading
This isn’t about total displacement (yet). It’s about getting “maimed” as innovative AI-first companies eat into your business—not by destroying you, but by steadily cutting away at your growth.

So it was just 8 months ago
we wrote “Is SaaS Dead?
” and the post not only took off, it summarized a zeitgeist, a malaise, a feeling across much of B2B at the start of 2024. That SaaS was Dead. A combination of AI and buyer retrenchment had killed it. What a difference 8 months makes. It’s not 2021 again, but so much has changed for the better as the year ends:
Many top SaaS and Cloud stocks are up +40%-60% or more in the back half of the yea
r. Not all of them, but so many. This makes everyone feel … richer. They are richer. Many top SaaS and Cloud leaders have seen growth re-accelerate
. This is a bigger deal. Shopify is growing far faster today at $9B ARR (a stunning 26%) than it was just a year before (21%). Even folks that were struggling to rebound from pandemic-fueled growth like Twilio have bounced back, to an extent at least. Twilio is now above 10% growth again. This isn’t 2020 levels of growth, but acceleration is acceleration. Many SaaS leaders are now benefitting from selling AI
. Salesforce has seen a boost. Dialpad has seen
stunning re-acceleration, from $200m ARR last year to $300m+ this year
. Not everyone has benefitted from selling AI to their base. But a number have. IPOs are restarting — and really good ones are coming
. There have only been 4 SaaS IPOs since 2021, but they’ve done well, and ServiceTitan had a big pop in its recent IPO. The pipeline looks strong for the back half of 2025 and into 2026, from Canva to Databricks to Stripe to Wiz to Snyk and on and on. More liquidity makes everyone feel better, for many reasons.

SaaS isn’t dead, even with the massive sell off this year (and really since July 2025)

But … what is dead is the classic pattern and way to scale:

- 1, maybe 2 players, take over a space by $20m ARR
- Massive sales & marketing spend gets you to $100m+ ARR, often takes years
- Product then mostly stagnant, quarterly releases,  big platform advance only every 5 years or so
- High NRR of 130%+ in enterprise, 110%+ in SMBs basically on autopilot
- Customers happily renew and keep spending more with you

That is dead

It’s been replaced with:

- Prototype built in days
- AI creating 100s of new competitors, many dramatically better at agentic functionality 
- Outliers get to $100m in 12 months, become budget magnets
- AI radically expanding functionality, obliterating prior pace software development 
- Massive reluctance to buy more products or seats from slow moving vendors they already pay for 
- High reluctance to contribute any budget that doesn’t show massive ROI almost immediately (from AI)
- Endless price increases since 2022 leading to frustration and even anger at existing leaders and brands

That is "SaaS" today.  If you want to win.

[train_5411]
The Era of Slow SaaS Evolution is Dead
SaaS and B2B software is experiencing an unprecedented transformation. From 2011 to 2023, the SaaS world was … predictable. You’d build a product, add a couple features annually, make quarterly releases, and if you hit $10M ARR with 110-120% net retention, your ticket was pretty much punched to $100m+ ARR and beyond. But that playbook is now obsolete. Revenue is still recurring in SaaS, of course. But the rate of change, and the threats from AI, are making the model far tougher than it was just 12 months ago. The stable, predictable SaaS world we knew has been replaced by rapid AI-driven evolution that’s breaking all the old rules. What worked yesterday is aging out FAST. The truth is harsh but necessary:
if you’re still running your 2023 playbook in 2025, you’re already falling behind. The 4 Red Flags You’re Getting “Maimed” by AI-First Competitors
You might not see competitors taking all your business overnight, but the “death by a thousand cuts” has begun:
Deals are getting smaller
Net Retention is steadily declining
Win rates dropping by 10-15%
(from 90% to 78%)
Existing customers downgrading
This isn’t about total displacement (yet). It’s about getting “maimed” as innovative AI-first companies eat into your business—not by destroying you, but by steadily cutting away at your growth.

answer:
Figma just reported its first quarter as a public company—and the results are everything you need to know that AI doesn’t mean SaaS is dead.
The Numbers:
$303.8 million quarterly revenue (up 41%)
$822 million trailing twelve-month revenue (up 46%)
Adjusted operating margin of 18%
Net income of $125-135 million for full year guidance
That’s how you grow when your product becomes essential infrastructure. Not hypergrowth at any cost—sustainable, profitable growth with genuine unit economics. The Profitability Story Nobody’s Talking About
Here’s what most analysts missed: Figma isn’t growing by cutting marketing expenses and hoping for the best. They’re actually building real operating leverage while maintaining investment discipline. The key insight? Figma achieved an adjusted operating margin of 18% while investing heavily in product development. This isn’t temporary optimization—it’s structural positioning. The Revenue Breakdown That Matters
$243.2M of Q1 revenue came from subscriptions—a massive increase over previous quarters. But here’s where it gets interesting: professional services revenue surged 71% year-over-year to $60.6 million. Translation: enterprises are spending more on implementation services because they see Figma becoming mission-critical infrastructure, not just design tooling. Customer Metrics That Tell the Real Story
We’ve all heard “land and expand” strategies before. Figma’s actual execution is worth studying. Their data shows that:
Customers using two or more products grew 28 percentage points year-over-year
Professional services adoption accelerated significantly
Enterprise expansion represents their fastest-growing segment
The average enterprise customer now uses five products per month
This isn’t accidental cross-selling. It’s proof that once companies embed Figma deeply enough into workflows, switching costs become real and the expansion path is obvious.

answer:
So you know we've been talking on this podcast for years that SaaS was back. We've seen it. We've seen all these public leaders just accelerate at scale again over the past year. But now I think there's no question anymore that it really is back.
We're seeing new IPOs break out. We're seeing everyone raise capital at historic valuations. Everyone's growing faster than ever before. It's like nothing we've ever seen before. So let me share one story today with you. This isn't an investment idea. I'm not recommending anyone buy anything here. No, I want to tell you about something much bigger than any individual stock or company.
The other day, Figma hit almost $300 million in a single quarter. A record-breaking $304 million in a single quarter. They just closed their largest-ever enterprise deal—$50 million per year. Their CEO said they'd never seen demand like this before. Now imagine if you were running Salesforce, or ServiceNow, or Adobe Sign, or Zendesk. You look at this and you go, "Wow, what have you done? How do I tap into some of those tailwinds?"
And then the other week, Figma announced its first ever dividend payment—a $47 million quarterly payout. Not bad for a company founded by two designers who graduated from college five minutes apart.
Figma's business has delivered. Let me give you the facts as reported:
LTM revenue $821 million
YoY growth 46%
Non-GAAP operating margin 18%
Cash balance $1.5 billion plus zero debt
Gross margins 91%
Net dollar retention 132%
Enterprise penetration—78% of Fortune 2000 companies using them
Multi-product usage—76% of customers on two-plus platforms
ARR crossing $1 billion
ARR growth 41%
Free cash flow margins 24%
Now, $100 million in net income
They got 1,119 customers above $100k ARR. Up +16% QoQ.
